SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/introducing-http-anomaly-rank  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; the full body was read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/introducing-http-anomaly-rank.txt`, 8,837 chars) — `web_extract` was not needed. Published Tuesday, 11 November 2025 by James Kettle (@albinowax); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: this is a TOOLING/ANALYSIS article (HTTP Anomaly Rank added to Turbo Intruder and to Burp's API in 2025.10). It teaches no vulnerability class, no entry point and no request shape, so it is recorded as a DETECTION/triage upgrade to the recorded error-diff harness (§17.238), not as a hunting technique of its own.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — the ranking was not reimplemented and no fuzzing result set was ranked; the weights, the example table and the O(N) claim are the author's own.
CLASS: fuzzing-result TRIAGE / response-anomaly ranking — a detection-stage aid for injection and desync hunting (NOT a standalone vulnerability class; recorded per doctrine §5, which asks for reusable detection technique, not only vuln classes).
CORE METHOD:
  1. For a set of responses to payload variations, compute a list of ATTRIBUTES per response — the article's table uses Status, Content-Type, Word-count and CRC32 (a byte hash); the technique's lineage ("Backslash Powered Scanner: Automating Human Intuition", 2016) used "status code, line count, exact byte sequence".
  2. WEIGHT each attribute by how STABLE it is across the whole set: an attribute with FEW unique values gets a HIGH weight (the example's `Status` has two unique values ⇒ high); an attribute that NEVER changes is USELESS (`Content-Type`); an attribute that is UNIQUE ON EVERY RESPONSE is USELESS too (`CRC32` — "perhaps the username is reflected", i.e. a reflection makes the hash always-unique and therefore worthless as a signal).
  3. SCORE every response by how unique its attribute values are, combined with those weights, and rank descending. In the article's table `ADMIN` scores highest purely because it is the only response with a unique word-count (811 vs the 812 shared by `administrator`/`admin`/`accounting`/`test`), while the responses whose status was the ordinary `403` sink to the bottom.
  4. Cost/mechanics: the score is O(N) and is only computed when the attack completes; Turbo Intruder now auto-sorts by the anomaly-rank column (`table.setSortOrder()` overrides it), and an always-zero column means Burp Suite is older than 2025.10.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a payload-variation result set (thousands of responses) too noisy to read by eye, where the only tell of a real differential is one word, one status, one header or one byte; a reflected input that makes a byte hash / CRC unique on EVERY response (so hash attributes must be discarded, not trusted).
CHAIN: n/a on its own (it is a triage aid, not a primitive). It is the ranking front-end for two RECORDED detection primitives: the §17.238 error-detection harness (13 response parameters, stable-attribute diffing of payload PAIRS, which finds blind SSTI/code injection) and the §17.236 evaluation primitive (a control response re-measured after a candidate desync trigger on a separate connection).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: when you fuzz a parameter/header and cannot read the noise, stop sorting by length by hand — compute from the raw responses the attributes you can (status, Content-Type, byte length, character length, word count, line count, header count, cookie count, byte hash), tally UNIQUE values per attribute across the whole set, KEEP only the attributes with ~2–4 unique values (drop the constant ones AND the always-unique ones), then rank the responses by their rarity within those attributes and open only the top few. This is the GRADED version of the harness rule "a parameter is STABLE if constant or within 5% of the average": the harness keeps stable attributes and diffs payload pairs; this ranks the attributes that are neither stable nor always-unique and diffs the whole set.
DEDUPE: `Anomaly Rank`, `setSortOrder`, `Backslash` as a RANKING method, `HTTP Anomaly Rank` = 0 hits across all three write targets (`anomaly` hits 5/5/1 are the Elasticsearch ML-anomaly index entry, the sync-anomaly-detector entry and the `linux_anomalous_network_activity_ecs` path; `Backslash` 5/11 hits are ExifTool/URL-parser/markdown-autolink material with no ranking content; `Turbo Intruder` hits are generic tooling mentions). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the §17.238 error-detection harness (stable-attribute diffing of near-identical payload PAIRS) — the NEW atoms here are the WEIGHTED set-wide ranking and the "unique-on-every-response is useless (a reflection)" rule.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/websocket-turbo-intruder-unearthing-the-websocket-goldmine  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/websocket-turbo-intruder-unearthing-the-websocket-goldmine.txt`, 17,456 chars). Published Wednesday, 17 September 2025 (updated 18 September 2025) by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: part tool-release (WebSocket Turbo Intruder, BApp store / CLI / WS logger) — the in-class atoms recorded are the WS-as-HTTP adapter, the Socket.IO handshake, the Socket.IO prototype-pollution payload and the THREADED race model; the install/BApp/CLI/logger features are deliberately excluded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no WebSocket target, Socket.IO server or Burp instance was stood up; every script, decorator, payload and frame is the author's own.
CLASS: the WEBSOCKET attack surface (BAC/IDOR, SQLi, command injection, race conditions inside WS frames) and in particular SERVER-SIDE PROTOTYPE POLLUTION reached through a Socket.IO protocol quirk — in-class: prototype pollution with a gadget = code execution / logic bypass. The WS transport is the entry point that "many testers and tools give up ... the moment a protocol upgrade to WebSocket occurs".
CORE METHOD:
  1. WRAP THE WEBSOCKET IN HTTP SO AN ORDINARY SCANNER CAN FUZZ IT: WebSocket Turbo Intruder's HTTP Middleware exposes a local endpoint whose `url` parameter is the WS endpoint and whose BODY is the WS message — `POST /proxy?url=https%3A%2F%2F<host>%2Fchat HTTP/1.1` / `Host: 127.0.0.1:9000` / `Content-Length: 16` / body `{"message":"hi"}` — the extension relays it over the WS connection and returns the reply, so Burp Scanner/Intruder can scan a WebSocket ("ideal for finding server-side vulnerabilities like SQL injection, authentication bypass, or command injection").
  2. FILTER THE NOISE: unlike HTTP, one outgoing WS message can produce MANY incoming messages (the article's lab answers one message with three), so lock the table to the responses you care about with an incoming-message decorator, e.g. `@MatchRegex(r'{"user":"Hal Pline"')` on `handle_incoming_message` (or `@MatchRegex(r'{"user":"You"')` for an echo).
  3. DETECT Socket.IO: "the easiest way to confirm that a server uses Socket.IO is by checking the mandatory query parameter `EIO`, which specifies the protocol version. If it equals 4, the server sends ping packets." Then complete the handshake yourself — create the connection with `upgrade_request.withUpdatedParameters(HttpParameter.urlParameter("EIO","4"))`, queue `'40'` (the Socket.IO connect packet), then send frames such as `connection.queue('42["message","hello"]')`, keeping the session alive with the built-in `@Pong("3")` / `@PingPong("2","3")` decorators. For the HTTP-adapter variant, return the connection after `connection.queue('40')` + `connection.decIn()`.
  4. TEST SERVER-SIDE PROTOTYPE POLLUTION THROUGH SOCKET.IO: Socket.IO's protocol quirks make it "a good candidate for server-side prototype pollution"; polluting the `initialPacket` property — `{"__proto__":{"initialPacket":"Polluted"}}` — "trick[s] Socket.IO into returning a new greeting message", i.e. the polluted prototype changes an OBSERVABLE server-side behaviour (the Express-feature differential from Gareth Heyes' "Server-side prototype pollution: Black-box detection without the DoS").
  5. RACES OVER WEBSOCKET: the default engine sends messages in chunks over ONE connection (good throughput, useless for races); switch to the `THREADED` engine, which "starts multiple worker threads, each with its own WebSocket connection, and sends messages in parallel", to trigger "logic bypasses, token reuse, or state desync bugs" (RaceConditionExample.py, thread count set in `config()`).
DETECTION SIGNAL: `Upgrade: websocket` (stop treating the protocol switch as the edge of scope); an `EIO=` query parameter / Socket.IO in the client bundle (then check `EIO=4`); WS frames the server trusts without re-authorising each message (test BAC by replaying a frame from another user's channel with your own or no session); a WS message handler that merges a JSON body into a config/state object (the prototype-pollution sink); any WS endpoint with a per-message state change that a single connection cannot race (the THREADED model is the test).
CHAIN: a WebSocket endpoint that tools abandon at the protocol upgrade (primitive: an untested attack surface holding BAC/SQLi/command-injection bugs) -> wrap it as HTTP and fuzz the frames, or complete the Socket.IO handshake and inject `{"__proto__":{"initialPacket":"Polluted"}}` (escalation: a server-side prototype pollution), -> a polluted prototype reaching a gadget = code execution, or an unauthorised frame = BAC/ATO the HTTP-only tooling never saw; the THREADED engine separately reaches race-condition logic bypasses (token reuse, state desync). The WS frame is the entry point; the polluted property / unauthorised action is the finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any `Upgrade: websocket` endpoint — (a) put the WS behind an HTTP adapter (`POST /proxy?url=<ws-url>` with the frame as the body) and run your HTTP scanner over it; (b) if `EIO` is present, handshake with `EIO=4` + `40` and send `{"__proto__":{"initialPacket":"Polluted"}}`, then diff the server's greeting/messages against the un-polluted run; (c) fire the same state-changing frame over N parallel connections (THREADED) before declaring "no race"; (d) replay each frame with no auth and as a second tenant. DO-NOT-TEST NOTE (doctrine §2(d)): the article's "ping of death" — a WS frame HEADER declaring a payload length of `Integer.MAX_VALUE` with no body sent, making a Java WS implementation allocate on the declared length and OOM the server — is a DoS primitive; it is recorded here only as a fingerprint of a naive WS implementation and must never be fired at a live target.
DEDUPE: `initialPacket`, `EIO=`, `MatchRegex`, `PingPong`, `Socket.IO` as a TECHNIQUE, `WebSocket Turbo Intruder` = 0 hits across all three write targets (`Socket.IO` 2/0/1 hits are a realtime-transport XSS detection-signal line and an unrelated FreeBSD kernel entry; `THREADED` 3/3/1 hits are "threaded comments", a multi-threaded coupon entry and the HTTP/3 engine option list — not a WS race engine; `prototype pollution` 16/13 hits are the client-side gadget entry, the Kibana ML-anomaly `__proto__.sourceURL` → RCE entry and the GitLab Mermaid entry — all HTTP/DOM merge sources). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the recorded prototype-pollution entries are HTTP/DOM merge sources; this adds a WEBSOCKET/Socket.IO frame as the merge source and the `initialPacket` greeting as the black-box oracle.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/cookie-chaos-how-to-bypass-host-and-secure-cookie-prefixes  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/cookie-chaos-how-to-bypass-host-and-secure-cookie-prefixes.txt`, 11,264 chars). Published Wednesday, 3 September 2025 by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. (Django's reply, quoted in the post: the attack relies on permitting cookies from untrusted subdomains, which their session docs already warn against, so "this will not be treated as a security vulnerability".)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Django/ASP.NET/Tomcat/Jetty instance was stood up; the PoC, the code-point list and the wire header are the author's own.
CLASS: COOKIE-PREFIX BYPASS (`__Host-` / `__Secure-`) via a browser↔server PARSER DISCREPANCY, escalating to session fixation / reflected-cookie XSS / privilege escalation — i.e. session-integrity forgery from a subdomain or an insecure origin. Chain-only: the disguised cookie is the first link; the XSS / session fixation / priv-esc it reaches is the finding.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TWO PROGRAMS DISAGREE ABOUT THE NAME: the browser enforces the prefix on the name it is handed; the server DECODES and normalises the bytes it receives ("the Cookie header is defined as a sequence of octets, not characters ... it's the server's responsibility to decode those bytes into a string").
  2. DISGUISE THE NAME WITH UNICODE WHITESPACE: `document.cookie = `${String.fromCodePoint(0x2000)}__Host-name=injected; Domain=.example.com; Path=/;`` — to the browser this is an unprefixed, unrestricted cookie, so it is accepted and sent to ALL subdomains (and over an insecure origin), while a trimming server sees the name as `__Host-name`.
  3. WHICH SERVERS TRIM: Django processes cookie keys/values with Python's `.strip()`, which removes a wide range of Unicode whitespace — `[133, 160, 5760, 8192–8202, 8232, 8233, 8239, 8287, 12288]` (U+2000 included); ASP.NET applies the same normalisation/trim. Safari is the exception: it refuses MULTIBYTE Unicode whitespace in a cookie name, but still permits the single-byte U+0085 (NEL) and U+00A0 (non-breaking space).
  4. LEGACY-PARSING VARIANT (Java): "if a Cookie header begins with `$Version=1`, some Java-based web servers, such as Apache Tomcat and Jetty, switch into a legacy parsing" mode where a single cookie string is read as SEVERAL cookies — `document.cookie = "$Version=1,__Host-name=injected; Path=/somethingreallylong/; Domain=.example.com;"` therefore forges a `__Host-` pair from a subdomain or an insecure origin, bypassing the browser's prefix check entirely.
  5. FULL CHAIN: from an XSS (or any unescaped cookie reflection) inject the forged protected cookie — `document.cookie = `${String.fromCodePoint(0x2000)}__Host-name=<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>;Domain=example.com;Path=/;`` — and the browser puts BOTH on the wire: `Cookie: __Host-name=Carlos; â€€__Host-name=<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>;`. Many frameworks (Django named explicitly) resolve a duplicate-cookie conflict by accepting only ONE value, "typically the last occurrence", so the attacker-controlled value takes precedence: a reflected XSS if the value is re-rendered unencoded, or session fixation / privilege escalation if the same cookie feeds CSRF protection or session identification. (A lightweight Burp Custom Action accompanies the post for detecting backends vulnerable to the prefix bypass; the "cookie sandwich" post is the earlier article in the same series.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: `__Host-`/`__Secure-` cookies in use (they are only meaningful if the server RELIES on the prefix, which is the bug); a backend that TRIMS/normalises cookie names — Django, ASP.NET — or a Java server (Tomcat, Jetty) that honours `$Version=1` legacy parsing; a duplicate-cookie resolution that silently picks one value; any sink that re-renders a cookie value or derives CSRF/session identity from it.
CHAIN: JS execution on a sibling subdomain or an insecure origin (primitive: normally blocked from writing a `__Host-` cookie) -> the U+2000-prefixed (or `$Version=1,`-prefixed) twin is accepted by the browser and NORMALISED into the protected name by the server (escalation: the cookie-prefix protection is gone) -> the server keeps the attacker's duplicate (last-wins) -> a reflected cookie value becomes XSS on the main origin, or the session/CSRF cookie becomes attacker-chosen giving session fixation and privilege escalation (escalation: account takeover / priv-esc). Doctrine note: cookie prefixes are a HARDENING control, so the finding is the escalation (XSS, session fixation, priv-esc), never the bypass on its own.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: when a target ships `__Host-`/`__Secure-` cookies and you have any JS execution on a sibling subdomain or an insecure origin (or a cookie value you can influence): (a) set the twin — `document.cookie = String.fromCodePoint(0x2000) + "__Host-<name>=x; Domain=.example.com; Path=/;"` — then confirm the value reaches the target origin and that the app treats it as the protected cookie; (b) try `$Version=1,__Host-<name>=x; Path=/a-very-long-path/; Domain=…` against Tomcat/Jetty; (c) on Safari use U+0085 or U+00A0 (multibyte whitespace is refused there); (d) check WHICH duplicate the server honours (last-wins is the exploitable case). Rule: **`__Host-`/`__Secure-` are enforced by the BROWSER on the raw name and by the SERVER after decoding — hide the prefix behind Unicode whitespace (U+2000, U+0085, U+00A0) or a `$Version=1,` legacy list, and a subdomain or insecure origin can plant a cookie whose NAME the server normalises into the protected one.**
DEDUPE: `String.fromCodePoint`, `U+2000`, `$Version=1`, `__Secure`, `cookie prefix`, `cookie chaos`, `cookie sandwich` = 0 hits across all three write targets (`0x2000` 2 hits are `CMD_RESOLVE`/`CMD_COMPLETE` command codes in an unrelated kernel entry; `__Host` 1/6 hits are an H2-race entry that merely NAMES `__Host-session` and playbook cookie-flag hardening material — doctrine §2(c) header-opinion items, not a prefix BYPASS; `cookie tossing` 4/2/3 hits are the recorded header-injection session-fixation technique). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: `cookie tossing` requires injecting a `Set-Cookie` into the response stream; THIS technique needs no header injection — it is a NAME-normalisation discrepancy between browser and server.

DETECTION SIGNAL: an injection point that is a `style` ATTRIBUTE only — a rich-text/markdown/template sink that strips `<style>` blocks but keeps inline styles, or an attribute you control next to the target element; any attribute (or attribute-bound DOM property) holding a short secret (user id, username, CSRF token, numeric code) because `attr()` reads ANY attribute; a sanitizer that blocks stylesheet imports but not inline `if()`/`attr()`/`image-set()`.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/how-to-distinguish-http-pipelining-from-request-smuggling  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/how-to-distinguish-http-pipelining-from-request-smuggling.txt`, 12,595 chars). Published Tuesday, 19 August 2025 by James Kettle (@albinowax); read in full 2026-11-08. (Triggered by http1mustdie.com; the companion Burp Custom Action is named "Smuggling or pipelining?" and the low-level extension is "HTTP Hacker".)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp/Turbo Intruder session and no desync-capable target were used; the request streams, the classes and the escalation ladder are the author's own.
CLASS: REQUEST-SMUGGLING FALSE-POSITIVE DISCRIMINATION / connection-reuse semantics — a METHODOLOGY for deciding whether a connection-reuse-requiring desync PoC is real, and the escalation ladder that turns a real one into impact. In-class: request smuggling / desync → cross-user response capture, cache poisoning, ACL bypass, auth bypass.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ALWAYS DISABLE CONNECTION REUSE WHEN TESTING SMUGGLING: "when creating a request smuggling proof of concept, always disable connection reuse where possible. If this breaks your attack, you have a choice — give up, or dive deeper." The usual false positive is a desync between YOUR HTTP CLIENT and the target, not between the front-end and the back-end — the article's CL.0 example (`POST / HTTP/1.1` / `Content_Length: 47` (malformed) / `GET /robots.txt`) only produced two responses because the author's own client appended the next request's bytes to the first request's body; the underlying stream shows `X: YPOST / HTTP/1.1` — "This is useless. In fact, hackxor doesn't even have a back-end so it's immune to request smuggling."
  2. THREE VALID CLASSES DO REQUIRE CONNECTION REUSE (so "breaks when reuse is off" is not proof of a false positive): (a) CONNECTION-LOCKED request smuggling — some front-ends only reuse the upstream connection if the client connection was reused, so the bug is only triggerable with client-side reuse; (b) CONNECTION-STATE attacks — not technically smuggling: some servers treat the FIRST request on each connection differently from subsequent ones (first-request routing), and they can occur even with no front-end; (c) CLIENT-SIDE DESYNC — restricted to a request the victim's browser can be made to send cross-domain, which rules out header-obfuscation techniques.
  3. PROVE A CONNECTION-LOCKED SMUGGLING IS REAL (not a client artefact): "see if you can send a request over HTTP/2 that triggers a response containing a separate HTTP/1 response nested inside it" — a nested HTTP/1 response proves the disagreement is in the server chain; alternatively "you can often distinguish connection-locked request smuggling using partial requests".
  4. REQUIRE EVIDENCE OF IMPACT: "to prove a vulnerability is really present, you need to obtain evidence of real impact beyond 'an attacker can make themselves receive a surprising response'". Connection-locked smuggling cannot be used for direct cross-user attacks, so escalate instead by: (i) poisoning the server CACHE if one exists — "an easy high-impact attack"; (ii) "look for an input reflection gadget and use it to reveal any headers the front-end is injecting. Sometimes internal headers enable complete authentication bypass!"; (iii) bypassing "any security controls applied by the front-end server" (paths it blocks) — "This is your pathway to a valid report!"; (iv) host-header tampering both directly and inside smuggled requests "to gain access to some previously off-limits internal systems, or launch other host-header attacks".
  5. TOOLING/ROUTE: explore with Turbo Intruder `requestsPerConnection=2`, or a Repeater tab group using 'Send group in sequence (single connection)'; HTTP Request Smuggler has a 'connection-state probe' that finds first-request routing automatically; use HTTP Hacker to see the raw request stream beneath Burp's abstraction.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a smuggling PoC that only works with connection reuse (Turbo Intruder `requestsPerConnection > 1`, Burp Intruder HTTP/1 Connection Reuse, Repeater 'Send group in sequence (single connection)' / 'Enable connection reuse', or "two HTTP/1 responses in one"); a front-end whose upstream reuse is keyed to client reuse (connection-locked); a server that treats the first request on a connection differently (first-request routing / connection-state); an open input-reflection gadget next to the desync (internal-header disclosure); a cache in front; front-end rules that block specific paths.
CHAIN: a smuggling PoC that only fires with connection reuse (primitive: ambiguous — most such PoCs are client-artefacts) -> confirm it belongs to one of the three valid reuse-requiring classes (HTTP/2 request yielding a nested HTTP/1 response, or a partial request, or a first-request-routing probe) (escalation: a REAL desync) -> then convert to impact: cache poisoning (site-wide), an input-reflection gadget that discloses front-end-injected internal headers (sometimes a COMPLETE AUTHENTICATION BYPASS), bypass of front-end security controls, or host-header tampering into internal systems (escalation: P1/P2 desync impact). If no impact path is found, the finding stays a lead.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: before ever reporting a desync that needs connection reuse — (a) re-run the PoC with reuse DISABLED; if it still works it is a normal desync, done; (b) if it breaks, test whether it is connection-locked / connection-state: send the same request over HTTP/2 and look for a nested HTTP/1 response in the reply, try partial requests, and run a connection-state probe for first-request routing; (c) for a confirmed connection-locked bug, spend the effort on IMPACT ONLY — poison the cache, use an input-reflection gadget to leak front-end-injected headers (→ possible auth bypass), bypass front-end path controls, and test host-header tampering toward internal systems. Rule: **"only works with connection reuse" is usually a client-side artefact, so disable reuse first; if it still fires, classify it as connection-locked smuggling / a connection-state attack / a client-side desync, and pay for it with cache poisoning, a reflection gadget that discloses internal headers (auth bypass), control bypass or host tampering — a desync that yields only "a surprising response to myself" is not a report.**
DEDUPE: `first-request`, `connection state`, `masked header`, `HTTP Hacker`, `Smuggling or pipelining` = 0 hits across all three write targets (`pipelining` 1/1 hits are the recorded "early read" sub-technique line inside Kettle's pause-based-desync entry; `connection-locked` 4/2/3 hits are that same entry plus the CRLF entry's connection-locked `0.CL` case; `Microsoft-HTTPAPI` 1/1 hits are an H2-downconvert false-positive identifier). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the ledger's pause-based-desync entry (line ~4370) already holds the "early read" resolution of the pipelining ambiguity for connection-locked CL.TE; the NEW atoms here are the THREE valid reuse-requiring classes (connection-locked smuggling, connection-state/first-request routing, client-side desync), the HTTP/2-nested-HTTP/1-response proof, the partial-request and connection-state-probe tooling, and the connection-locked ESCALATION LADDER (cache poisoning, reflection gadget → internal-header disclosure → complete auth bypass, front-end control bypass, host-header tampering).

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/http1-must-die.txt`, 49,411 chars). Published Wednesday, 6 August 2025 (updated Friday, 17 October 2025) by James Kettle (@albinowax); read in full 2026-11-08. DELTA ENTRY: the ledger already holds the CRLF/Nginx-`$uri` desync entry, the HTTP-Terminator entry (§17.236: protocol ruler, novel triggers, dangling byte, status-line injection, range cache poisoning, response forking, shared-parser confusion) and the `Expect: 100-continue` tunnel reveal — this entry records ONLY what those lack: the masked-header DISCREPANCY-DETECTION method (V-H vs H-V), the leading-space CL.0 / OPTIONS workaround, the IIS-behind-ALB H-V case, the 0.CL DEADLOCK and its EARLY-RESPONSE GADGET (`/con`), the DOUBLE-DESYNC 0.CL→CL.0 conversion, and the Expect-based desync TAXONOMY.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no nginx/IIS/ALB/CDN lab was stood up and no target was touched; every payload, status code, case study and bounty figure is the paper's own.
CLASS: HTTP request smuggling / desync via PARSER DISCREPANCIES — masked-header V-H/H-V detection, CL.0/0.CL desyncs with early-response gadgets, and Expect-based desyncs; the paper's impact is mass compromise of user credentials and full site takeover (Akamai, Cloudflare, Netlify). In-class: request smuggling → cross-user response capture, session/token theft, cache poisoning, ATO.
CORE METHOD:
  1. DETECT THE DISCREPANCY, NOT THE EXPLOIT (HTTP Request Smuggler v3, extending Daniel Thacher's 2021 header-smuggling idea): send a request with a PARTIALLY HIDDEN header — a leading space before the header NAME (` Content-Length: 23`, ` Host: x`) or a masked duplicate (`Xost: x`) — and compare the response against four references: the normal header, the header omitted, and an arbitrary other masked header. If the masked variant produces a response that CANNOT be triggered any other way, there is a parser discrepancy in the server chain. "Note that the specific status codes are not relevant, and can sometimes be confusing. All that matters is that they're different."
  2. CLASSIFY V-H vs H-V: VISIBLE-HIDDEN = the masked header is visible to the front-end but hidden from the back-end; HIDDEN-VISIBLE = hidden from the front-end but visible to the back-end. Distinguish by inspecting the responses and guessing which tier produced them (the paper's IIS/ALB example is unambiguous from the banners: unmasked `Host: foo/bar` → `400, Server: awselb/2.0` (front-end), masked `Xost: foo/bar` → `200, -no server header-` (back-end)).
  3. V-H → CL.0 BY HIDING `Content-Length` (hidden from the back-end, so the back-end treats the next request's bytes as this request's body): `GET /style.css HTTP/1.1` / `Host: <redacted-food-corp>` / `Foo: bar` / ` Content-Length: 23` (LEADING SPACE) / blank / `GET /404 HTTP/1.1` / `X: y` → the smuggled request is answered separately. CL.0 is preferred over TE.CL "as it's much less likely to get blocked by a WAF". BARRIER WORKAROUND: when the front-end rejects GET requests carrying a body, "I was able to work around this simply by switching the method to OPTIONS".
  4. H-V ON IIS BEHIND AWS ALB (a mass-vulnerable, DELIBERATELY UNPATCHED case): the malformed/masked `Host` is hidden from ALB and passed to IIS, so the classic exploit is CL.TE; AWS' Desync Guardian blocks it, and Thomas Stacey bypassed that with an H2.TE desync. Even with the H2.TE bypass fixed, the same discrepancy still allows smuggling HEADERS, "enabling IP-spoofing and sometimes complete authentication bypass". AWS will not patch it (compatibility with ancient HTTP/1 clients); self-mitigate with `routing.http.drop_invalid_header_fields.enabled` and `routing.http.desync_mitigation_mode = strictest`.
  5. 0.CL DESYNC AND ITS DEADLOCK: exploit an H-V discrepancy to hide `Content-Length` from the FRONT-END while the back-end sees it — `GET /Logon HTTP/1.1` / `Host: <redacted>` / `Content-Length:` / ` 7` / blank / `GET /404 HTTP/1.1` / `X: Y`. This normally DEADLOCKS (the front-end buffers the second request and forwards only the header block; the back-end waits for the 7-byte body; the front-end waits for the back-end; one times out and resets → `504 Gateway Timeout`).
  6. BREAK THE 0.CL DEADLOCK WITH AN EARLY-RESPONSE GADGET — a way to make the back-end respond WITHOUT waiting for the body: on nginx a STATIC FILE does it (nginx answered before the request was complete and broke the author's timing tests); on IIS, which ignored the static-file trick, use the WINDOWS RESERVED DEVICE NAME — request `/con` inside any filesystem-mapped folder and IIS "respond[s] without waiting for the body to arrive, and helpfully leave[s] the connection open" (the reserved list is `CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1, COM2 …`; "I've known about the /con quirk for over ten years but this was the first time I've been able to actually make use of it"). SERVER-LEVEL REDIRECTS also act as early-response gadgets on other servers; the author never found one for Apache ("too studious about closing the connection when they hit an error condition"). This is why the tool's "Mystery 400" responses are in fact usually exploitable.
  7. PROVE 0.CL, THEN CONVERT IT TO CL.0 WITH A DOUBLE-DESYNC: proof = give the first request a correct `Content-Length: 20` and put a second path inside the victim request's header block — the sliced request line is processed (`302 Found Location: /Logon?ReturnUrl=%2fwrtz`). A realistic attack needs the payload in the VICTIM's request, i.e. 0.CL → CL.0, which requires a DOUBLE-DESYNC: request 1 poisons the connection with a 0.CL; the poisoned connection weaponises request 2 into a CL.0 which re-poisons the connection with a malicious prefix; the prefix poisons the VICTIM's request. The clean form (`POST /nul` + `Content-length:` + ` 163` + a second `POST /`) is fragile because you must know the exact size of the front-end's injected headers ("virtually all front-end servers append extra headers ... often contain things like the client IP, which means the attack works for you but breaks when someone else tries to replicate it"). THE FIX: "Most servers insert headers at the END of the header block, not at the start. So, if our smuggled request starts before that, the attack will work reliably!" — reveal the inserted header with an input reflection (`Foo: GET /y HTTP/1.1` then `???: ???? // front-end header lands here`), measure its length with the `0cl-find-offset` Turbo Intruder script, and from there use traditional CL.0 techniques (the paper's `HEAD` technique served malicious JavaScript to random users). Free lab: Web Security Academy "0.CL Request Smuggling".
  8. EXPECT-BASED DESYNC — A TAXONOMY (the paper's "Expect complexity bomb"; the Expect header splits a request into header-block and body, and "significantly worse for reverse proxies"): VANILLA `Expect: 100-continue` causes a 0.CL desync on numerous servers — "a broken Expect implementation in the front-end server, which makes it correctly forward the headers, but get confused by the back-end's non-100 reply and forget it still needs to receive a body from the client" (`GET /logout HTTP/1.1` / `Host: <redacted>.t-mobile.com` / `Expect: 100-continue` / `Content-Length: 291` → `404`; T-Mobile paid $12,000 on a non-production domain). AN OBFUSCATED Expect exposes a much larger target set — `Expect: y 100-continue` produced a 0.CL desync on `h1.sec.gitlab.net` (the host holding GitLab's bug-bounty report attachments), exploited by Response Queue Poisoning: "27,000 requests later we got access to someone else's vulnerability report video and a $7,000 bounty" (some high-end payouts took the 0.CL Expect-based total to ~$95,000). Expect also causes CL.0 desyncs: VANILLA Expect on the Netlify CDN gave a CL.0 RQP "send[ing] us a continuous stream of responses from every website on the Netlify CDN" (third-party responses, reported, no bounty — "Websites utilizing Netlify are out of scope"), and OBFUSCATED `Expect:` (newline + space before `100-continue`) on Akamai gave a CL.0 desync serving arbitrary content to users of `auth.lastpass.com` ($5,000 max; the wider campaign — CVE-2025-32094 — produced 74 bounties totalling $221,000).
  9. EXPECT SIDE-EFFECTS WORTH ABUSING: (a) "All HTTP/1.1 responses have one header block — unless you send Expect", and the SECOND header block surprises front-end logic that tries to REMOVE sensitive response headers, so masked `Server:` banners and internal headers reappear (the Netlify example exposed `X-Bb-Account-Id`, `X-Bb-Cache-Gen`, `X-Bb-Deploy-Id`, `X-Bb-Site-Id`, `X-Nf-Cache-Key`, `X-Nf-Ats-Version`, `X-Nf-Proxy-Header-Rewrite` … — Netlify's reply: "this information is provided by design"); (b) several servers respond to Expect by DISCLOSING MEMORY — fragments of unrelated text and SECRET KEYS, e.g. `HTTP/1.1 100 ContinTransfer-EncodingzxWthTQmiI8fJ4oj9fzE"` / `X-: chunked`; (c) Expect can also make a server forget that HEAD responses have no body, causing an upstream deadlock (`HEAD` + `Content-Length: 6` + `Expect: 100-continue` + `ABCDEF` → `100 Continue` then `504`).
  10. DETECT HIGH-RISK PARSING: the same discrepancy scan finds servers that do NOT treat `\n\n` as terminating the header block (RFC-9112 says "a recipient MAY recognize a single LF as a line terminator") — send `POST / HTTP/1.1\r\n` / `Content-Length: 22\r\n` / `A: B\r\n` / `\nExpect: 100-continue\r\n` and a server that answers `100 Continue` + `302 Found` is lenient; harmless for direct access but exploitable behind a front-end (traced to the HTTP library; the paper's defence: upstream HTTP/2).
DETECTION SIGNAL: a masked/duplicated header (leading space, `Xost:`) that produces a response unreachable any other way; a body-ignoring method/framing mismatch; a "mystery 400" that HTTP Request Smuggler reports; a server that answers a request BEFORE its body arrives (the early-response gadget: `/con` on IIS, a static file on nginx, a server-level redirect); `Expect` accepted/ignored inconsistently between tiers, or a response that carries an extra header block; `\n\n` not terminating the header block; a front-end whose injected headers are appended at the END of the header block (the reliable double-desync precondition).
CHAIN: a parser discrepancy found by masked-header probing (primitive: normally a P4/P5 framing anomaly with no visible impact) -> classify V-H/H-V and weaponise: V-H hides `Content-Length` from the back-end (CL.0) or H-V hides it from the front-end (0.CL, needing an early-response gadget to break the deadlock) (escalation: a real front-end/back-end desync) -> convert 0.CL to CL.0 with a DOUBLE-DESYNC whose smuggled request starts before the front-end's appended headers, then smuggle the request that changes a victim's account / capture other users' responses / poison a cache (escalation: mass credential compromise, ATO, site takeover) -> and the Expect variants reach the same impact from a single un-obfuscated header (0.CL on numerous servers; `Expect: y 100-continue` and `Expect:`-with-newline corners exposed GitLab's report attachments to RQP and served arbitrary content on `auth.lastpass.com`), while Expect's second header block defeats response-header removal and Expect can leak memory/secret keys. Impact evidence in the paper: 24M websites exposed by the Cloudflare H2.0 case, Akamai CVE-2025-32094 (74 bounties, $221,000), Netlify CDN-wide RQP, GitLab/Lastpass/T-Mobile payouts.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any HTTP/1 front-end→back-end chain — (a) run the masked-header permutation probe (leading space before the name; a masked duplicate such as `Xost:`; a duplicate with an invalid value) against a control and treat ANY unique response as a discrepancy, then infer V-H vs H-V from the server banners; (b) V-H → try a CL.0 by hiding `Content-Length` behind a leading space (switch the method to OPTIONS when the front-end rejects GET-with-body); H-V → hide `Content-Length` from the front-end (`Content-Length:` + ` 7`) for a 0.CL; (c) if 0.CL deadlocks (a `504`), find an early-response gadget — `/con` on IIS, a static file on nginx, a server-level redirect — then convert it to CL.0 with a double-desync (front-end headers are appended at the END, so start the smuggled request before them; measure the injected length with a reflection and `0cl-find-offset`); (d) test `Expect` in two forms — vanilla `Expect: 100-continue` and obfuscated (`Expect: y 100-continue`, `Expect:` + newline + `100-continue`, `Expect :\t100-continue`) — expecting a 0.CL or a CL.0 on a CDN edge; (e) diff the response HEADERS with and without Expect to see headers the front-end tried to remove (and check for memory disclosure). Published Tuesday, 15 July 2025 by Gareth Heyes (@garethheyes); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: a TOOL-RELEASE post (Repeater Strike, a Burp AI extension on the Early Adopter channel) — the atoms recorded are the DETECTION METHOD (structural response regexes + probe mutation + proxy-history replay), not the tool; the tool narrative, the extension plumbing and the token-cost trivia are deliberately excluded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp/Burp-AI session was run; the JSON shapes, the regex examples and the limitation notes are the author's own on-page examples.
CLASS: IDOR/BOLA DISCOVERY AMPLIFICATION — turning ONE hand-confirmed access-control break into a parameterised rule that finds its siblings across the whole proxy history. Detection-stage method (doctrine §5); the class it serves is BAC/IDOR → cross-user/cross-tenant data (P2), and write-method siblings → account modification.
CORE METHOD:
  1. CONFIRM ONE INSTANCE BY HAND in Repeater (the post's example: `…?id=wiener` returns `Your username is: wiener` and `Your API Key is: <32 chars>`) — the rule is derived FROM a proven primitive, never hypothesised.
  2. EXTRACT THE FINGERPRINT, NOT THE VALUE. The identifying side is the parameter and its probe: `"param": {"values": ["wiener"], "name": "id", "type": "URL", "vulnerabilityClass": "IDOR"}`. The success side is a STRUCTURAL regex for the leak — `Your username is: wiener`, `Your API Key is: [A-Za-z0-9]{32}`, `<a href="/my-account\?id=wiener">My account<\/a>` — matching the SHAPE of the secret/key, never the literal secret.
  3. RE-PLAY the probe to reproduce the finding, then persist the rule (a "Strike Rule").
  4. MUTATE BOTH SIDES, keeping the structure: candidate identifiers `admin`, `testuser`, `anonymous`, `user123`, … each with its mutated-but-structurally-identical regex set (`Your username is: admin` + the same `[A-Za-z0-9]{32}` key regex + the same account-link regex).
  5. SCAN THE PROXY HISTORY with the rule — "taking what you do in Repeater and scanning your proxy history to discover more of it": every request you have already made anywhere that both hits the parameter shape and returns the leak shape is a NEW sibling BOLA. This is the amplification step: one confirmed bug becomes an inventory.
  6. AUTOMATION: the extension can create a Strike Rule automatically on every Repeater request (~61 tokens to build a rule, zero tokens to apply it), and the generated rule is editable and re-runnable without further model calls.
  7. STATED LIMITS (do not over-trust): long responses (Facebook-scale) defeat the analyser; unescaped regex metacharacters caused runtime errors (escape programmatically on exception); rules generalise badly ACROSS sites; isolating meaningful UI change from header noise (response diffing) was left unsolved by the author.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an object reference (numeric id, uuid, slug, email, filename) that returns a page repeating YOUR identifiers back; a response carrying a per-object STRUCTURE (key/token/balance/email shape) rather than only a display name; the same parameter name reused across many endpoints of one app — the sibling surface the history replay sweeps; an access-control test you already won once (it is now a rule, not a data point).
CHAIN: one hand-confirmed IDOR (primitive: a single object read — doctrine §2(b) keeps "an id in a URL" as a lead only) -> structural regex + identifier enumeration + proxy-history replay convert it into every sibling endpoint leaking the same object shape (escalation: a mass BOLA surface at once) -> the escalated finding is other users'/tenants' data of the same shape (PII, API keys, tokens) and, on the siblings that accept PUT/PATCH/POST, modification of another account (P2 → ATO path). The rule never becomes the report; the cross-user data/action it proves does.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: after confirming ONE access-control bug by hand — (a) write down the parameter, the probe value and a STRUCTURAL regex for the sensitive field leaked (token/key/email shape), not the literal value; (b) enumerate candidate identifiers (`admin`, `root`, `support`, `test`, `anonymous`, `1`, `2`, `1000`, plus own-vs-neighbour ids) and replay the request with each, using the structural regex as the pass/fail oracle; (c) grep/replay the ENTIRE recorded proxy history for the same parameter name + response structure — every hit is a sibling instance to verify; (d) check whether the siblings accept write methods before rating. Rule: **a confirmed IDOR is a PATTERN, not a point — generalise the leak to a structural regex, enumerate identifiers, and replay the rule over your whole proxy history to turn one finding into the endpoint inventory that carries it.**
DEDUPE: `Repeater Strike`, `Strike Rule`, `mutatedProbesToUse`, `responseRegexes`, `vulnerabilityClass` = 0 hits across all three write targets (`proxy history` appears only as a workflow noun in tooling lines). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: every recorded IDOR/BOLA entry tests ONE endpoint at a time; this entry records only the AMPLIFICATION step (one proven primitive → rule → history-wide sibling scan).

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/drag-and-pwnd-leverage-ascii-characters-to-exploit-vs-code  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b72-drag-and-pwnd-leverage-ascii-characters-to-exploit-vs-code.txt`, 11,823 chars). Published Wednesday, 30 April 2025 (updated Thursday, 1 May 2025) by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the author's own MSRC outcome is recorded as-is — "they do not consider it a security issue … existing mitigations - such as workspace trust warnings and the requirement for significant user interaction - lower the severity" — so the technique is recorded as a class-level method with its interaction precondition stated, not as an accepted vendor finding.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no VS Code/terminal lab was stood up this pass; the payloads, the two cases and the platform notes are the author's own (he reports reproducing on macOS and Ubuntu).
CLASS: COMMAND INJECTION / CODE EXECUTION through TERMINAL CONTROL CHARACTERS — untrusted bytes that reach a PTY are reinterpreted as line-editing keystrokes (SOH = cursor-to-line-start, ETX = abort line, CR = execute) and reassemble a command the user never typed. In-class: OS command injection (the shell-escaping layer is bypassed, not broken), reaching code execution on whatever host owns the terminal.
CORE METHOD:
  1. FIND A SINK THAT FORWARDS RAW BYTES TO A PTY. `node-pty` — VS Code's terminal, and by the author's own generalisation "any web application that blindly passes raw bytes into a terminal without proper control characters sanitization" — "forwards raw bytes directly to a shell, trusting that everything downstream will 'do the right thing'". The Readline layer behind it maps the ASCII communication-control characters onto line editing: `\x01` SOH = Ctrl+A (move to the beginning of the line), `\x02` = Ctrl+B (back one character), `\x03` = Ctrl+C (interrupt / abandon the line), `\x04` = Ctrl+D (delete at cursor), `\x0d` = Enter (EXECUTE).
  2. CASE 1 — ARGUMENTS. A VS Code run configuration `{"args": ["hello","\u0001\t--args\u0001\tCalculator\u0001\t-a\u0001open\t"]}` does not run the Python script: the resulting command line is `open -a Calculator --args cd /tmp/; /usr/bin/env /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 script.py hello`. Each `\x01` moves the cursor to the start so the remaining text is typed IN FRONT of the line — "repeated four times in the given example to build the payload in reverse". Works on Ubuntu with `gnome-calculator`.
  3. CASE 2 — FILENAMES / DRAG-AND-DROP. Name a file `very very very long name \x03 open -a Calculator \x0d.txt` and drag it into the terminal: the shell sees `'very very very long name` [Ctrl+C: abandon the line] newline `open -a Calculator` [Enter] `'.txt'`. "when a file is dragged and dropped, the carriage return character `[\x0d]` automatically executes a command. This prevents the user from examining the potentially harmful input in the terminal window."
  4. WHY THE ESCAPER DOES NOT HELP. The post's `shellEscape` escapes `[$!'"();`*?{}[\]<>&%#~@\\ ]` — it has NO control-character branch, so `\x01`/`\x03`/`\x0d` pass through every shell-quoting/escaping layer untouched; the injection carries no shell metacharacter at all.
  5. PLATFORM / TARGETING: reproduced on macOS and Ubuntu; Windows is mitigated twice over (the filesystem disallows control characters in filenames AND VS Code defaults to PowerShell, which does not honour them as cursor moves / command breaks); macOS Terminal warns on drag-and-drop of special characters and Ubuntu's terminal escapes control characters, so the technique needs the app's own PTY path, not the OS terminal.
  6. GENERALISED HUNTING SURFACE (author's conclusion): "the underlying issue lies in how applications communicate with the terminal … any web application that blindly passes raw bytes into a terminal" — web SSH/console UIs, CI "run configuration" editors, notebook cells, log/chat viewers printing untrusted bytes, and filename/argument fields echoed into a terminal. The effective payloads were merged into the Active Scan++ Burp extension.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any feature that sends your string (filename, argument, comment, ticket title) into a terminal or PTY — web SSH / K8s `exec` / browser consoles, IDE or CI run configurations, drag-and-drop-to-terminal, a log viewer that prints raw bytes; a filename/path/argument validator that accepts `\x01`–`\x1f` or `\x0d`; a shell-escaping function with no control-character branch.
CHAIN: an untrusted string (filename, arg, log line) reaches a PTY (primitive: treated as inert text — the bug is in the terminal/line-editor layer, not the shell) -> `\x01` rewrites the pending command line from the left, or `\x03`+`\x0d` abandon it and execute a fresh command, so the attacker composes an arbitrary command with NO shell metacharacters for the escaper to catch (escalation: every quoting/escaping layer is bypassed while remaining "correct") -> OS command execution as the terminal's user: on a workstation IDE that is the developer's machine, on a server-side web terminal it is the HOST (escalation: code execution / RCE). Precondition stated for severity (doctrine §4/§8): the victim must have a terminal pointed at the file/argument the attacker supplied and must drop/run it (user interaction), which is exactly the vendor's reason for not rating it — so the finding is the RCE on the HOST for a SERVER-side PTY (no interaction), and a workstation RCE where a spec'd workflow runs an untrusted artifact.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find a field whose content a PTY will echo or execute (a filename printed on drag-and-drop, an IDE/CI run-configuration `args` entry, a log line, a web-terminal input). Submit `aaa\x01echo PWNED\x0d` (in JSON: `\u0001` … `\u000d`) and watch whether the command executes; also try the filename form `x \u0003 echo pwned \u000d.txt`. Confirm the escaper in front of the sink is regex-based shell escaping with no control-character branch. Rule: **treating "it only goes to a terminal" as inert is wrong — SOH (`\x01`) moves the cursor to the start of the line, ETX (`\x03`) abandons the line and CR (`\x0d`) executes it, so raw bytes entering a PTY reassemble an attacker command that no shell escaper ever sees; only a sanitizer that strips control characters stops it.**
DEDUPE: `SOH`, `node-pty`, `terminal escape`, `readline`, `carriage return`, `\x01`/`\x03`/`\x0d` as a technique = 0 hits across all three write targets (`ANSI` 14/41/4 hits are escape-sequence/colour material and WorstFit-adjacent charset work; `control character` 1 hit is unrelated; the recorded command-injection entries are shell-metacharacter, argument-splitting and interpreter-flag classes). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the recorded command-injection corpus routes through metacharacters; this one routes through the terminal's own line editor.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/document-my-pentest  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b72-document-my-pentest.txt`, 11,846 chars). Published Wednesday, 23 April 2025 (updated Thursday, 24 April 2025) by Gareth Heyes; read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: a TOOL-RELEASE post (Document My Pentest, BApp store) — the recorded atoms are the INPUT→REGEX REFLECTION CANARY and the prompt-language discipline; the installation/Organizer plumbing is excluded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp AI session; the regex, the encoding examples and the prompt before/after are the author's own.
CLASS: REFLECTED-INPUT TRANSFORMATION MAPPING — translating the payload you sent into a regex that matches its ENCODED forms, so a reflection is found and its filter/encoder identified without an extra request. A detection technique serving XSS with real impact (and path traversal); chain-first-link only (doctrine §2(b): "it reflects" is a lead, the impact is the finding).
CORE METHOD:
  1. DO NOT burn a second request and do not alter the user's request with a separate canary: "why don't we just use the tested input as the canary and translate it to a regular expression".
  2. TRANSLATE the input into a GAP-TOLERANT regex: keep every alphanumeric token verbatim, replace everything between them with a bounded wildcard. `<script>alert(1)</script>` becomes `.{1,6}script.{1,6}alert.{1,6}1.{1,6}.{1,6}.{1,6}script.{1,6}` — the author's rule: "often the alphanumeric characters will stay consistent".
  3. ONE regex then matches the raw, HTML-entity, URL-encoded and DOUBLE-encoded reflections — `&lt;script&gt;alert(1)&lt;/script&gt;`, `%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E`, `%253Cscript%253Ealert(1)%253C%252Fscript%253E` — and the bytes visible around the match tell you WHICH transformation the app applied, letting the analysis "quote what the input was transformed to without any specific instructions".
  4. USE IT AS THE FILTER TEST: the set of characters that survive (vs are dropped/rewritten) is the filter's signature — this is the same question the sibling Shadow Repeater post answered empirically ("spaces are allowed in an XSS vector").
  5. PROMPT DISCIPLINE (why the analysis stopped labelling encoded reflections as XSS): vague negative guidance — "if HTML entities are found they very rarely indicate an XSS vulnerability" — makes a model report encoded reflections as XSS; use a PRECISE negative: `If the response reflection contains HTML-encoded input (e.g., &lt;script&gt;), that is not a vulnerability.` Then meta-prompt the model about its own output — "Look at this LLM response and point out why it thinks there's XSS when there clearly isn't" — and feed the resulting fix back ("How can I improve this prompt to prevent this kind of issue?").
  6. OBSERVED LIMITS (honest): whole request/response analysis worked poorly for some classes ("The AI isn't very good at analysing a whole request and response, especially for vulnerabilities like XSS") and worked for path traversal where the response showed the directory listing; for classes where "parameter/header modifications couldn't be detected" (request smuggling) the whole raw request+response had to be sent with a different prompt.
DETECTION SIGNAL: your input reflected anywhere in the response; a reflection in which some characters are rewritten (entities, percent-escapes) — i.e. a filter/encoder sits in the path; a sink where the number of surviving metacharacters differs from the input (partial filtering); the same input reflected twice under different encodings on one page.
CHAIN: inject a known input and translate it into the gap-tolerant regex (primitive: you learn WHERE it reflects and HOW it is transformed) -> the transformation fingerprint names the sink/sanitiser you are behind (HTML-encode-only ≠ strip-chars ≠ JS-string-escape ≠ attribute-context escape), so you pick the correct context breakout instead of guessing (escalation: "it reflects" → a working vector in the right context) -> a vector that survives the discovered transformation in a sensitive origin = XSS with session impact (P2) or token theft (the impact is the finding; the reflection alone stays a lead).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take the exact payload you sent, replace every run of non-alphanumeric characters with `.{1,6}`, and match it against the response — a hit proves the reflection and the encoding visible at the match names the filter. Then vary ONE metacharacter at a time (`<`, `>`, space, `(`, `"`, `'`, backtick) and diff which survive to map the filter before designing the breakout. Rule: **turn your own payload into a gap-tolerant regex (`.{1,6}` between the alphanumeric tokens) and the reflection finds itself in every encoded form — the match position and the surrounding bytes tell you where it landed and which encoder you are behind.**
DEDUPE: `Document My Pentest`, `.{1,6}`, input-to-regex canary translation = 0 hits across all three write targets (`canary round-trip` hits are marker-based file-read / blind-injection checks — they prove a FILE was read, not how a reflection was encoded; `input to regex` = 0). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: recorded reflection entries assert that a reflection exists; this records the transformation-mapping step and the precise-negative prompt rule.

ROUTE: assigned source 4; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b72-saml-roulette-the-hacker-always-wins.txt`, 15,665 chars). Published Tuesday, 18 March 2025 (updated Monday, 31 March 2025) by Gareth Heyes (@garethheyes) with Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY / DELTA: §17.237 (the sibling paper "The Fragile Lock") merely ASSERTS in its dedupe line that "the `saml-roulette` DTD material" is already recorded — a grep shows `ATTLIST` = 0 hits and NO saml-roulette entry exists anywhere in the three write targets; that reference is an unbacked dedupe note, not a recorded method. This entry is therefore a DELTA entry over §17.237/§17.1: those hold attribute pollution by ORDER, reserved-`xml` namespace confusion WITHOUT DTDs, void canonicalization and plain XSW — the ROUND-TRIP mutation and the free-signature route below are new.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no SAML SP/IdP pair or GitLab instance was stood up; the document mutations and the chain are the authors' own (patched in GitLab CE/EE 17.9.2, 17.8.5, 17.7.7).
CLASS: OAUTH/OIDC/SSO BYPASS + AUTHENTICATION BYPASS via an XML PARSE→SERIALIZE→RE-PARSE ROUND TRIP plus NAMESPACE CONFUSION in ruby-saml (REXML vs Nokogiri) → unauthenticated administrator. In-class: SSO/auth bypass → full ATO, and privilege escalation to admin.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ROUND TRIP IS THE BUG: "SAML libraries often parse an XML document, store it as a string, and later re-parse it" — ruby-saml parses and validates the signature with REXML and reads attributes with Nokogiri, so "if any mutations occur during this process, the document may not be identical when parsed a second time": the document that is VERIFIED and the document that is USED are different trees, and the attacker controls the difference.
  2. MUTATE INSIDE THE DOCTYPE, IN THE SYSTEM IDENTIFIER: a single-quoted system identifier is re-serialised with DOUBLE quotes; because the identifier contains double quotes internally, the re-serialised XML terminates the string early, the following XML COMMENT becomes processed markup, and "an entirely different node" results — first parse sees the original trusted `assertion`, second parse sees the attacker's `assertion`. This refines Juho Forsén's notation/quote-inconsistency finding; Zak Fedotkin then reduced the mutation to a streamlined vector.
  3. WHAT STILL HAS TO MATCH (the whole exploit budget): the library first checks the certificate embedded in the SAMLResponse against the server's stored fingerprint, then validates the signature — and that validation happens on the ORIGINAL element while "all other validation checks operate on the attacker assertion rather than the original signed document". Only two things must agree: the signed element's `ID` in both documents, and the canonicalization properties. NameID, attributes, conditions, session index — all freely attacker-controlled "without breaking the signature verification process".
  4. NAMESPACE CONFUSION TO SATISFY THE XSD: Nokogiri validates against SAML schema files, so the signed element must be a valid SAML protocol element (no hunting for a signed response on a forum). Instead exploit the XPath lookup: ruby-saml searches for the `Signature` element with an XPath using the `ds` namespace prefix. Declare that namespace NOT on the `Signature` element but IN THE DOCTYPE via `<!ATTLIST>` — "Both REXML and Nokogiri support doctype-based namespace declarations, but REXML has a crucial flaw: XML standards prohibit duplicate attributes with the same name. However, REXML ignores this restriction in doctype declarations" — so define two conflicting namespace attributes and the SECOND overrides the first. "As a result, REXML reads a FAKE digest value, while Nokogiri reads the REAL one." Ship TWO `Signature` elements (one valid digest, one forged) and Ruby-SAML's Digest Validation is bypassed.
  5. RUBY < 3.4.2 MAKES BOTH HALVES NECESSARY: before 3.4.2, REXML TRUNCATED `!ATTLIST` strings in doctype declarations, which alone breaks GitLab — combining the two flaws restores it: on the FIRST parse REXML ignores the `!ATTLIST` value (treats it as a string literal), on the SECOND parse it recognises the declaration → full exploitation.
  6. FAIL AROUND HARDENING BY EXPLOITING THE FLAW (an earlier 2-year-old class was fixed; this refines it), because "Security experts often focus on !ENTITY declarations in XXE attacks, but !ATTLIST declarations can also be used for exploitation."
  7. FREE SIGNED XML — THE PRECONDITION DELETED: "Identity Providers (IdPs) silently support Single Sign-On protocol: WS-Federation by default for every tenant. WS-Federation provides signed metadata XML endpoints" — e.g. `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>.onmicrosoft.com/...` — and "Federation metadata documents are publicly accessible to any unauthorized user — all that's required is the application's unique ID, which can be easily extracted from the Identity Provider's URL or found using a search engine." It need not be SAML metadata: "a namespace confusion attack only requires a valid Signature element — one that is signed with the same certificate stored at the Service Provider. And it is."
  8. RESULT / ESCALATION: extract a legitimate `Signature` from that public document, graft it onto a forged assertion, POST to the SP's ACS → log in as ANY user (Zak's part of the paper then escalates it to unauthenticated ADMINISTRATOR on GitLab Enterprise).
  9. MITIGATION (the fingerprint to look for): "ensure that the same library is used for both parsing and validating signed XML documents. Avoid marshaling and unmarshaling untrusted user data." Fixed in GitLab 17.9.2 / 17.8.5 / 17.7.7.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a SAML/OIDC SP in the Ruby ecosystem (`ruby-saml`, REXML+Nokogiri split) or PHP (DOM+xmlseclibs); a signature validated on a RE-SERIALISED copy of the document instead of on the transmitted bytes; a validator that locates the Signature by PREFIXED name via XPath while its schema/attribute reading happens in a different parser; a DTD accepted at all inside a SAMLResponse (and a library that tolerates duplicate attribute/namespace declarations in it); any PUBLICLY fetchable XML the IdP has signed — WS-Federation federation metadata, signed SAML metadata, a signed error response.
CHAIN: an unauthenticated request → a public WS-Federation metadata document signed by the IdP certificate the SP already trusts (primitive: a legitimate signature obtained with no credentials, no MITM, no key compromise) -> the DOCTYPE SYSTEM-identifier quote conversion makes the parse→serialise→re-parse round trip swap the `Assertion` the app consumes, while the `!ATTLIST` duplicate-namespace trick makes REXML read a forged digest and Nokogiri the real one (escalation: signature validation passes on the ORIGINAL node while the application acts on the ATTACKER's assertion, with only `ID` + canonicalization needing to agree) -> log in as any user, assert an administrative attribute/NameID → unauthenticated ADMINISTRATOR on GitLab Enterprise (escalation: full SSO authentication bypass → ATO and privilege escalation; P1/Critical).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any SAML SP — (a) fetch the IdP's public WS-Federation metadata for the tenant (the app's unique ID is in the IdP URL or a search engine hit) and keep the `<Signature>` plus the certificate; (b) round-trip your SAMLResponse document: mutate the DOCTYPE SYSTEM identifier so single/double quotes flip (`'…"'` → `"…'"`) so the re-serialised copy terminates the string early around an XML comment, and compare the tree parsed on pass 1 vs pass 2; (c) split the two parsers — move the `ds` namespace declaration into the DOCTYPE with `<!ATTLIST>` and duplicate it so REXML honours the second declaration and Nokogiri the first, then ship two `Signature` elements (real digest + forged digest); (d) keep the signed element's `ID` and canonicalization identical to the original; (e) POST to the ACS with your chosen NameID/`memberOf` and see whether a session is issued — compare `xmlsec1 --verify` (should fail) against the app's own validator, because the technique lives in the gap. Rule: **the verifier and the consumer are different parsers — mutate the document in the DOCTYPE (SYSTEM-identifier quote conversion) so the re-parsed tree differs, split the two with an `<!ATTLIST>` duplicate namespace declaration and a forged second digest, and never hunt for a signed assertion: the IdP signs XML you can fetch for free (WS-Federation metadata).**
DEDUPE: `ATTLIST`, `System identifier`, `single-quoted system`, `Forsén`, `GitLab Enterprise`, `entities were parsed` = 0 hits across all three write targets; no `saml-roulette` entry exists in any of them (`saml-roulette` appears ONLY inside §17.237's and the batch-70 entry's dedupe lines as an unbacked assertion that the material was recorded). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: §17.1/#3827674 Rocket.Chat XSW, §17.45/#136169 OneLogin signature stripping (missing `<ds:Signature/>` accepted), §17.38 Grammarly `entityId` normalization, and §17.237 Fragile Lock (attribute pollution by attribute ORDER, reserved-`xml` REXML namespace confusion WITHOUT DTDs, void canonicalization / empty-string digest). NEW here = the parse→serialise→re-parse ROUND TRIP mutated in the DOCTYPE SYSTEM identifier, the `!ATTLIST` DUPLICATE-namespace digest split, the pre-3.4.2 REXML truncation combination, and WS-Federation federation metadata as a free source of an IdP-signed Signature.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/shadow-repeater-ai-enhanced-manual-testing  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b72-shadow-repeater-ai-enhanced-manual-testing.txt`, 10,611 chars). Published Thursday, 20 February 2025 (updated Tuesday, 25 February 2025) by Gareth Heyes; read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: a TOOL-RELEASE post (Shadow Repeater, BApp store, Early Adopter channel) — the recorded atoms are the REQUEST DIFFER, variant generation and the CONTROL-VALUE RESPONSE DIFFING rule; the install/Organizer narrative and the "Dragons Den" backstory are excluded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp/AI session; the design and the three example discoveries are the author's own.
CLASS: VARIATION TESTING WITH CONTROL-VALUE RESPONSE DIFFING — a cross-class detection method (demonstrated on XSS, path traversal and URL/email splitting), i.e. a chain-first-link detector for injection classes; not a vulnerability class by itself.
CORE METHOD:
  1. DIFF THE REQUEST AND SEND ONLY WHAT CHANGED. A Java Request Differ "analyse[s] the headers, parameters and URL path and only send[s] the changing values" — before that, sending whole requests to the model failed: "Parsing entire requests was of course a bad idea", and the lesson was that only a small, focused slice of data should reach the model.
  2. ASK FOR VARIANTS, NOT FOR UNDERSTANDING. Rather than telling the model what vulnerability is being tested, "I simply told it to find variations of it … giving the AI general instructions to find variations but not going to detail about what it's actually testing" — the context comes from the differ, so the same rule generates variants for path traversal, XSS, encodings and unknown classes.
  3. DIFF THE RESPONSE AGAINST A NOISE FLOOR (the transferable rule). Add to the analysis list BOTH the user's own request AND "some random control values", then "look for invariant attributes of the response that changed when a variation was sent". A variant only counts if it moves an attribute that is otherwise STABLE across the controls — that is what suppresses reflective noise. (The author credits James Kettle's Backslash-Powered-Scanner diffing logic for the code samples.)
  4. WHAT THE MODEL FOUND THAT A HUMAN MISSED: that spaces are allowed in an XSS vector, that a path-traversal vector actually resolved, and an unknown class — email splitting attacks. In other words the target of the technique is the NEAR MISS ("how many vulnerabilities you've missed by a hair's breadth, due to a single flawed choice") — wrong syntax, wrong encoding, wrong file path, a typo.
  5. OPERATION (so the trigger is understood): it fires on the 5th Repeater request and requires a parameter or header to have been CHANGED; findings are pushed to the Organizer for inspection instead of interrupting the workflow.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a manual payload that returns an "almost" answer (error text, partial reflection, `403` vs `404`, a truncated resource list) where you are unsure whether a variation changed the code path; a target where encoding/syntax guesses are the only uncertainty left; responses whose STABLE attributes (status, byte length, a marker string, a timing floor) move when exactly one parameter changes; a reflection that masks the signal (discard any byte-hash attribute — the Anomaly Rank rule: an attribute unique on every response is a reflection, not a signal).
CHAIN: a near-miss payload (primitive: your syntax/encoding/path was wrong but the surface is real) -> mechanically varied payloads scored against RANDOM CONTROL values, accepting only variants that move an INVARIANT response attribute (escalation: the working variant is isolated without a human guessing encodings; and the same run reveals the filter's character policy) -> the confirmed variant becomes the actual finding in its class (stored/reflected XSS with session impact, an LFI/path-traversal file read, an email-parsing access-control bypass) — the diffing is the lead generator, the class impact is the finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any parameter you test, send a small batch — your payload, 5–10 mechanically varied forms (case, encoding, comment/whitespace insertion, path shape, doubled characters) and 2 RANDOM CONTROL values — then diff ONLY the attributes that are stable across the controls; a variant that moves a stable attribute (status, byte length, marker text) is the one to inspect by hand. Rule: **the signal in variation testing is not "the response changed" but "an attribute that is INVARIANT across random controls changed" — send only the fields that differ, and score every variant against a control noise floor.**
DEDUPE: `Shadow Repeater`, `response diffing` as a named technique, `invariant attribute`, `Request Differ` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the §17.238 error-detection harness diffs near-identical payload PAIRS and keeps stable attributes; the HTTP Anomaly Rank entry ranks one result SET by attribute rarity — neither uses RANDOM CONTROL values plus a stable-attribute requirement, which is the atom recorded here.
