SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/bypassing-character-blocklists-with-unicode-overflows  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b73-unicode-overflows.txt`, 6,314 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈2.8k). Published Tuesday, 28 January 2025 at 13:58 UTC (updated Wednesday, 29 January 2025 at 08:10 UTC) by Gareth Heyes (@garethheyes), investigated with Zakhar Fedotkin; read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: a SHORT micropost — the recorded atoms are the two truncation primitives and their arithmetic; the tooling announcements (ActiveScan++ truncation checks, a Hackvertor tag, the Shazzer unicode truncation table) and the credit to Ryan Barnett are named as provenance only, not as the method.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no byte-truncating sink was built or tested this pass; both primitives and all arithmetic are the author's own.
CLASS: CHARACTER-BLOCKLIST / WAF-SIGNATURE BYPASS via CODEPOINT TRUNCATION ("unicode overflow") — a filter-escape primitive that escalates in whichever class the sink sits (XSS, SQLi/NoSQLi, path traversal, command/template injection). Chain-first-link only: "the filter was bypassed" is a lead; the synthesised character's impact is the finding.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TRUNCATION IS THE BUG: "Unicode codepoint truncation - also called a Unicode overflow attack - happens when a server tries to store a Unicode character in a single byte. Because the maximum value of a byte is 255, an overflow can be crafted to produce a specific ASCII character."
  2. COMPUTE THE WRAPPED CODEPOINT FOR THE CHARACTER THE BLOCKLIST BANS: for target byte b, send the codepoints b + n*256 — "here are a couple of examples that end with 0x41 which represents A: 0x4e41 0x4f41 0x5041 0x5141", proof `String.fromCodePoint(0x4e41 % 256, 0x4f41 % 256, 0x5041 % 256, 0x5141 % 256) // AAAA`.
  3. THE SAME OVERFLOW EXISTS IN JAVASCRIPT — `String.fromCharCode()`: "This method allows you to generate a character between 0-0xffff but if you go above this range it will be overflowed and produce a character by the overflow amount" — `String.fromCharCode(0x10000 + 0x31, 0x10000 + 0x33, 0x10000 + 0x33, 0x10000 + 0x37) //1337` (0x10000 is "one above the maximum codepoint supported"; each addition wraps back to the intended character). So a client-side filter that inspects the code POINTS but a sink that truncates them is bypassable too.
  4. WHERE IT FIRES: only where the pipeline casts codepoint→byte — an 8-bit/Latin-1 store, a C-string/buffer write, a single-byte charset or BMP-ignoring conversion. The arithmetic is exact and deterministic: the same wrap that hides the banned character from the validator recreates it at the sink.
  5. WHAT IT BUYS: for any character a WAF/validator refuses (`<`, `>`, `(`, `)`, `'`, `"`, `;`, `/`, `.`, or a keyword letter), substitute `char + n*256` (or the `0x10000 +`-style JavaScript overflow) and re-send — if the response is identical to sending the raw character, the blocklist is decoration. The post notes this is "being actively used by bug bounty hunters".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a blocklist/WAF that refuses a specific character or letter but accepts the same request with it removed; a sink that stores/compares as bytes (Latin-1 columns, fixed-width char fields, C-string handling, single-byte charset conversions); a sanitiser that runs before a later cast or a second decode; a JS path reached through `fromCharCode`/`fromCodePoint` wrappers (the overflow produces the banned character after the filter).
CHAIN: a blocked character (primitive: the input is refused by the WAF/validator, so the class is unreachable) -> send each blocked character as its wrapped codepoint `b + n*256` (escalation: a byte-truncating layer between validator and sink recreates the character after the filter has passed) -> the reconstructed metacharacter or keyword reaches the real sink = the impact of that class (XSS with session impact, SQLi, path traversal to internal file read, command execution). The bypass alone stays a lead.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for each character the target blocks, send `chr(ord(c)+256)`, `chr(ord(c)+512)`, … (and for JavaScript paths `String.fromCharCode(0x10000 + code)`); if the response or behaviour is the same as sending the raw blocked character, the pipeline truncates codepoint→byte and every "character policy" it declares is bypassable. Rule: **a single-byte store overflows — a banned character is re-synthesised from codepoint `char + n*256`, so probe every character blocklist with wrapped codepoints wherever a stage in the pipeline casts a codepoint to a byte.**
DEDUPE: `unicode overflow`, `codepoint truncation`, `fromCharCode`, `codepoint % 256`, `ActiveScan++` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: `WorstFit` (A 3 / B 3 hits) is Windows Best-Fit ANSI conversion at the OS layer; §17.109 (A/C) is a fixed 256-BYTE hostname truncation (string LENGTH differing between validator and resolver) — neither is codepoint-modulus truncation; the `%00`/overlong-UTF-8 material in the upload playbook is the dead legacy null-byte family.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/stealing-httponly-cookies-with-the-cookie-sandwich-technique  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`b73-cookie-sandwich.txt`, 14,810 chars incl. chrome; body ≈7.6k). Published Wednesday, 22 January 2025 at 14:45 UTC (updated Monday, 30 June 2025 at 16:01 UTC) by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the real-world section is a redacted case study (hosts shown as `example.com` / `tracking.example.com`) — the request/response shapes, the cookie-ordering rule and the exploit JS are as published; no host, token or value is invented here.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Tomcat/Flask pair, CORS endpoint or victim cookie jar was stood up; the wire examples, the ordering rule and the final exploit are the author's own.
CLASS: HttpOnly-BYPASS → SESSION/CREDENTIAL THEFT (cookie-header syntax smuggling) — an ATO chain. In-class: sensitive information disclosure with PoC + session forgery/account takeover.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SERVER SPLITS THE COOKIE HEADER ON THE WRONG SEMANTICS: Tomcat "handles both RFC6265 and RFC2109 standards, defaulting to legacy parsing logic if a string starts with the special `$Version` attribute", and "if cookie value starts with double quotes, it will continue reading until the next unescaped double quotes char" — so one quoted value swallows every `; name=value` pair between its opening and closing quote (it also unescapes anything after a backslash).
  2. THE BROWSER IS WHAT LETS YOU BUILD IT: "Because the Chrome browser doesn't support legacy cookies, it lets attackers create a cookie name that starts with a `$`, like `$Version`" (a name a server-side caller could never set), and quotes are legal inside any cookie value: `document.cookie = '$Version=1;'`; `document.cookie = 'param1="start'`; `document.cookie = 'param2=end";'` — on the wire `Cookie: $Version=1; param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end"`, and the server reflects `Set-Cookie: param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end";` with the HttpOnly session cookie folded into param1's value.
  3. CONTROL COOKIE ORDER WITH THE `path` ATTRIBUTE (this is what makes it work against a victim whose cookie you did not set): "For the $Version cookie to be sent first, it must either be created earlier or have a path attribute longer than all other cookies. While we cannot control the creation time of the victim's cookie, we can manipulate the path attribute" — set `$Version` and the OPENING quoted cookie with `Path=<the endpoint's own path>` (e.g. `/json`) and the CLOSING quoted cookie with `Path=/`.
  4. TARGET A COOKIE-REFLECTING ENDPOINT: the case study's tracking service "reflects cookie value in the response body" and "allows cross origin request from vulnerable domain" — `GET /json?session=ignored` with `Origin: https://www.example.com`, answering `HTTP/2 200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://www.example.com`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, body `{"session":"deadbeef"}`; the URL `session` parameter is mandatory but "the server overwrites its value with the one from the Cookie header", so the sandwich's value is echoed.
  5. DELIVERY NEEDS ANY JS ON THE ORIGIN — in the write-up a reflected XSS on an error page (link/meta attributes reflected without escaping) with the AWS WAF beaten by an unpatched event handler: `<link rel="canonical" oncontentvisibilityautostatechange="alert(1)" style="content-visibility:auto">` (credit @garethheyes) — then the exploit JS plants the three cookies inside a hidden iframe of the target path, `fetch(target, {credentials:'include'})` to the CORS endpoint, and reads the HttpOnly `PHPSESSID` out of the JSON.
  6. PYTHON VARIANT WITHOUT `$Version`: "Python frameworks support quoted strings by default, eliminating the need for the special $Version attribute" and they "recognize the semicolon as the browser's cookie pair separator, automatically encoding all special characters into a four-character sequence: a forward slash followed by the three-digit octal equivalent" — `Cookie: param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end"` → `Set-Cookie: param1="start\073 sessionId=secret\073 param2=end";`.
  7. SCOPE + FIX: "Apache Tomcat versions 8.5.x, 9.0.x and 10.0.x support the RFC2109" by default; the recommendation is to disable legacy RFC2109 support unless required and to stop trusting assumptions about which characters a cookie value can contain.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any endpoint that echoes a cookie value back (body, JSON, or `Set-Cookie`) — analytics/tracking/`visitorId` endpoints are named as the ideal target because the id "is rarely validated"; a `Set-Cookie` that reflects the request's own cookie string; a Tomcat/Java backend (RFC2109 on by default) or Flask/Django/`SimpleCookie` (quoted strings + octal decoding); a CORS endpoint with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <the vulnerable origin>` + `Allow-Credentials: true` that reads a cookie; the presence of an HttpOnly session cookie (which is exactly the thing the sandwich is for).
CHAIN: any JavaScript execution on the origin (reflected/stored XSS, or an unescaped cookie reflection) [primitive] -> JS plants `$Version=1` plus an opening quoted cookie on the endpoint's own long path and a closing quoted cookie on `/` (escalation: the server's legacy parser folds the HttpOnly cookie into the quoted value — the flag is bypassed, not removed) -> request a cookie-reflecting endpoint same-origin or cross-origin with credentialed CORS and read the session id out of the response (escalation: HttpOnly no longer protects the secret; the CORS misconfiguration is the second link) -> replay the session cookie = account takeover (P1/P2 with scale). The XSS alone is the first link; a permissive CORS endpoint alone is §2(b) chain material.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any endpoint that reflects a cookie value, send `Cookie: $Version=1; session="deadbeef; <HttpOnlyCookieName>=secret; dummy=qaz"` (Tomcat) or `Cookie: param1="start; <HttpOnlyCookieName>=secret; param2=end"` (Flask/Django) and check whether the response contains the whole sandwiched string; then confirm the ordering rule is satisfiable client-side by creating the `$Version` and opening cookies from JS with `path=` set to the endpoint's own (longest) path. Rule: **a server that starts legacy parsing on `$Version=1` (or on a `"`-opened value) treats everything up to the next unescaped quote as ONE value — sandwich the HttpOnly cookie between two attacker-set quoted cookies, order them with the `path` attribute, and read the secret back from any endpoint that reflects cookies (credentialed CORS counts).**
DEDUPE: `cookie sandwich` hits (A 3 / B 3 / C 1) are ONLY dedupe lines of the § Cookie Chaos entry ("the 'cookie sandwich' post is the earlier article in the same series") and a 0-hit dedupe list — the technique itself is nowhere in the three write targets. `$Version` (A 10 / B 10 / C 8) is recorded ONLY as the cookie-NAME normalisation vector inside the Cookie Chaos entry (`$Version=1,__Host-<name>=x` to smuggle a protected name past browser→server parsing) — a prefix bypass, NOT the quoted-value sandwich; `RFC2109` = 0 hits. Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: `cookie tossing` (header-injection session fixation), Cookie Chaos (Unicode-whitespace name normalisation), and the recorded OAuth cookie-tossing entry.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/bypassing-wafs-with-the-phantom-version-cookie  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 4; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`b73-phantom-version-cookie.txt`, 13,056 chars incl. chrome; body ≈6.4k). Published Wednesday, 4 December 2024 at 15:03 UTC (updated Monday, 30 June 2025 at 16:01 UTC) by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: part 1 of the cookie-parsing series whose part 2 is the cookie-sandwich post (previous entry).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no WAF, Tomcat or Flask instance was stood up; the parser tables, the AWS WAF verdicts and the Burp `HttpHandler` snippet are the author's own.
CLASS: WAF/SIGNATURE BYPASS via COOKIE-PARSER DOWNGRADE — a filter-escape primitive carrying SQLi / command-injection / XSS payloads, plus reflected `Set-Cookie` attribute injection. Chain-first-link.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE HEADER IS LEGAL AND EVERY STACK PARSES IT DIFFERENTLY: `Cookie: $Version=1; foo="bar"; $Path="/"; $Domain=abc;` is a valid RFC2109 header; the post tabulates the result — Flask/Django `{"foo":"bar","$Version":"1","$Path":"/","$Domain":"abc"}` (quotes stripped), PHP/Ruby keep the quotes (`"foo":"\"bar\""`), Spring `{ "foo": "\"bar\"" }`, Python `SimpleCookie` `{ "foo": "bar" }`. `$Version` is the switch: Tomcat "handles both RFC6265 and RFC2109 standards, defaulting to legacy parsing logic if a string starts with the special $Version attribute", additionally supports `$Path`/`$Domain` ("may enable users to change reflected cookie attributes") and "will also unescape any character starting with backslash" — `Cookie: $Version=1; foo="\b\a\r"; $Path=/abc; $Domain=example.com` → `Set-Cookie: foo="bar"; Path=/abc; Domain=example.com`.
  2. QUOTED-STRING ENCODING DEFEATS VALUE ANALYSIS: per RFC 2068 "many HTTP/1.1 header field values consist of words separated by LWS or special characters. These special characters MUST be in a quoted string to be used within a parameter value" — so `$Version=1; name="<payload with every char backslash-escaped>"` is a legal cookie that hides `(`, `'`, `;`, spaces and `=` from signature matching. The AWS WAF example: `eval()` → allowed, `eval('test')` → forbidden, `"\e\v\a\l\(\'t\e\s\t\'\)"` → allowed, and `"\145\166\141\154\050\047\164\145\163\164\047\051"` (octal escapes) → allowed, because all Python frameworks "automatically decode octal escape sequences within quoted strings" (`"\012"`=LF, `"\015"`=CR, `"\073"`=`;`).
  3. BYPASS COOKIE-NAME BLOCKLISTS WITH THE COMMA SEPARATOR: "Another crucial aspect of RFC2109: a server should also accept a comma (,) as a separator between cookie values" → `$Version=1; foo=bar, abc = qux` parses to `"abc": "qux"`; "the specification permits any number of space or tab characters before or after the equal sign", so a blocked name/`=`-shaped signature can be concealed.
  4. SPLIT THE COOKIE ACROSS MULTIPLE HEADERS: "Like many other HTTP headers, the Cookie header can be sent multiple times in a single request", and Ruby/PHP/Django/Flask "combine headers into a single comma-separated string (with an optional space between parameters)" — `Cookie: param1=value1;` + `Cookie: param2=value2;` → Flask/Django `{ ",param2": "value2"}`, PHP `{ ",_param2": "value2"}`, Ruby `{ ", param2": "value2"}`, while Spring keeps them apart. The joining comma is the exploitable artefact: `Cookie: name=eval('test//` on the first header and `Cookie: comment')` on the second gives the server "Resulting cookie: name=eval('test//, comment') => allowed" — the server's own inserted `,` is swallowed by an inline comment, so the reassembled payload still executes while the WAF saw two innocent halves.
  5. AUTOMATION: these techniques are implemented in Param Miner; the post's Burp `HttpHandler` snippet rewrites every parameter as `$Version=1; name="\<char>"` with each character backslash-escaped.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a WAF that blocks a payload in a cookie value while allowing the same bytes in a quoted string (retry as `"…"` with backslash escapes, then as octal escapes `"\145\166…"`); a backend in the PHP/Ruby/Python family that concatenates two `Cookie:` headers with a comma (send the header twice and diff the parsed value); Tomcat/Java behind the WAF (legacy RFC2109 path live); a `Set-Cookie` that echoes a request-supplied `$Path` or `$Domain`.
CHAIN: the WAF passes a request the backend re-assembles into a payload the WAF never saw (primitive: signature evasion on the only detector in the path) -> the quoted/octal/split-encoded payload arrives intact at the SQL/command/XSS sink (escalation: the application's own parser performs the decode) -> the class impact (SQLi read/write, command execution, XSS with session impact). Secondary link: a reflected `$Path`/`$Domain` becomes a `Set-Cookie` attribute you chose — scope widening / cookie shadowing, only ever a chain step (doctrine §2(c): cookie attributes are not a finding on their own).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take a payload the WAF blocks in a cookie, then resend it (a) wrapped as `$Version=1; name="…"` with every character backslash-escaped, (b) as octal escapes `"\145\166…"`, (c) split across two `Cookie:` headers with `//` placed just before the break so the server's joining comma is commented out, (d) with the cookie NAME hidden behind a `, ` separator. Whichever variant produces the application's normal behaviour is the parser differential to keep. Rule: **the WAF reads the raw Cookie header while the backend re-parses it — force legacy parsing with `$Version=1`, hand the value over as a quoted/backslash/octal string, hide names after a `, `, or split the header in two and let an inline comment absorb the server's joining comma.**
DEDUPE: `RFC2109` 0, `quoted-string` 0, `comma separator` 0, `header continuation` 0, `RFC2068` 0 hits across all three write targets; `octal escape` hits (A 2 / C 3) are CSS `\00003c`-style escapes in the sanitizer-rewriter entries — a different decoder in a different protocol; `$Version` is recorded only in Cookie Chaos as a cookie-NAME normaliser (see previous entry). Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: `cookie tossing` and Cookie Chaos.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/new-crazy-payloads-in-the-url-validation-bypass-cheat-sheet  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`b73-url-validation-bypass.txt`, 8,858 chars incl. chrome; body ≈4.2k). Published Tuesday, 29 October 2024 at 13:59 UTC (updated Friday, 22 November 2024 at 09:06 UTC) by Zakhar Fedotkin (@zakfedotkin); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the payloads are community submissions (@e1abrador's Encode IP extension, @SeanPesce's userinfo payload, @t0xodile's CORS entries) and the userinfo payload is MASKED IN THE PUBLISHED PAGE SOURCE as `https://***@attacker.com` (a link to the cheat-sheet entry `#id=1da2f627…`) — the character named in the prose is the left square bracket `[`; nothing beyond that mask is asserted here.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — the browsers/Spring instance were not exercised this pass; the notation list, the userinfo discrepancy and the CORS examples are the authors' own.
CLASS: SSRF / OPEN-REDIRECT FILTER BYPASS via IP-NOTATION and URL-USERINFO PARSER DIFFERENTIALS, plus CORS ALLOW-LIST VALIDATION BYPASS. Chain-first-link: the notation or parser discrepancy is the primitive; cloud metadata / internal service access / authenticated cross-origin read is the impact.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SAME IP HAS MANY EQUIVALENT NOTATIONS — for the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254 the cheat sheet now generates formats "supported by Chrome, Firefox, Safari": `169.254.43518` (Partial Decimal **Class B** — "combines the third and fourth parts of the IP address into a decimal number"), `169.16689662` (Partial Decimal **Class A** — "combines the second, third, and fourth parts") and `0xA9.254.0251.0376` (Mixed Encodings — "each segment of the IP address can be presented in different formats: hexadecimal, decimal, or octal"; the tool's default is segment1 hex, segment2 decimal, segments 3-4 octal). Arithmetic check: 169*256+254 = 43518 and 254*65536+169*256+254 = 16689662, i.e. the address is one 32-bit integer written in parts — the validator and the resolver need not agree on the split.
  2. NORMALISATION ENCODINGS ON TOP: the generated host can be re-encoded with "Circled Latin letters and numbers, Fullwidth Forms, or even Seven-segment display characters" (Advanced → Normalization settings) — payloads aimed at the stage that normalises or blocklists, not at the resolver.
  3. IPv6 SIDE: a valid IPv6 address is expanded to its full form, and an embedded IPv4 is extracted and expanded into all the IPv4 formats above.
  4. THE USERINFO BRACKET DIFFERENTIAL (the structurally new atom): the payload shown as `https://***@attacker.com` — "the 'left square bracket' character `[` in the userinfo segment can cause Spring's UriComponentsBuilder to return a hostname value that differs from how major browsers interpret it. This discrepancy can potentially lead to vulnerabilities such as open redirects or SSRF" (submitted by @SeanPesce; the author also reproduced a separate, patched exploit with it).
  5. CORS ALLOW-LIST REGEX BYPASS (same update, @t0xodile): `https://example.com.{.web-attacker.com/`, `https://example.com.}.web-attacker.com/` and `https://example.com.`.web-attacker.com/` — "an edge case related to localhost regex implementations and Safari-specific domain splitting attacks … where attackers can manipulate domains using special characters to bypass validation checks".
DETECTION SIGNAL: an SSRF/allowlist check that string-matches the literal (`169.254.169.254`, `127.0.0.1` denylist) instead of resolving the address; a user-supplied URL fetched by a Java/Spring stack (`UriComponentsBuilder`); an origin allow-list built from a regex (a `localhost` pattern, a `example.com` pattern) with a client that tolerates `{`, `}`, backtick or a trailing-dot sibling domain; any "validate then fetch" pair where your tool and the target disagree about the parsed host.
CHAIN: a user-controlled URL that must pass an allow/deny check (primitive: the filter is the only gate) -> re-express the same target in an accepted equivalent notation (partial-decimal Class A/B, per-segment mixed radix, normalised digits) or move the real host behind a masked userinfo so VALIDATOR and HTTP CLIENT disagree about the host (escalation) -> the request lands on loopback/link-local/cloud metadata or on the attacker origin while validation reported success = SSRF to internal services → metadata credentials → RCE, or open redirect → OAuth token theft; the CORS variants instead read authenticated cross-origin responses = BAC/ATO. The notation trick alone is a lead.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every URL/SSRF parameter, send the SAME internal target in: `<a>.<b>.<c*256+d>` (Class B), `<a>.<b*65536+c*256+d>` (Class A), per-segment mixed radix (`0xA9.254.0251.0376`), an IPv6 expansion (and its embedded-v4 form), then a `[` inside the userinfo before the real host (Spring stack), then a `{`/`}`/backtick/trailing-dot sibling domain against any regex origin allow-list — and diff which pass and which reach the internal target. Rule: **an IPv4 address is one 32-bit integer and a URL authority has a userinfo segment — validators string-match while clients normalise, so retry the same internal host as partial-decimal / per-segment mixed-radix, hide it behind a `[...]`-bearing userinfo, and test `{`/`}`/backtick domains against every regex-based origin allow-list.**
DEDUPE: `UriComponentsBuilder` 0, `partial decimal` 0, `0xA9` 0, `169.254.43518` 0, `circled` 0, `seven-segment` 0, `web-attacker` 0, `example.com.{` 0, `localhost regex` 0, `Safari domain` 0, `url-cheat-sheet` 0, `CORS bypass` 0 hits across all three write targets. Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the recorded SSRF material already lists userinfo `@` tricks and generic "decimal/octal/hex IPv4" (`2130706433`, `0x7f000001`, `0177.0.0.1` for 127.0.0.1) — NEW here is the PARTIAL-DECIMAL Class A/B segmentation, PER-SEGMENT MIXED RADIX, the digit-NORMALISATION encodings, and the `[`-in-userinfo → Spring `UriComponentsBuilder` hostname discrepancy; the `fullwidth`/homoglyph hits in C (10) are Unicode path/parameter ROUTING bypasses (V-series CSRF/path material), not host-literal normalisation.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/concealing-payloads-in-url-credentials  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`b73-url-credentials.txt`, 8,322 chars incl. chrome; body ≈4.1k). Published Wednesday, 23 October 2024 at 12:59 UTC (updated 23 October 2024 at 14:03 UTC) by Gareth Heyes (@garethheyes); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the payloads are masked IN THE PAGE SOURCE as `https://***@portswigger-labs.net` (the CMS hides the credentials segment) — the mask is reproduced verbatim and no substitute payload is invented; the `foo:bar` example, the JS, the anchor examples and the limitations are exact. Builds on Johan Carlsson's original discovery (linked from the post).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no browser lab was run; the property difference, the Shazzer fuzzing result and the clobbering examples are the author's own.
CLASS: DOM XSS via PAYLOAD CONCEALMENT IN URL CREDENTIALS + DOM CLOBBERING of `username`/`password`. In-class: XSS with real impact; chain-first-link (the concealed payload by itself is not a finding — the DOM XSS or the clobbered-object effect is).
CORE METHOD:
  1. `location` AND `document.URL` DISAGREE: `https://foo:bar@portswigger-labs.net` gives `alert(location)` = `https://portswigger-labs.net/` but `alert(document.URL)` = `https://foo:bar@portswigger-labs.net/` — "document.URL contains the credentials part of the URL whereas location doesn't". Chrome and Firefox hide the credentials in the address bar and it "even persists through same origin navigations".
  2. A SINK THAT READS `URL`/`document.URL` READS YOUR CONCEALED PAYLOAD: `https://***@portswigger-labs.net` plus `<img src onerror=alert(URL.slice(8,16))>` — "you can use just URL inside an event [handler to] grab the payload from the credentials".
  3. THE BYPASS THAT REVIVES A DEAD DOM XSS: after fuzzing which characters are encoded in the credentials segment (Shazzer vector linked in the post), "Firefox doesn't URL-encode single quotes" — so against `function getBase(url){ return url.split(/[?#]/)[0]; } document.write(\`<script>const url='${getBase(document.URL)}';<\/script>\`)` the credentials segment closes the single-quoted string: "useful in DOM XSS scenarios, if the site removes the query string and hash". Delivery: "redirection or user navigation".
  4. ANCHOR PROPERTIES CARRY THE SAME DATA: every `<a>` has `username`/`password` properties holding the URL credentials, and "if it's a relative link, it inherits the parent credentials, allowing you to clobber these values" — `https://***@example.com` + `<a href=# onclick=alert(username)>test</a>`.
  5. DOM-CLOBBERING PAYLOAD: `https://user:pass@example.com` + `<a href id=x>test</a>` then `eval(x.username) //user` and `eval(x.password) //pass` — "You can combine this with DOM Clobbering to give you control over objects with username or password properties"; a blank `href` still works, so any app code reading `obj.username`/`config.password` from a clobbered element is attacker-controlled.
  6. LIMITS (honest): "Safari discards URL credentials. All the examples shown only work on Chrome and Firefox. Also Chrome blocks sub-resources from using URL credentials" — top-level navigation/redirect only, and the parent credentials only reach the same-origin child.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any sink that interpolates `document.URL`/`URL`/`document.baseURI` into HTML or a JS string, especially where `?`/`#` stripping is the site's protection; a DOM-XSS candidate whose vector dies on query/hash filtering; application JS (or the client bundle) reading `.username`/`.password` off an element or a config object (clobberable); an open redirect or auth flow that lets you place arbitrary text before the `@` of the final URL.
CHAIN: a sink that consumes `document.URL` (primitive: an under-appreciated source, invisible in the address bar) -> place the payload in the credentials segment and break out with Firefox's unencoded `'` — or read it back with `URL.slice(...)` — so stripping the query string and hash, the site's stated XSS mitigation, no longer removes the attack surface (escalation) -> injected JavaScript in a victim's authenticated session = XSS with session impact / actions as the victim (P2/P3 by the sink); separately, clobbering an anchor's `username`/`password` feeds any code that reads those fields = logic/authorization manipulation. The concealed payload alone is a lead.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any DOM-XSS candidate whose vector dies because `?`/`#` is stripped or sanitised, retry with the payload inside the authority — `https://<payload>@<host>/<path>` (top-level navigation or a redirect) — and check whether the site's JS reads `document.URL`/`URL` rather than `location` and interpolates it into HTML or a quoted JS string; in Firefox single quotes survive. In parallel, add `<a href id=x>test</a>` under a credential-bearing parent URL and see whether the app's own script reads `x.username`/`x.password`. Rule: **`location` hides URL credentials and `document.URL` keeps them — hide the payload before the `@` where query/hash filters never look; Firefox leaves `'` unencoded so it breaks out of JS strings, and every anchor's `username`/`password` inherit the parent credentials, which is a DOM-clobbering primitive for any object the app reads those fields from.**
DEDUPE: `document.URL` hits in C (5) are generic DOM-XSS source lists (`location.*`, `document.URL`, `window.name`, `postMessage`, …) — no entry records the credentials-retention difference; `credentials part` 0, `anchor username` 0, `password property` 0, `concealed payload` 0, `Shazzer` 0, `UriComponentsBuilder` 0 hits. Related-but-distinct and NOT re-recorded: the recorded DOM-XSS/DOM-clobbering entries map sources→sinks generally — this adds the USERINFO source (invisible, filter-escaping) and the anchor `username`/`password` properties as clobberable fields.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/gotta-cache-em-all  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b74-src2.txt`, 30,812 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈24k). Published Thursday, 8 August 2024 at 22:27 UTC, UPDATED Thursday, 8 January 2026 at 12:21 UTC (Martin Doyhenard @PortSwiggerRes; DEF CON/BH USA paper); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: several request/response examples are rendered as IMAGES in the published page (the exploit diagrams, the CDN static-extension tables and the two normalisation tables) and did not survive local stripping — the ones quoted below are the ones present as text; the tables' contents are described only where the prose states them (Cloudflare/Google Cloud/Fastly do not normalise before evaluating cache rules; Azure/Imperva and CloudFront/Azure/Imperva do — as written in the post). The two named techniques ("Static Path Deception", "Cache Key Confusion") are named in the batch's sixth source, the DEF CON/BH preview, which was also opened this pass.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no cache/CDN pair (Nginx+Cloudflare, Apache+CloudFront, Azure) was stood up; every delimiter, normalisation and rule behaviour below is the paper's own text.
CLASS: WEB CACHE DECEPTION + WEB CACHE POISONING via URL-PARSER DISCREPANCIES (CDN/cache delimiter & normalisation rules vs origin delimiters & normalisation) — reaches session/token theft (deception) and site-wide XSS / defacement (poisoning). Chain: a delimiter or normalisation artefact is the primitive; the sensitive-response theft or the arbitrary-key injection is the impact.
CORE METHOD:
  1. DETECT ORIGIN DELIMITERS with a three-request control: (a) find a NON-cacheable request (`POST`, or a response with `Cache-Control: no-store`/`private`) = R0; (b) send the same request with a random suffix on the path (`/home` -> `/homeabcd`) = R1 and require R1 == R0 (else pick another endpoint); (c) send `/home<CANDIDATE_DELIMITER>abcd` = R2 — if R2 == R0 the candidate is a delimiter. Fuzz all ASCII with Burp Intruder, testing both raw and URL-encoded forms. Cache-side: find a CACHEABLE request (proven by `X-Cache: hit` or response time) and compare `GET /static-endpoint<DELIMITER><Random>` against it.
  2. THE DELIMITERS THAT EXIST IN THE WILD (step 1's payloads): semicolon in Spring/Java matrix variables — `/MyAccount;var1=val` -> path `/MyAccount`, `/hello;var=a/world;var1=b;var2=c` -> `/hello/world`; the dot in Rails formatter extensions — `/MyAccount.html`, `/MyAccount.css`, `/MyAccount.aaaa` all -> `/MyAccount` (default HTML view); the NULL byte in OpenLiteSpeed — `/MyAccount%00aaa` -> `/MyAccount`; the encoded newline in Nginx when a rewrite maps a PREFIX (`rewrite /user/(.*) /account/$1 break;` -> `/users/MyAccount%0aaaa` becomes `/account/MyAccount`).
  3. DETECT DECODING: compare `/home/index` with its fully percent-encoded twin `/%68%6f%6d%65%2f%69%6e%64%65%78` (encode each character individually, as reserved chars may not be decoded). Same body and NOT from cache => the origin decodes the path before using it; if the encoded twin comes back with the same cache headers, the cache KEY was decoded before comparison. Proxies often decode and forward the decoded value, so `"/myAccount%3Fparam" -> "/myAccount?param"` and the next parser sees a delimiter.
  4. DETECT DOT-SEGMENT NORMALISATION: non-cacheable `GET /home/index?cacheBuster` vs `GET /aaa/../home/index?cacheBuster` (and the backslash form `aaa\..\home/index`) — identical responses => the path is normalised before endpoint mapping; repeat against a cacheable resource and compare `X-Cache`/`Cache-Control` to learn whether the CACHE normalises.
  5. ARBITRARY WEB CACHE DECEPTION — static-EXTENSION rule: if a character is a delimiter at the origin but is NOT special to the cache, append an arbitrary suffix that trips a "static" rule: `GET /<Dynamic_Resource><Delimiter><anything>.css` (the paper's example is `/myAccount$<suffix>` with `$` backend-only) — the cache stores the dynamic, victim-specific response and the attacker fetches it by URL. Encoded delimiters work where the raw one would be dropped (`#` is never sent by the browser unless encoded), and multiple encodings/delimiters can be stacked to reach a specific proxy in a rewriting chain.
  6. …static-DIRECTORY rule (a published prefix such as `/static`, `/assets`, `/wp-content`, `/media`, `/templates`, `/public`, `/shared`), two directions: front-end normalises, backend does not => `GET /<Dynamic_Resource><Delimiter><ENCODED_Dot_Segment><Static_Directory>` (CloudFront/Azure/Imperva normalise before evaluating the rules by default); backend normalises, front-end does not => `GET /<Static_Directory><ENCODED_Dot_Segment><Dynamic_Resource>` (Cloudflare/Google Cloud/Fastly do not; Nginx/IIS/OpenLiteSpeed normalise before mapping). The dot-segment MUST stay encoded or the victim's browser resolves it locally. IIS + any cache that does not convert backslashes to slashes is a variant.
  7. …static-FILE rule (`/robots.txt`, `/favicon.ico`, `/index.html` — stored by default on e.g. Cloudflare): same shape with the filename in place of the directory and a cache buster: `GET /<Dynamic_Resource><Delimiter><Encoded_Dot_Segment><Static_File>`.
  8. ARBITRARY CACHE POISONING via KEY NORMALISATION (assumes the key is normalised — configurable in most CDNs, default on Azure and Imperva): a self-reflected XSS or 404 body that is stored under its own URL (`/<script>X</script>` cached as `public`) becomes a poisoned hot path once the key is normalised — `GET /<Backend_Path><Path_Traversal><Poisoned_Path>` stores the malicious body under the resolved hot endpoint (`/home`). Adjust the number of dot-segments to the payload's own slashes. With a BACK-END delimiter the same works as `GET /<Backend_Path><Delimiter><Path_Traversal><Poisoned_Path>`; with a FRONT-END delimiter (the hash, on Azure which normalises the path AND treats `#` as a delimiter) as `GET /<Poisoned_Path><Front-End_Delimiter><Path_Traversal><Backend_Path>`. Requirement: the key is normalised and the suffix after the delimiter is still forwarded.
  9. "CACHE-WHAT-WHERE": take any bug that is NOT exploitable through a browser (headers/characters a browser will not send) and store it in the cache under a hot path. Demonstrated escalation: an `X-Forwarded-Host`-driven open redirect (`GET /home` + `X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com` -> `302 Location: http://evil.com/index.html`) is key-confused onto `/main.js`, so every visitor of the homepage loads attacker-controlled JavaScript from that path = cross-domain script execution / full site takeover; if the redirect response itself carries `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` (the paper's `/redirect?somePage` example) no static extension is needed and the result is arbitrary cache poisoning / full website defacement.
  10. DEFENCE (so a target that does this is NOT reachable): dynamic responses marked `Cache-Control: no-store, private`; cache rules verified not to take priority over that header; cache keys NOT normalised; the suffix after a cache delimiter not forwarded.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any front-end cache in front of an origin that treats the URL differently — a `;`, `.ext`, `%00`, `%0a`, or backslash variant of a path that returns the SAME body as the clean path; a static-extension/directory/file rule (`Cf-Cache-Status: HIT` or `X-Cache: hit` on a path that is not actually static); a cacheable response to a request that carries user-specific data while unauthenticated; a `Cache-Control: public` on anything dynamic; a front-end that normalises dot-segments (or the hash) while the origin does not, or vice versa.
CHAIN: a dynamic, victim-specific response that the cache can be tricked into storing (primitive: one delimiter or dot-segment that one parser honours and the other ignores) -> the attacker's crafted URL makes the cache treat that response as a static resource under a path the victim will visit, and the attacker reads it unauthenticated (escalation: session tokens/API keys out of the cached body => account takeover — the paper's stated outcome) OR the same mechanism normalises the KEY so a self-reflected XSS/open-redirect body is stored under a hot path like `/main.js` (escalation: attacker JS on a highly visited URL = site-wide XSS/defacement, and with a stored open redirect, arbitrary poisoning). Every link above is one request shape; the delimiter artefact alone is chain material, not a finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for the next target, (1) fingerprint the front-end and the origin, then run the three-request delimiter control and the encoded-twin decoding control on a non-cacheable endpoint, and the same on a cacheable one with `X-Cache` inspection; (2) for every delimiter you find, append a static-looking suffix (`<delim><x>.css`, `<delim>%2e%2e%2fstatic`, `<delim>%2e%2e%2frobots.txt`) and check whether an authenticated, user-specific response is now served to you unauthenticated out of the cache; (3) if the key normalises, append `<dot-segment><attacker payload>` or `<front-end delimiter><dot-segment><backend path>` and check whether the reflection is stored under the clean hot path. Rule: **whenever a cache and an origin disagree about a delimiter or about dot-segment/encoding normalisation, the attacker gets to decide BOTH what is stored and under which key — so enumerate the origin's delimiters (`;` Spring, `.` Rails, `%00` OpenLiteSpeed, encoded newline after an Nginx prefix rewrite) and normalisation order, then aim the discrepancy at a static extension/directory/file rule (deception: read someone else's response) or at the cache key (poisoning: put your body on a hot URL).**
DEDUPE: `matrix variab` 0, `OpenLiteSpeed`/`LiteSpeed` 0, `formatter extension` 0, `static directory` 0, `Cache-What-Where` 0, `Cache Key Confusion`/`cache key confusion` 0, `Static Path Deception` 0, `hybrid caching` 0, `cache buster` 0, `deep cache` 0, `dot segment` (unhyphenated) 0 hits across all three write targets; `rewrite /user` 0. Pre-existing hits that ARE related material and were therefore NOT re-recorded as new: `dot-segment` hits are the OAuth `redirect_uri` prefix-check traversal entry (§17.195) and the Nginx `alias` path-traversal entry (a filesystem join, not a cache rule); `cache deception` hits are the ChatGPT wildcard (`/share/*` + `%2F..%2F`, §8.8) and the cache-deception+CSPT static-extension entry (§12.4) — both use a static extension rule and a traversal, but neither records a DELIMITER matrix for an origin server, the normalisation ORDER test, static directory/file rules, key normalisation, or Cache-What-Where; `X-Forwarded-Host` hits are host-header reset poisoning and the OAuth `url`-helper entry (no cache key confusion); `static extension` (A 1) is §12.4's own wording.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/splitting-the-email-atom  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b74-src3.txt`, 44,827 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈41k). Published Wednesday, 7 August 2024 at 21:32 UTC, updated Friday, 27 June 2025 at 13:49 UTC (Gareth Heyes @garethheyes; BH USA + DEF CON, accompanied by a Web Security Academy CTF and a Joomla docker lab); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: this paper renders MANY payload examples as IMAGES — the GitHub and GitLab splitting payloads, the Joomla style-injection tag, the punycode subdomain chains and parts of the encoded-word examples did not survive local stripping, and NO substitute payload is invented here; everything quoted below was read as TEXT in the page. The unicode-overflow section of this paper duplicates the standalone "Bypassing character blocklists with unicode overflows" post already recorded this ledger (see DEDUPE).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no mailer (Sendmail/Postfix), Ruby `Mail`-based app, PHP IDN library or Joomla instance was stood up; every address, probe and decode result below is the author's own.
CLASS: ACCESS-CONTROL BYPASS via EMAIL-ADDRESS PARSER DISCREPANCIES — email-domain spoofing to defeat domain-based authorisation (registration allow-lists, IdP e-mail-domain trust / "Zero Trust" gateways, support-centre domain restrictions), plus CODE INJECTION (blind CSS injection -> CSRF token exfiltration -> template edit) reaching RCE. Chain-first-link: an address that merely "parses oddly" is not a finding; the verified-but-not-owned domain and the injection are.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE MAILER CAN ROUTE THE MAIL SOMEWHERE ELSE THAN THE DOMAIN YOU READ. Sendmail 8.15.2, UUCP syntax (its separator runs the other way round; a trailing backslash escapes the `@`): `oastify.com!collab\@example.com` is delivered to oastify.com, not example.com (author's original discovery was the same shape with every local-part special character: `!#$%&'*+\/=?^_`{|}~-collab\@psres.net`). Postfix 3.6.4, source routes + the "percent hack" (the mailer converts `%` to `@` and forwards) with a parenthetical comment that removes the real domain: `collab%psres.net(@example.com` is delivered to psres.net. Two more Postfix behaviours, sent regardless of quoting: `"psres.net!collab"(\"@example.com` -> `collab@psres.net`, and a source route survives the bracket syntax `collab%psres.net@[127.0.0.1]` -> `collab@psres.net`. Bonus vector: SMTP ORCPT smuggling — `"foo\\"@psres.net> ORCPT=test;admin"@example.com` changes the destination by abusing the application's mishandling of escapes in a quoted local-part.
  2. RFC2832 QUOTED LOCAL-PARTS AND COMMENTS ARE LEGAL: `"@"@example.com`, `"\\""@example.com` and `(foo)user@(bar)example.com` are valid addresses; anything may live inside a comment. This is the ground truth that makes an application's "domain" decision unreliable.
  3. ENCODED-WORD (RFC 2047) IS A FULL DECODER STACK INSIDE THE ADDRESS. Syntax `=?<charset>?q?<Q-encoding>?=` (Q-encoding is hex with `=` prefixes, e.g. `=41=42=43` -> `ABC`) or `=?<charset>?b?<base64>?=`. Ruby's `Mail` gem (>508M downloads) decodes UTF-7 and base64, IN THE LOCAL-PART AND IN THE DOMAIN; the layers compose — base64 whose charset is UTF-7 is decoded twice; in Q-encoding `_` is a space (`=20` also works). The consequence: blocked characters (`@`, `>`, `"`, `<`, whitespace, NUL) can be assembled from allowed ones after validation.
  4. PROBE FIRST (the author's two-probe method): send addresses that place an encoded `@` + collaborator domain inside an encoded-word local-part (his probe method: keep the probe short by using a one-letter charset like `x` where the platform accepts it, but prefer the common charsets because some systems reject unknown ones), and watch for an SMTP interaction in Burp Collaborator whose `RCPT TO:` shows the DECODED address — that proves encoded-word decoding, and it is common on Ruby-based sites.
  5. SPLIT THE ADDRESS at the SMTP layer so the site verifies a domain you do not own: encode `@` (`=40`) and `>` (`=3e`) so the mailer's RCPT TO command ENDS at your encoded `>`, then append an encoded NUL (`=00`) plus a harmless valid local-part (`foo`) so the mailer discards the tail while the application's own validation still accepts the whole string (GitHub: charset irrelevant, so `x`); for other stacks the same split needs an encoded SPACE (`=20`, or `_` in Q-encoding) and a widely accepted charset such as `iso-8859-1`. Results: verify addresses on microsoft.com, mozilla.com, github.com from a GitHub test account (the author did), and — because GitHub is an IdP for Cloudflare Zero Trust where the e-mail DOMAIN decides access — reach an internal network protected by Zero Trust.
  6. ZENDESK, a worked differential: input `=?x?q?=41=42=43collab=40psres.net=3e=20?=@psres.net` came back in the SMTP conversation as `RCPT TO:<"ABCcollab@psres.net> "@psres.net>` — which tells you uppercase and decoded spaces are allowed and that the parser re-quotes values that are illegal in a local-part. The successful split then combined DOUBLED encoded quotes (decoded by the parser) with `=3c22`, which yields a `<` that the application REMOVES — removing it completes the quote and satisfies their validation/exception path; `=3e=00` finishes RCPT TO and swallows the rest as on GitHub. Effect: bypass the "only these domains may register" restriction on a support centre.
  7. GITLAB (enterprise + web app are different mailers): the enterprise instance (Postfix) fell to an encoded SPACE written as an underscore (`_` — "1 character and I love elegant vectors", `=20` also works) in a domain-restricted registration; the web app needed a real charset plus a space. Either way: unauthorised registration/access on a domain-restricted GitLab.
  8. MALFORMED PUNYCODE -> HTML/CSS INJECTION. The IDN PHP library (IdnaConvert) mis-decodes crafted `xn--` labels into arbitrary ASCII: `psres.net.com.xn--0049.com.psres.net` -> `psres.net.com.,.com.psres.net`, `foo@xn--0117.example.com` -> `foo@@.example.com`, and from the fuzzer `x@xn--42` -> `x@,`, `x@xn--694` -> `x@;`, `x@xn--svg/-9x6` -> `x@<svg/`. Because Joomla ESCAPES the stored address and then a display path PUNYCODE-DECODES it, the decoded `<` becomes live markup. The single-subdomain constraint means the only reachable opening tag was `<style>`; the injected address is persistent on the users list page and needs no activated account.
  9. THE CSS CHAIN TO RCE (Joomla, CVE-2024-21725, fixed 20 Feb 2024; idn-convert library fixed 14 Feb 2024): account 1's name carries `{}` so the rest of the page's HTML is parsed as an invalid CSS selector, account 2's name carries an `@import` pointing at the attacker's stylesheet (inline style, so Chrome's MIME check does not apply), the imported CSS exfiltrates the super-admin's CSRF token via import chaining (tools by d0nut / Pepe Vila), and the token is replayed to edit a backend template with PHP calling `system()` = RCE.
 10. METHODOLOGY + TOOLING: "Probe, Observe, Encode and Exploit" (probe with Collaborator, observe the decoded address, repeat until the needed characters are available, then exploit); Hackvertor tags `_unicode_overflow(0x100,...)`, `_unicode_overflow_variations(0xfff,...)`, `_encoded_word_encode/_decode`, `_email_utf7/_decode`, `_encode_word_meta('iso-8859-1',...)`; a Turbo Intruder script that replays all known splitters (null vs space, per-mailer) against a `%s` marker with a configurable sleep for rate limits; a punycode fuzzer with random-number/whitespace placeholders plus regex match/contains filters. Defence stated by the author: disable encoded-word, or block `=[?].+[?]=`, always validate even an SSO-provided address, and never use the e-mail domain as the sole authorisation signal.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any feature where an e-mail DOMAIN decides something — registration allow-lists, "your-company-only" signup, IdP/Zero-Trust domain trust (e.g. GitHub as IdP), support-centre access, invite domains; a Ruby stack behind e-mail (the `Mail` gem decodes encoded-word by default); verification mails that arrive with a domain you did not type; a Collaborator/DNS interaction when the address contains `=`, `?`, `_`, `(`, `)`, `%` or an `xn--` label; `xn--` labels displayed as text anywhere (avatars, user lists, admin views) — the punycode decode is a display-time injection.
CHAIN: an application that authorises on the e-mail domain (primitive: the domain string it checks) -> craft an RFC-valid address whose DECODED destination is your own domain, so verification mail lands with you while the app sees the victim domain (escalation 1: verified e-mail on a domain you do not own) -> use that verified identity where the domain is the trust signal: IdP/Cloudflare Zero Trust domain rules = access to internal systems, registration allow-lists = unauthorised account, GitLab EE = enterprise access (escalation 2: BAC / auth bypass / internal access). Parallel chain from the same parser bug: a crafted `xn--` address that decodes to `<style>` (primitive: malformed punycode -> markup) -> persistent style injection -> `@import` chaining exfiltrates the admin CSRF token (escalation: token theft through CSS) -> authenticated request edits a backend template to PHP = RCE (CVE-2024-21725). The misrouted mail or the odd-looking address alone is chain material.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target that trusts an e-mail domain, (1) send the two encoded-word probes and check Collaborator's SMTP `RCPT TO:` for a DECODED address (Ruby/PHP presence raises the odds); (2) build a split for the local mailer — encoded `@` + `>` + NUL with a trailing valid local part (Postfix/GitHub shape) or encoded SPACE/`_` with `iso-8859-1` (GitLab-web/GitLab-EE shape) — and check whether a verification mail for the target domain arrives at your collaborator while the application still accepts the address; (3) where the address is DISPLAYED, throw `xn--` fuzz labels at it and look for injected punctuation/tag characters; (4) if the domain is the sole authorisation signal (IdP / Zero Trust / allow-list), treat a successful spoof as access-control bypass, not as "email spoofing". Rule: **an e-mail address is a string several parsers disagree about — the application validates one parse, the mailer delivers by another, and display code may decode a third (punycode), so never treat the domain as an authorisation input, and always test `=40`/`=3e`/`=00`, `_`/`=20`, `(`, `%`, `!` and malformed `xn--` labels against it.**
DEDUPE: `encoded-word` 0, `utf7` 0, `idn-` 0, `xn--` 0, `CVE-2024-21725` 0, `UUCP` 0, `ORCPT` 0, `percent hack` 0, `collab%psres` 0, `RCPT TO` 0, `Kobold` 0 hits across all three write targets; `Harvest`… `Hackvertor` hits (A 3 / B 2 / C 2) are the Hackvertor tag usage recorded from other PortSwigger posts, not these tags. Pre-existing hits that ARE related material and were therefore NOT re-recorded as new: the UNICODE-OVERFLOW section of this paper is the same primitive as §17.247 (standalone post, read in batch 73: codepoint % 256 / `fromCharCode` overflow) — only the e-mail-specific use of it (spoof a blocked `@`) is referenced here, and even that is not re-recorded; `email splitting` hits are an unrelated AI-variation-testing entry that merely mentions the class; `Punycode`/`IDN` hits are homoglyph/near-duplicate tenant-identifier material (registration DoS/provisioning) and an SSRF trailing-dot note — none is the malformed-`xn--` decode to markup; `email atom` hits are the SAML-roulette entry's mention of this same paper as a chain partner (no method recorded).

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/listen-to-the-whispers-web-timing-attacks-that-actually-work  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 4; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b74-src4.txt`, 44,578 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈41k). Published Wednesday, 7 August 2024 at 18:10 UTC, updated Monday, 18 November 2024 at 08:32 UTC (James Kettle @albinowax; BH USA + DEF CON, tooling in Param Miner/Turbo Intruder, CTF at listentothewhispers.net); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the paper's response-time tables, diagrams and videos are images — the millisecond values quoted below are the ones written in the text; the request-line/loop listings quoted are the ones present as text.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no single-packet timing harness was built this pass and no target was touched; the primitives, the measurements and the case studies are the author's own (research run over a 30,000-site bug-bounty corpus).
CLASS: TIMING-SIDE-CHANNEL DRIVEN DISCOVERY AND SSRF/BAC ESCALATION — high-precision timing (single-packet attack + bottom-quartile sampling) is used to (a) find hidden parameters/headers that never change the response, (b) detect SCOPED SSRF (a reverse proxy that only forwards to the company's own hosts, invisible to OAST), (c) enumerate hidden internal routes, and (d) bypass front-end rules and impersonate the front-end. Impact classes: SSRF to internal services, admin/internal panel access, authentication/authorisation bypass.
CORE METHOD:
  1. MAKE THE MEASUREMENT LOCAL — the single-packet attack, adapted for timing: "disable TCP_NODELAY | send a ping frame for each request with no body | send the headers | withhold an empty data frame | for each request with a body: send the headers and the body except the final byte, withhold a data frame containing the final byte | wait for 100ms | send a ping frame | send the final frames". Two requests then reach the server together, and you compare the ORDER the responses arrive in (a delay only needs to change the ordering, not the measured latency) — the sacrificial ping frame makes the OS coalesce the header frames so the sticky request-order bias of plain HTTP/2 de-sync disappears, with no per-target tuning.
  2. MAKE IT FEASIBLE — sample 30 times per variant and compare the BOTTOM QUARTILES of the two sets: distinct = a real difference, overlapping = noise (this is what Param Miner does with 'response time' added as an attribute, "measured the time from the last byte of the request to the first byte of the response"). Reduce noise by taking the shortest code path and reusing caches/objects/connections; raise signal with random inputs (defeat server-side caching), slow resources and workload multiplication — the text's payload `GET / HTTP/1.1` plus `X-Uaa: a`, `X-Ubb: a`, `X-Ucc: a`, …{256} repeats a fixed prefix to amplify the delay of a lookup loop; ReDoS, batching, recursive XML entities and hashtable collisions all amplify too ("a DoS attack is just a really easy timing attack").
  3. FIND HIDDEN PARAMETERS/HEADERS THAT NEVER CHANGE THE BODY: `commonconfig: x` returned in 55 ms where `foo: x` took 50 ms, and `commonconfig: {}` returned in 50 ms — a header that costs time unless the value is valid JSON. A connection-resetting server still leaked one header (`authorization: x` took 50 ms vs `foo: x` 30 ms before the reset). Most useful of all: `GET /?id=random` 310 ms vs `GET /?foo=random` 22 ms proves `id` is in the CACHE KEY (parameter-based cache-poisoning exposure) and, because that is configured site-wide, the parameter also applies to other pages.
  4. DETECT SCOPED SSRF (the paper's biggest breakthrough): if the app routes by `Host` but only to its own hosts, OAST never fires. Ask "did the server try to connect to that hostname?" with timing instead: `foo.example.com` -> 404 in 25 ms vs `foo.bar.com` -> 403 in 20 ms shows validation; the PROOF is the DNS-cache pair — `abc.example.com` twice, 25 ms then 20 ms (the second is faster because the first resolution was cached) — and where failed resolutions are not cached, use an over-long DNS label so the client refuses before querying: `aaa{62}.example.com` 25 ms vs `aaa{63}.example.com` 20 ms. Validated on the corpus: 375 vulnerable domains, 206 with a DNS pingback, 217 visibly cached.
  5. USE THE SAME ORACLE ON IP-SPOOFING HEADERS: `True-Client-IP: xyz.example.com` produces a delay (in-band DNS lookup) and hits the resolver cache on the repeat; ~170 of the 375 did not ping back — one target answered `Random-header: x.psres.net` in 170 ms and `True-Client-IP: 1.1.1.1` in 170 ms, but `True-Client-IP: x.psres.net` in 90 ms, and the site's login history then recorded the spoofed `1.1.1.1` (Cloudflare) as the client IP: an INVALID IP raised an exception and short-circuited the slow third-party geo-lookup, which is exactly why the response came back faster. Lesson: exceptions short-cut large code paths, so timing is exceptionally good at detecting them (and at revealing WAF processing: the `exec`-looking delay turned out to be a WAF, whose stacking behaviour was then turned into a full WAF bypass, now implemented in `nowafpls`).
  6. BLIND SERVER-SIDE PARAMETER POLLUTION AND BLIND INJECTION: pair a reserved URI character against a non-reserved one — `/path?objectId=57%23` returned in 180 ms where `/path?objectId=57%21` took 430 ms (the encoded `#` either broke a server-side path into a fast static response or made the app's HTTP client refuse to send it) — and "it's crucial not to assume which way around the delay will land". 50 request pairs per probe, report when the response order is ≥80 % biased to one payload. A blind SQLi was found this way with `mic='` vs `mic=''` (162 ms vs 170 ms) but it was a duplicate and the lesson is stated: for SQLi/command/code injection timing only matters where a WAF blocks the classic detection; timing comes into its own for the "injection underclass" (JSON/XML/CSV/server-side query params/headers).
  7. TURN A DETECTED REVERSE PROXY INTO ACCESS: once a proxy is proven, compile target hostnames (generic wordlist + Project Sonar `fdns` — reversed, sorted, searched with `look` — + columbus.elmasy.com), then request each hostname twice, directly and through the proxy, and diff status / header names / `Location`. Outcomes: (a) FIREWALL BYPASS — `sonarqube.redacted.com` resets from outside, but `app.redacted.com` with `Host: sonarqube.redacted.com` returns 200 (and the invisible-route variant finds internal-only pre-prod/staging systems and admin consoles); (b) FRONT-END RULE BYPASS — reach endpoints the edge blocks/rewrites; (c) FRONT-END IMPERSONATION — the back-end trusts headers the front-end normally overwrites (`X-Forwarded-For`, custom auth headers; the author fully compromised New Relic's core internal API via a header called `Service-Gateway-Is-Newrelic-Admin`), which a misconfigured proxy lets you send directly.
  8. CHAIN UP: because a reverse proxy lets you choose the back-end, taking over a subdomain of the target and pointing its DNS at an arbitrary IP upgrades a SCOPED SSRF into a full SSRF (analogous to SSRF + open redirect). Param Miner's scans: 'Detect scoped SSRF' -> 'Exploit scoped SSRF' -> 'Guess headers' on each alternate route.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a `Host`-routed front-end that answers differently (403 vs 404) for non-owned vs owned domains — the tell that a scoped proxy may exist; a second identical request to the same hostname coming back faster (DNS cache) or a faster/ slower response to a 63-octet DNS label; a header whose presence costs milliseconds without changing the response; a parameter that changes response time while the body stays identical (cache-key tell); an edge that overwrites `X-Forwarded-*`/custom auth headers (the only defence against front-end impersonation) — a difference in that overwriting between routes is the bug.
CHAIN: a question the response body cannot answer (primitive: "did the server resolve/connect to that hostname?") -> answer it with the single-packet/bottom-quartile timing oracle via DNS-cache or over-long-label differentials (primitive: scoped SSRF proven with no OAST interaction) -> enumerate the proxy's reachable hosts and diff direct vs proxied responses (escalation 1: firewall bypass / hidden internal routes — the author reached an internal SonarQube and pre-launch admin consoles) -> send the back-end the headers the front-end normally overwrites (escalation 2: front-end impersonation = authentication/authorisation bypass against an internal API, demonstrated as full compromise of New Relic's core internal API) -> and where a target subdomain can be taken over, point DNS at an arbitrary IP to upgrade scoped SSRF to full SSRF (escalation 3: internal services -> credentials -> RCE). Timing evidence alone is chain material; the internal route plus the impersonated header is the finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target, (1) build the single-packet pair (headers + body-minus-last-byte, 100 ms ping, final frames) and compare response ORDER, 30 samples per variant, bottom quartile; (2) ask the Host-header question — send `Host: <random>.<target domain>` twice and a 63-octet-label variant, and treat "second request faster" / "63-octet label faster" as proof the server resolved it: that is scoped SSRF; (3) if proven, request every known hostname directly and through the proxy and diff status/headers/`Location`; (4) on each alternate route, replay the front-end's own trust headers (`X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, `True-Client-IP`, and any `Service-Gateway-Is-*`/custom auth header you find by guessing) to become the front-end. Rule: **the response body is not the only output — with the single-packet attack and bottom-quartile sampling a sub-millisecond differential is measurable, and a DNS-cache or over-long-label differential turns "did you connect to that hostname?" into a yes/no answer, which is how a scoped SSRF (invisible to OAST) is proven and how the proxy is then used to bypass firewalls, reach hidden internal routes and impersonate the front-end.**
DEDUPE: `scoped SSRF`/`Scoped SSRF` 0, `front-end impersonation` 0, `True-Client-IP` 0, `64-octet`/`64 octet` 0, `DNS caching` 0, `nowafpls` 0, `bottom quartile` 0, `h2spacex` 0, `timing attack` 0 hits across all three write targets; `Param Miner` hits (2/2/2) are tool references, not this method; `t-test` hits (3/2/8) are statistical/other-topic mentions. Pre-existing hits that ARE related material and were therefore NOT re-recorded as new: `timing oracle` hits are the generic blind-SQLi oracle, a format-string `%<N>c` oracle (§17.206) and honest-reporting advice — the timing SIDE CHANNEL as a discovery engine is not recorded anywhere; `single-packet` hits (A 7 / B 6 / C 7) are the race-condition/smuggling material (the attack as a prerequisite of this technique, not the timing application); `Timeless` hits are the HEIST-derived cross-site search material; `reverse proxy` hits are request smuggling, the GlobalProtect Nginx path and recon templates — none is the scoped-SSRF proxy-as-route method; `vhost` hits are smuggling/vhost-bypass and the nginx mTLS session-ticket entry, not "bruteforce vs proxy enumeration".

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/fickle-pdfs-exploiting-browser-rendering-discrepancies  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b74-src5.txt`, 9,236 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈5.5k). Published Tuesday, 9 July 2024 at 12:51 UTC, updated Monday, 15 July 2024 at 09:02 UTC (Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin; inspired by Konstantin Weddige's "Kobold Letters"); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the CONSTRUCTED FILE and the PDF source are in the linked repo (`github.com/PortSwigger/research-labs/tree/main/pdf-rendering-discrepancies`); the java snippet quoted below is the pseudo-code printed in the post. The screenshots are images; the ChatGPT transcription is quoted as text.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no PDF was built with pdfbox and no browser/LLM was exercised this pass; the rendering behaviour per viewer is the author's own.
CLASS: PARSER/RENDERER DISCREPANCY IN A DOCUMENT WORKFLOW with MONETARY IMPACT (business-logic / approval-bypass class) — the same file shows different values to different readers, so the human who approves, the system that pays, and any AI assistant that ingests it each act on a different number.
CORE METHOD:
  1. BUILD A HYBRID PDF: one interactive text field whose plain/default value is the string the "safe" viewer shows, plus a WIDGET ANNOTATION whose appearance stream draws a DIFFERENT string (`PDDocument` + `PDAcroForm` + `PDTextField.setValue("£399")`, then a `PDFormXObject` appearance stream whose `appearanceContents.showText("£999")` — the post notes `PDTextField#setValue` would normally update the appearance unless `PDAcroForm.getNeedAppearances()` is true, so the custom annotation is what carries the second value). Manual PDF editing achieves the same; an annotation "can contain any text and theoretically, nothing prevents you from overwriting the entire page".
  2. KNOW WHICH PARSER SHOWS WHICH VALUE: Chrome (PDFium) supports form fields AND annotations and "dynamically updates the displayed text from the annotation value to the form field's default value upon user interaction" (so it can flip value mid-review); Firefox (PDF.js) and Google Drive's preview prioritise the annotation and ignore the default; Safari's engine and macOS Preview render the FIELD value only, ignoring annotations; ChatGPT "doesn't support annotations" and reports the field value.
  3. THE WORKED SCENARIO (quoted): a CEO opens an invoice PDF, "in Safari and MacOS Preview, the total price displayed is £399. After approval, the invoice is sent to the accounting department, which operates on Windows OS. However, when the same PDF file is opened in Google Chrome or Google Drive, the price changes to £999" — and the LLM transcription of the same file reports `Unit Price: £399 / Total: £399`.
  4. GENERALISE THE PRIMITIVE: whenever two stages of a workflow read a document through different parsers (approver's viewer vs payer/OCR/extraction pipeline vs AI assistant vs e-mail client preview), the file is a place to hide a value; the same shape applies to any rich document format with redundant/overriding representations (annotations, comments, alt text, metadata, layers, hidden text).
  5. DEFENCE STATED: treat PDFs as untrusted input in payment and AI-ingestion workflows (the author's closing advice to accounting departments and to anyone granting a chat assistant access to a mailbox).
DETECTION SIGNAL: a workflow where a document is rendered by one system and its VALUE extracted by another (approval + payment, e-mail preview + OCR, upload + AI summarisation); a PDF with form fields plus widget annotations, or any duplicate/overriding representation of a displayed value; a discrepancy between what a screenshot shows and what the text extraction returns.
CHAIN: an attacker who can submit a document into an approval/payment workflow (primitive: a file the victim opens, no exploit code required) -> the file's default field value and its widget annotation disagree, and the renderer decides which one a given reader sees (primitive: two parsers, two numbers) -> the approver sees the low amount while the system that pays, or the AI that summarises the invoice, uses the other one = invoice manipulation / payment fraud with monetary impact (P2 where the workflow is real); the same differential is an AI-review bypass where a reviewer model ignores the annotation. The differential alone is chain material; the paid invoice is the impact.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target that accepts documents (invoices, receipts, tickets, KYC evidence), submit a file with two disagreeing representations of one value (form field default vs annotation appearance stream via pdfbox, or doubled/overriding text layers) and record what each reader returns — the approver's browser, the e-mail/Drive preview, the OCR/extraction service, and any AI assistant that the workflow feeds it to; a workflow that pays or provisions on the extracted value while the human approves the rendered one is the finding. Rule: **a document is not a value, it is a set of parsers — build the file so the field default and the widget annotation disagree, and you choose which reader sees which number; the same trick hides a value from an AI reviewer that ignores annotations.**

HONESTY: this is the CHEAT SHEET'S ANNOUNCEMENT post — an inventory of generated payload classes with worked example values, not a case study; several wordlist tables are images and did not survive stripping, so only the payloads printed as text are reproduced. Its classes overlap the DELTA already recorded from the later update post (batch 73, §17.250) — the genuinely new atoms are listed in DEDUPE and this entry is a DELTA, not a re-record.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no validator/client pair was exercised this pass; the notation arithmetic below is checked by hand, the behaviour claims are the authors'.
CLASS: SSRF / CORS-ALLOW-LIST / OPEN-REDIRECT FILTER BYPASS — the generated payload families are chain-first-link primitives whose impact is internal-service/cloud-metadata access or authenticated cross-origin read.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THREE CONTEXTS, ONE WORDLIST ENGINE: a fully qualified absolute URL (for a URL used in a query parameter; Burp-Intruder-friendly, i.e. pre-encoded), hostname only (for a `Host` header), and a CORS `Origin` — the same bypass families are applied to whichever string the target validates.
  2. PAYLOAD FAMILIES the tool generates: "Domain Allow List Bypass" (domain-confusion payloads built from an allowed domain plus an attacker domain), "Fake Relative URLs" (absolute URLs a browser accepts but client-side validation mis-parses) and "Loopback Address" (IP representations and their normalisations).
  3. IPv4/IPv6 NOTATION SET TO RETRY FOREVERY INTERNAL HOST (defaults computed for 127.0.0.1): octal, each segment padded to 4 digits — `0177.0000.0000.0001`; hexadecimal, each segment `0x`-prefixed and padded to 2 digits — `0x7F.0x00.0x00.0x01`; binary, each segment as 8 bits — `01111111.00000000.00000000.00000001`; Partial Decimal — `127.0.1`; DWORD — `2130706433`; **DWORD with overflow — the DWORD plus `2^32 * 10` = `45080379393`**; and the IPv6-mapped form — `[::FFFF:7F00:0001]` ≡ `::FFFF:127.0.0.1`. Rationale: an address is one 32-bit integer, so a resolver/parser can accept a value no "is this an IP" check would.
  4. STRING-ENCODING LAYERS aimed at the VALIDATOR rather than the resolver: Intruder's percent-encoding, "Everything" (percent-encode all non-alphanumerics), a "Special Chars" set that leaves `!$'()*,-./\:;[]^_{|}~` unencoded, and Unicode escapes written as six-character `\uXXXX` for everything outside `['"','\\','\b','\f','\n','\r','\t']` and `[0x0020-0x007f]`.
  5. NORMALISATION PAYLOADS — characters that normalise to the EMPTY STRING and therefore disappear from whatever the validator sees (named in the post): ZeroWidthSpace and the NegativeVeryThin/NegativeThin/NegativeMedium/NegativeThick spaces, the Word Joiner (U+2060), and the Soft Hyphen (U+00AD) — "These techniques can be used to bypass Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)".
  6. MULTILINE-REGEX BYPASS for an allow-list written as `^allowed_domain$`: if the regex engine treats a UNICODE LINE SEPARATOR as a line break, `attacker_domain(U+2028)allowed_domain` (Line Separator) or `attacker_domain(U+2029)allowed_domain` (Paragraph Separator) matches while the resolved host is the attacker's.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an SSRF/redirect/allow-list check that string-matches rather than resolves (a literal `127.0.0.1`/`169.254.169.254`/domain denylist, a `^allowed$` regex, a `startswith`); a validator that fails differently for a value whose characters have been altered but which resolves identically; a domain check that is bypassed by invisible characters; a CORS origin check that matches a substring/pattern rather than the exact origin.
CHAIN: a URL or origin that must pass a check before the server/client fetches or trusts it (primitive: the filter is the only gate) -> re-express the same target so the check and the resolver disagree — an equivalent IP notation (padded octal/hex/binary segments, partial decimal, DWORD, DWORD-with-overflow `45080379393`, IPv6-mapped), invisible characters or a U+2028/U+2029 line break inside the checked string (escalation: the validated string and the used string are no longer the same) -> the request lands on loopback/link-local/cloud metadata (SSRF -> cloud credentials -> RCE) or an attacker origin is trusted (CORS read of authenticated data -> BAC/ATO). A notation bypass alone is a lead.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every URL/SSRF parameter and every origin/domain allow-list, replay the SAME internal target in the whole notation set (`0177.0000.0000.0001`, `0x7F.0x00.0x00.0x01`, the binary form, `127.0.1`, `2130706433`, `45080379393`, `[::FFFF:7F00:0001]`), then with invisible characters embedded (U+200B/U+200C/U+2060/U+00AD) and with `attacker<U+2028>allowed` for any `^allowed$` check. Rule: **an IP is a 32-bit integer and a checked domain is a string — generate every equivalent notation of the internal address (including the DWORD plus 2^32*10, which no "looks like an IP" test rejects) and every codepoint that normalises to nothing or to a line break, and re-send until one form passes the check that the resolver ignores.**
DEDUPE: `DWORD` 0, `45080379393` 0, `0177.0000` 0, `0x7F.0x00` 0, `url-cheatsheet-data` 0, `Fake Relative URL` 0, `Domain Allow List` 0, `ZeroWidth`/`zero width` 0, `soft hyphen`/`Soft Hyphen` 0, `Line Separator` 0, `IPv4 representation` 0, `binary notation` 0 hits across all three write targets. Pre-existing hits that ARE related material and were therefore NOT re-recorded as new: batch 73's batch-74-predecessor entry (§17.250) already records the LATER update post's partial-decimal Class A/B, per-segment mixed RADIX, digit-normalisation (circled/fullwidth/seven-segment) and the `[`-in-userinfo Spring discrepancy — this entry's NEW atoms are the PADDED-4-DIGIT OCTAL / 2-DIGIT-HEX / 8-BIT-BINARY per-segment forms, the PLAIN DWORD and above all **DWORD WITH OVERFLOW (`2130706433 + 2^32*10 = 45080379393`, which keeps the resolved value while defeating both a literal-DWORD blocklist and an "integer < 2^32" check)**, the empty-string normalisation codepoints (U+200B family, U+2060, U+00AD) and the **U+2028/U+2029 multiline-`^allowed$` bypass**; `2130706433` (A 5 / B 2 / C 5) is the already-recorded generic decimal IPv4 in the SSRF ladder; `U+2028`/`U+2029` (A 3 / C 2) are the Kibana prototype-pollution RCE gadget (a JS line terminator in generated source) and a tag-name XSS entry — neither is a REGEX line-anchor bypass; `Paragraph Separator` hits are the same XSS entry; `::FFFF:7F00` (A 1 / C 2) is the SSRF ladder's `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`; `url validation bypass cheat sheet` (A 2 / B 2 / C 1) is the batch-73 records of the update post.
