SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/new-exotic-events-in-the-xss-cheat-sheet  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b75-src1.txt`, 6,584 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈1.5k). Published Tuesday, 11 June 2024 at 14:58 UTC, updated Tuesday, 11 June 2024 at 14:58 UTC (Gareth Heyes @garethheyes, Researcher; contributions credited to @amirmsafari, @Wcraft-log, @Filipnyquist, @RenwaX23, @lbherrera_, @zhenwarx and Mozilla); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: this is a SHORT cheat-sheet UPDATE post — a handler/payload inventory with one line of context per item, not a case study; every payload string below was read as TEXT in the page (the post only uses Ray.so for syntax-highlighted images of the same strings), and the interaction requirements are the contributors' statements as printed. DELTA, not a re-record: the `autofocus` + `onfocus` zero-interaction family is already all over this ledger; the new atoms are the three unlisted handler families and the Safari media event.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no browser was exercised to confirm which handler fires in which engine this pass.
CLASS: XSS — an EVENT-HANDLER DICTIONARY for a filter/WAF that blacklists the common handlers (`onerror`/`onload`/`onfocus`) and for the "requires user interaction" severity downgrade.
CORE METHOD:
  1. WHEN THE COMMON HANDLERS ARE BLOCKED, ROTATE THE EXOTIC SET (all printed as text in the post): `<xss onpointercancel=alert(1)>XSS</xss>`; `<xss onwebkitmouseforceup=alert(1)>XSS</xss>`; `<xss onwebkitmouseforcewillbegin=alert(1)>XSS</xss>`; `<xss onwebkitmouseforcedown=alert(1)>XSS</xss>`; `<xss onwebkitmouseforcechanged=alert(1)>XSS</xss>`.
  2. THE ONE THAT FIRES WITHOUT A GESTURE: `onwebkitplaybacktargetavailabilitychanged` on `<audio>`/`<video>` — described in the post as "a wonderfully obscure Safari only vector that used the event `onwebkitplaybacktargetavailabilitychanged` from @amirmsafari that works on audio and video tags" (Safari/WebKit only).
  3. THE ZERO-INTERACTION TRIGGER (already recorded here, restated by this update): `autofocus` works on "pretty much every element", not just form fields — `<xss onfocus=alert(1) autofocus tabindex=1>` (credited @RenwaX23 and @lbherrera_, submitted by @Filipnyquist).
  4. FORGET THE MARQUEE: Mozilla contributed the removal of events that "no longer work with the marquee tag on Firefox" — do not carry old `onstart`/`onbounce`/`onfinish` payloads into a Firefox-heavy target.
  5. INTERACTION COST IS THE SEVERITY: `onpointercancel` "requires heavy user interaction"; the `onwebkitmouseforce*` family needs trackpad pressure; only the media event and the autofocus path avoid the downgrade.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an injection point that strips/encodes `onerror=` but passes an unknown `on<word>=` attribute; a payload that fails only because the blocked handler never fires; a WebKit/Safari-rendering target (or one whose renderer you cannot pin down) where a media element can be injected; an event attribute surviving a sanitizer that only knows the famous handlers.
CHAIN: a reflected or stored injection point (primitive) -> the common handlers are neutralised by a blacklist (primitive) -> an unlisted handler fires anyway, and with `autofocus` on any element, or `onwebkitplaybacktargetavailabilitychanged` on an injected `<video>`, it fires with ZERO user interaction (escalation) -> script in the victim's origin without a click = session/token theft (ATO chain). The handler atoms are chain material; the interaction-free ones are what stop a real XSS from being written down as "requires user interaction".
TRANSFERABLE TEST: at the next injection point whose `onerror`/`onload` is filtered, replay exactly this update's set — `onpointercancel`, `onwebkitmouseforceup`, `onwebkitmouseforcewillbegin`, `onwebkitmouseforcedown`, `onwebkitmouseforcechanged`, and `onwebkitplaybacktargetavailabilitychanged` on a `<video>` — and in parallel retry `<x onfocus=<payload> autofocus tabindex=1>` on any element. Rule: **a handler blacklist is a stale list; an unlisted handler plus `autofocus` on any element is a zero-interaction XSS, and only the autofocus path and the Safari media event escape the "user interaction required" downgrade.**
DEDUPE: `onwebkitplaybacktargetavailabilitychanged` 0, `onpointercancel` 0, `onwebkitmouseforce` 0 hits across all three write targets. Pre-existing related material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded as new: `autofocus` (A 20 / B 20 / C 25) and `onfocus` (A 36 / B 36 / C 35) are the already-recorded attribute-injection and focus-chaining XSS family, including the explicit statement that "any element can be made focusable with `tabindex` (plus `autofocus`)", so only the three new handler families are admitted here; `oncontentvisibilityautostatechange` (A 1 / B 1 / C 1) is the §17.248 delivery atom and the nearest existing "unlisted event handler beats a WAF" precedent, which is exactly why this source's slot (§17.257) is written as a DELTA over it rather than as a new general method.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/introducing-signsaboteur-forge-signed-web-tokens-with-ease  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b75-src3.txt`, 13,759 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈8.5k). Published Wednesday, 22 May 2024 at 12:37 UTC, updated Tuesday, 4 June 2024 at 07:25 UTC (Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin; the tool is the open-source Burp BApp `SignSaboteur`, with a self-hosted lab in the linked GitHub repo); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: the methodology, the attack lists and the brute-force strategies are printed as text and are quoted below; the demo is a GIF (image) and is not reproduced; the post's own attack references (Apache Airflow CVE-2020-17526, "Baking Flask cookies with your secrets", Redash default config, an RCE on a Facebook server, the PortSwigger OIDC labs) are named, not re-read.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — the tool was not installed and no signed token was brute-forced or re-signed this pass.
CLASS: JWT / SIGNED-SESSION FORGERY -> AUTHENTICATION BYPASS + PRIVILEGE ESCALATION, with an OIDC-claim side channel (server-side fetch = SSRF) and an identity-provider token-forgery variant.
CORE METHOD:
  1. FIND THE TOKENS: "Observe request/response cookie, url, body parameters for potential signed tokens: base64 encoded or hex strings of known length common for HMAC"; if a token contains a timestamp, "observe whether the signature changes when the token expires" (that tells you what is inside and when it rotates).
  2. FINGERPRINT THE FRAMEWORK, THEN ITS SECRETS: identify the stack (the tool ships support for Django, Flask, Express, plus generic "unknown signed web tokens"), then "search for common secret keys and salts, for example hardcoded values or configuration files, including docker environment variables" — the post's own discovery list is source code, configuration files, documentation pages and error messages.
  3. BRUTE FORCE WITH THE RIGHT DERIVATION, not raw guessing — the tool's ladder is the method: `Known keys` (secrets already found), `Fast` (default hashing + key derivation only), `Balanced` (all derivations except slow PBKDF2-HMAC with big iteration counts), `Deep` (all, "including different types supported by Ruby on Rails framework"). Extend the wordlist with everything from step 2; JSON-encoded wordlists are supported so non-ASCII secrets can be included.
  4. TEST ACCEPTANCE BEFORE YOU OWN THE KEY: "If you couldn't find the secret key, try to re-sign a message with a default key and send it to the application. If the server accepts your forged message that means that a vulnerability exists." A default/hardcoded key is a finding without ever learning the deployment's real secret.
  5. ONCE YOU CAN SIGN, FORGE PRIVILEGE: "If the token structure is known, change id to high privilege account, usually 1"; "If the token structure is unknown, brute force parameters names with a commonly used list: id, user_id, username, etc."; then "visit all pages with a new token and also try to get access to administrative functionality."
  6. THE OIDC LAYER (the escalation most testers skip) — with the key, mint tokens carrying OpenID Connect Standard Claims: the `user claims` attack "tries to inject a collaborator payload for different potential SSRF vulnerable claims, like the user's picture" (the claim VALUE is dereferenced by the server/IdP, so claims are SSRF surface); wrapped user claims inject into the `user` JSON attribute; `username`/`password` claims generate an admin placeholder; Flask claims use `id`/`_id`/`user_id`/`_user_id`; Express claims use the `passport` attribute; account-wrapper and "authenticated" flags are covered too; and `User access_token` "generates JWT OpenID connect ID token signed with the same key and same hashing algorithm without any key derivation performed" — a forged IdP access token.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a cookie/URL/body value that is base64 or hex of HMAC length; a signature that changes when the token's timestamp rolls; a framework fingerprint (Django/Flask/Express/Rails) with a small, default or config-file secret ("docker environment variables" is the post's own hint); a decoded token whose inner JSON has an obvious privilege or identity field (`id`, `user_id`, `role`, `passport`, `_user_id`); a claim value the server fetches (avatar/`picture` URL).
CHAIN: a signed session/bearer token you can read but not yet forge (primitive) -> framework fingerprint plus a config/source/docker-env secret, or a default key the server accepts after a re-sign (primitive: the signing key is recoverable) -> forge the same token with `id`/`user_id` aimed at the privileged user (escalation 1: authentication bypass to admin functionality; the post cites Apache Airflow CVE-2020-17526, Flask-cookie forging, Redash default config and an RCE on a Facebook server as precedents) -> mint a same-key OIDC `access_token`/ID token for the identity provider and put a Collaborator URL in the `picture` claim to make the trusted component fetch it (escalation 2: authenticated SSRF from inside the IdP trust boundary, and full impersonation at the IdP). Key discovery alone is chain material.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target that carries a signed token, (1) fingerprint the stack and try its documented default/hardcoded secrets with the framework's OWN derivation (Fast -> Balanced -> Deep, including Rails/PBKDF2 variants), (2) the moment you have any key candidate, RE-SIGN YOUR OWN token and send it — acceptance is the finding, (3) set the identity claim to `1`/`admin` (brute the claim name from the usual list if the structure is opaque), (4) then mint a same-key OIDC token and put a Collaborator URL in `picture` (and the wrapped `user` attribute) to test for claim-driven SSRF. Rule: **a signed token is only as strong as the secret you can guess with the framework's own derivation — re-sign a message with a default key BEFORE you have anything else, and once you can sign, the claim names (`id`, `user_id`, `passport`, `picture`) are the privilege and SSRF surface.**
DEDUPE: `SignSaboteur` 0, `signsaboteur` 0, `PBKDF2` 0, `signed web token` 0, `oidc claim` 0, `picture claim` 0, `claims brute` 0, `default secret` 0, `flask-unsign` 0, `django-shares` 0 hits across all three write targets. Pre-existing related material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded as new: `secret_key_base` (A 8 / C 8) is a Rails secret obtained by FILE READ through a path traversal (the GitLab archive/`SafeMirror`-adjacent family) — a different entry point from guess-the-secret-with-derivation; `re-sign` (A 5 / C 7) and `jwt claim` (A 2 / B 1 / C 3) are the already-recorded `alg:none`/JWKS/`alg`-confusion and IdP-JWKS material; `hardcoded secret` (C 4) is unrelated tool text; `key derivation` (A 1 / B 1) is a passing mention only.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/trace-desync-attack  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 4; full body read with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip (`/root/.hermes/cache/scratch/b75-src4.txt`, 17,897 chars incl. page chrome; body ≈12k). Published Tuesday, 19 March 2024 at 14:00 UTC, updated Wednesday, 19 June 2024 at 13:58 UTC (Martin Doyhenard @PortSwiggerRes); read in full 2026-11-08. HONESTY: every request/response listing cited below is printed as TEXT in the post and is reproduced as such; the exploit diagrams are images and are not reproduced.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no desync victim, proxy or cache was stood up this pass.
CLASS: HTTP DESYNC (request smuggling) -> RESPONSE CONCATENATION / RESPONSE SPLITTING -> WEB CACHE POISONING -> SITE-WIDE STORED XSS, using the TRACE method as the attacker-controlled reflection.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT — the author's case was an HTTP/2 desync reached through a header-value line-break injection: "it was possible to inject a line break character in a header's value, letting me smuggle transfer-encoding header which would eventually split the request at backend." The point of the article is what to do when that is ALL you have: the program's answer was "Being able to smuggle a request is not a vulnerability in itself. How are you able to exploit the smuggling request?", and the app had no reflected parameter, no other bug, and per-user backend connections.
  2. USE TRACE AS THE ORACLE FIRST: the backend answered TRACE. `TRACE / HTTP/1.1` with any header returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: message/http`, and the whole request echoed in the body (including the `X-Forwarded-For` the proxy added) — so TRACE shows "exactly what is being received by the backend": modified/added headers and protocol downgrades (HTTP/2 -> HTTP/1.1, "which is the source of many desync vulnerabilities"). TRACE is default-on in "Apache and many Microsoft IIS and Tomcat versions" and must be disabled explicitly.
  3. RESPONSE CONCATENATION REFRESHER: smuggle a `HEAD` (a headers-only response whose `Content-Length` must equal what the GET body would be, and which a proxy would ignore) so that "as the HEAD message was smuggled and the proxy never noticed this, the content-length will not be ignored, causing a concatenation with the next available response". The post's CL.0 example: `GET / HTTP/1.1` + `Host` + `Content-Length: 108`, then a smuggled `HEAD /`, then `GET /reflect?value=myReflectedString`.
  4. THE TRACE PAYLOAD — swap the reflected GET for a TRACE carrying the script: outbound `GET / HTTP/1.1` + `Host` + `Content-Length: 150`, then smuggled `HEAD /` + `Host`, then smuggled `TRACE /` + `Host` + `SomeHeader: <script>alert("reflected")</script>` + `Other: aaaaaa…` (padding sets the length). The TRACE response body — the reflected header — is glued onto the forwarded response: "The response will be forwarded to the next request that arrives through the same connection, taking control of the browser with a malicious JavaScript!"
  5. BYPASS THE TRACE FIREWALL RULE: proxies commonly forbid TRACE, but "as smuggling can be used to bypass firewall rules, it is possible to hide a TRACE message from the proxy and deliver it directly to the backend. So even if the method is forbidden, exploitation through desynchronization is still possible."
  6. WHEN BACKEND CONNECTIONS ARE PER-USER (why the naive attack dies): the malicious response reaches only you, so escalate with `Web Cache Poisoning` or `Client-Side Desync` — in this case client-side desync was out (HTTP/2 injection was required) and the app "was storing static responses in the cache". The author's own fallback: run the desync, then request a static resource such as `/payload.css` over the same HTTP/2 connection so the evil response is cached for that URL (noting the difficulty of overwriting an existing resource with a max-age).
  7. THE STRONGER FORM — FULL RESPONSE SPLITTING: instead of relying on a static resource, inject a COMPLETE response so the cache stores arbitrary headers and body for a URL you choose: a body-reflecting `POST /reflect` returns padding plus injected CRLFs, `HTTP/1.1 200 Ok\r\n` / `Cache-Control: max-age=1000000\r\n` / `Content-Type: text/html\r\n` / `Content-Length: 44\r\n` / `\r\n` / `<script>alert("arbitrary response")</script>`; the first 78 bytes complete the HEAD and, because the remaining bytes ARE a valid HTTP response, "the message will be forwarded as the response of the next available request" and stored in the cache for that URL. "Finding an endpoint that allows us to reflect any byte sent in the body is extremely rare, but if TRACE requests are permitted, the attack is completely practical."
  8. WHEN TRACE REFUSES A BODY: "depending on the configuration, TRACE requests cannot contain a content-length header bigger than 0" — then build the payload from several responses: "the message length header can be added using a smuggled transfer-encoding or with an extra response which will be appended right after the last header of the TRACE message" (the post's listing writes `A: HTTP/1.1 200 Ok` / `A: Cache-Control: max-age=1000000` as TRACE header values, then a second smuggled `TRACE /` carrying `A: <script>alert("XSS")</script>`). "Some servers like Apache will allow a body If the 'TraceEnabled extended' directive is present, which makes the attack even more simple."
  9. LAST RESORT: store a REDIRECT response in the cache — "to a stored payload (using the cache deception/poisoning technique), or to an attacker's page to launch another attack like client-side desync or classic phishing."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a backend that answers `TRACE` (or answers it when the request is smuggled past an edge rule that blocks it); `Content-Type: message/http`; a desync primitive (HTTP/2 header-value CRLF, CL.0, TE.CL) on an app with NO reflected parameter and NO other bug; per-user backend connections (which force the cache-poisoning variant); a cache front-end that stores responses whose `Cache-Control` came out of a smuggled message.
CHAIN: a desync primitive (primitive: a line break in a header value -> smuggled `Transfer-Encoding`) -> the backend's TRACE reflection gives attacker-controlled bytes inside a `message/http` body with no application endpoint (primitive: reflection of the whole request) -> a smuggled HEAD concatenates that reflection into the response queue, so the script lands in the body of the response the NEXT request on the connection receives (escalation 1: response smuggling, cross-user XSS on a shared connection) -> where connections are per-user, aim the same trick at a cached static resource (escalation 2: web cache poisoning = the script is served to every visitor of that URL) -> or inject a complete response with `Content-Type: text/html` + `Cache-Control: max-age=1000000` + a `<script>` body, or store a redirect (escalation 3: arbitrary-response cache poisoning = site-wide stored XSS; the redirect variant is an open redirect plus a client-side-desync delivery vector). P1 where the poisoned URL is site-wide or the poisoned body is a token-carrying response.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target with any desync primitive, (1) send `TRACE / HTTP/1.1` with a junk header and look for `Content-Type: message/http` with your header echoed (default-on in Apache/many IIS/Tomcat; if the edge blocks it, smuggle it past the rule); (2) build the concatenation — outbound `GET /` with a `Content-Length`, then a smuggled `HEAD /`, then a smuggled `TRACE /` carrying `SomeHeader: <script>alert(1)</script>` and a padding header; (3) confirm whose response carries the script by issuing the next request on that connection (or fetch a static resource over the same connection and check the cache); (4) if TRACE will not take a body, split the payload across an extra smuggled response or exploit Apache's `TraceEnabled extended`. Rule: **TRACE echoes the entire request, so it is both the oracle that shows what the backend really receives and the only reflection an uneventful desync needs — smuggle a HEAD in front of it and the reflected header becomes the body of someone else's response, which the cache will happily store.**
DEDUPE: `response concatenation` 0, `message/http` 0, `TraceEnabled` 0, `cache-control: max-age=1000000` 0 hits across the three write targets. Pre-existing related material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded as new: the recorded `TRACE / HTTP/1.1` hits (A 5 / B 5 / C 5) are desync FUZZ payloads — a smuggled `TRACE` used as a canary to detect a desync (connection-desync / CVE-2026-63078 material) and the "self-replicating desync worm" note — none of them uses the TRACE response BODY as the attacker-controlled script that rides a smuggled HEAD into the response queue; `smuggled HEAD` (A 4 / C 3) and `HEAD /` hits are the existing HEAD technique for response splitting (a form field or a searched-for reflection being the body), and `response splitting` / `client-side desync` / `cache poisoning` hits are the pre-existing desync and cache-deception families; `Varnish` hits are the backend-desync entry, not the TRACE carrier.

Please contact us…"), `r.jina.ai` answered HTTP 403, and the Wayback availability API answered 429 — so the route that WORKED was HackerOne's disclosed-report JSON endpoint: `curl -A "<desktop UA>" -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/301432.json` (HTTP 200, 8,241 bytes, `application/json`), which carries `title`, `severity_rating`, `weakness`, `cve_ids`, dates and the FULL `vulnerability_information` body (4,732 chars). Metadata as served: title "GitLab CI runner can read and poison cache of all other projects", state closed/resolved, severity **critical**, weakness **Path Traversal**, CVE-2017-0918, reporter `jobert`, submitted 2017-12-30, disclosed 2018-04-27. HONESTY: the two `.gitlab-ci.yml` listings and the build-log excerpt below are quoted from that body; this report is NINE YEARS OLD (see the freshness warning in this batch's notes) and is recorded because it was an assigned source that teaches a transferable method, not because it is recent.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no GitLab instance, runner or cache service was stood up; the configs and the download URL behaviour are the report's own text.
CLASS: PATH TRAVERSAL IN A CI/CD CACHE KEY -> CROSS-TENANT CACHE READ + SHARED-CACHE POISONING -> RCE ON OTHER PROJECTS' BUILD RUNNERS.
CORE METHOD:
  1. PREMISE (from the report): "The GitLab CI runner allows users to cache files and directories in between runs. These files are stored in a ZIP file and uploaded to a shared cache instance." The reporter saw uploads to `runners-cache-4-internal.gitlab.com` and `runners-cache-3-internal.gitlab.com` "even for dedicated runners"; the download URL is `http://runners-cache-4-internal.gitlab.com:444/runner/project/5024150/cache`.
  2. READ ANOTHER PROJECT'S CACHE — create a project whose `.gitlab-ci.yml` is exactly: `a:` / `  script:` / `  - ls -lashR` / `  cache:` / `    key: ../1/cache` / `    policy: pull` / `    paths:` / `      - .`. The report's explanation: "By default, the project ID will be prepended to download the cache. But because it's an HTTP request and there's no additional checks on the `key` input, a path traversal vulnerability can be exploited to move up a directory and select the cache from a different project", so the runner "request[s] http://runners-cache-4-internal.gitlab.com:444/runner/gitlab/project/1/cache instead of the project ID of the build".
  3. MAKE THE READ VISIBLE: `paths: - .` extracts the ENTIRE cache ZIP into the working directory ("it (conveniently) allowed me to use `.` as path, extracting all files from the cache into the working directory"), and `ls -lashR` prints it into the build log (the excerpt downloads `cache.zip` from `.../runner/project/13083/ruby-235-with-yarn` and then "Successfully extracted cache"); contents are read with `cat` or captured as build artifacts. Cache keys are weak or absent — "The cache key seems to be guessable pretty easily or even unused when no key is specified, since most will correlate with the step they're executed in."
  4. POISON ANOTHER PROJECT'S CACHE — the same traversal with `policy: push`: `a:` / `  script:` / `  - echo 1 > file-to-poison` / `  cache:` / `    key: ../1/cache` / `    policy: push` / `    paths:` / `      - file-to-poison`. "The attacker has to run a build, which will overwrite the `file-to-poison` file in the cache for project ID 1. Now, when the targeted project starts another CI run, the poisoned cache files will be downloaded and used in the CI run."
  5. AIM THE WRITE AT CODE, NOT DATA: "an attacker could poison `13083/ruby-235-with-yarn`, which would overwrite the Ruby 2.3.5 executable that is being used for GitLab CE CI runs. As you can imagine, someone could enumerate over other projects that use cached executables and overwrite them with their own code."
  6. IMPACT AS STATED: "Depending on the files that are cached, this may allow an attacker to run arbitrary code on a victim's Docker instance running a CI run. This may expose confidential data, inject artifacts in a build pipeline to ship additional code, among other things."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a CI runner whose cache is a SHARED HTTP service rather than per-project object storage; a cache `key`/`policy`/`paths` field a pipeline author controls that is concatenated into a URL or filesystem path with no traversal check (a leading `../` in a cache key is the probe); a build log that prints the cache URL and shows a path that does not contain your own project id; a cache key that is guessable (step name) or omitted; a download URL shaped `.../runner/project/<id>/<key>`; cached EXECUTABLES (interpreters, toolchains) in the shared store.
CHAIN: an attacker-controlled pipeline config that names the cache `key` (primitive: a user-controlled path segment in a server-side URL) -> the runner resolves `.../project/<myId>/cache` after the traversal to ANOTHER project's cache id and downloads it (primitive: cross-tenant read of the cache ZIP, exfiltrated through the build log and artifacts — a multi-tenant data leak on its own) -> the same traversal with `policy: push` writes attacker bytes into that project's cache (escalation: integrity loss on a shared artefact store) -> the victim's next pipeline downloads and uses the poisoned file, and where the poisoned entry is an executable the build already trusts (the report's Ruby 2.3.5 example) the attacker's code runs inside the victim's runner container (final: cross-tenant RCE / supply-chain injection into other teams' builds). P1 as cross-tenant RCE; the read half alone is a cross-tenant sensitive-data leak.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target that runs CI/CD (GitLab, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, CircleCI, or any remote build cache), (1) find a user-supplied cache path/key/namespace that the runner concatenates into a URL or file path, (2) set it to a traversal (`../<otherId>/cache`, `..\..\`) with the pull policy and dump the result (`paths: - .` plus `ls -lashR`), (3) switch to the push policy and overwrite one file, then watch whether another project's next run consumes it, (4) prefer entries the pipeline EXECUTES (interpreters, tool wrappers, build scripts) over plain data. Rule: **a CI cache key is a path and a shared cache is a shared filesystem — traverse out of your own namespace to read, push to write, and aim the write at something the victim's pipeline executes.**
DEDUPE: `runners-cache` 0, `ci cache` 0, `cache.zip` 0 hits across the three write targets. Pre-existing GitLab-CI material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded as new: `.gitlab-ci.yml` as an attacker-controlled CARRIER is already recorded (mirror-triggered pipelines that resolve to the victim's identity and leak `CI_JOB_TOKEN`; the `environment.kubernetes.namespace` injection; artifacts-based XSS) — those are all pipeline-config AUTHORITY bugs, none is the cache-path traversal above; `secret_key_base` entries are Rails secrets harvested by a path traversal in a different service; `artifacts`/`pipeline`/`runner` hits are those entries and generic tool text.

ROUTE: assigned source 6; same SPA problem as source 5, same working route — the disclosed-report JSON endpoint `curl -A "<desktop UA>" -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/3734676.json` (HTTP 200, 11,816 bytes, `application/json`) returns the full `vulnerability_information` body (6,162 chars). Read in full 2026-11-08. Metadata as served: title "Taskcluster web-server OAuth2 authorization codes are reusable and the exchange handler checks the wrong expiry column", state closed/resolved, severity **medium** (program rating; the class is an authentication bypass with a Critical-Site asset impact), weakness **Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay**, reporter `anshuman_bh`, submitted 2026-05-14, disclosed 2026-06-23, no CVE assigned. HONESTY: file/line references, the PoC commands, the Mocha test output and the fix SQL below are quoted from that body; the referenced test patch attachments were not downloaded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — the reporter verified it with a Mocha test against Taskcluster's own source; no instance was brought up this pass.
CLASS: OAUTH2 AUTHORIZATION-CODE REPLAY / BROKEN CODE LIFETIME -> IDENTITY TAKEOVER OF THE ORIGINAL USER -> CI INTEGRITY (privileged scopes).
CORE METHOD:
  1. READ THE TOKEN-EXCHANGE HANDLER FOR TWO THINGS — whether it CONSUMES the code, and WHICH expiry field it checks. Both failed in the same handler (`services/web-server/src/servers/oauth2.js`, lines 165-199): "The exchange handler validates `redirect_uri` and code existence, mints a bridge access token, and returns — it never deletes or otherwise consumes the `authorization_codes` row" (against RFC 6749 §4.1.2: "The client MUST NOT use the authorization code more than once…"), and "The expiry check at line 66 reads `entry.client_details.expires`, which is the requested lifetime of the resulting Taskcluster credentials (capped by the registered OAuth client's `maxExpires`, e.g. `"1 year"` in the test config). The authorization-code row's intended 10-minute lifetime (`entry.expires`, set at line 33 to `taskcluster.fromNow('10 minutes')`) is never checked at exchange time."
  2. THE BUG IS A FIELD-NAME COLLISION: an `expires` exists on the authorization-code row AND on the client details the row carries, and the handler reads the longer one, so "Expired codes remain usable until the daily `cleanup-expire-auth-codes` cron deletes them" (`services/web-server/procs.yml:20-24`) — a window of hours instead of ten minutes.
  3. THE SAME MISTAKE REPEATS ONE HANDLER ALONG — check the whole chain, not just the exchange: "The same expiry-column mismatch repeats in the bridge-token-to-credentials handler at `oauth2.js:318-375` (`/login/oauth/credentials`), which checks `entry.client_details.expires` rather than the access-token row's `entry.expires`."
  4. THE REPLAY TEST (the reporter's Mocha case `TC-002`, run against unmodified source at commit `246cb765672da1fdc1b7e6901002725bf0e50090`, `yarn mocha --grep "TC-002" test/third_party_test.js` → `✔ TC-002 (PoC): authorization code is reusable in violation of RFC 6749 §4.1.2`, "1 passing"): (1) authorize a code through `GET /login/oauth/authorize` with a registered client (here `test-code-whitelisted`); (2) exchange it through `POST /login/oauth/token` — assert 200, take token A; (3) REPLAY the same code through `POST /login/oauth/token` — assert 200 again, token B, and `token A != token B`; (4) `GET /login/oauth/credentials` with `Authorization: Bearer <token B>` — assert 200 and a credential with `clientId` + `accessToken` in the ORIGINAL user's identity.
  5. THE PRECONDITION IS AN ORDINARY LEAK: "a captured authorization code (referer in narrow conditions, redirect-page logs, TLS-inspecting proxy, browser-history access on the redirect page)" — exactly the material that is normally dismissed as a P4/P5 information disclosure becomes a durable key because the code neither expires nor dies.
  6. BOUNDS AND SCOPE OF THE FORGE: replay is bounded by (a) `client_details.expires` (the OAuth client's `maxExpires`, "up to 1 year" in the report) and (b) the daily cleanup cron, so "the window extends to many hours past the intended 10-minute code lifetime"; the minted credential is "in the original user's `identity`, `identity_provider_id`, and consented scope set", and on `firefox-ci-tc.services.mozilla.com` those are "the user's Firefox-CI scopes, which directly impacts the Firefox build CI integrity boundary" (the reported asset was a Critical Site, and a `mozilla-employee` role is privileged — "a meaningful integrity exposure").
  7. THE FIX IS THE DIFFERENTIAL TO TEST FOR: consume the code atomically — a single statement deleting the row only `WHERE code = code_in AND client_id = client_id_in AND redirect_uri = redirect_uri_in AND expires > now() RETURNING code, client_id, redirect_uri, identity, identity_provider_id, expires, client_details` — and use the returned row as the ONLY gate for minting; apply the same correction to `/login/oauth/credentials` by checking the access-token row's top-level `entry.expires`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an OAuth2/OIDC token endpoint that mints a token without a consuming DELETE/UPDATE of the code row; an `authorization_codes`-style table with an `expires`/`expiry` column that is never read at exchange time; a `cleanup-*-auth-codes` cron standing in for a real expiry check; a code lifetime that outlives the documented window (exchange a code, wait past the documented lifetime — or past the `maxExpires` the client asks for — and exchange it again); a field-name collision where the client's requested credential lifetime is visible to the handler (`client_details.expires` vs the row's own expiry); a second handler in the same file that validates a DIFFERENT row's expiry.
CHAIN: any leak of one authorization code — Referer, redirect-page logs, a TLS-inspecting proxy, browser history on the redirect page (primitive: a raw code string, otherwise a P4/P5 disclosure) -> the exchange handler neither consumes nor expires the code (primitive: the code is a durable bearer secret valid for hours) -> replay `POST /login/oauth/token` repeatedly, each replay minting a FRESH bridge access token in the victim's identity (escalation 1: token minting long past the intended window, undetectable to the victim) -> `GET /login/oauth/credentials` converts any of those bridge tokens into the victim's real credentials (escalation 2: full identity takeover inside the OAuth provider) -> those credentials carry the victim's scopes, here Firefox-CI roles, so the attacker acts inside the CI trust boundary (final: CI/build-integrity compromise, i.e. supply-chain impact). The leaked code alone is chain material; the durable, replayable code is the finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on the next target running an authorize+token OAuth2/OIDC flow, (1) obtain one code and exchange it once; (2) exchange the SAME code a second time and diff the tokens — two HTTP 200s with different tokens is the RFC 6749 §4.1.2 violation; (3) hold a code past the documented lifetime and exchange it — success proves the expiry check reads the wrong field; (4) read every handler that mints a token or a credential and confirm WHICH row's expiry it checks (a `client_details`-style nested object is the tell); (5) walk the rest of the chain (`/login/oauth/credentials`, bridge/exchange endpoints) and confirm the resulting credentials belong to the original identity. Rule: **an authorization code must die on first use and on its own clock — replay it; if the handler checks a DIFFERENT row's `expires` (the client's requested credential lifetime, which is longer by design), a leaked code becomes a durable key in the victim's identity.**

CLASS: A URL-VALUED PARAMETER THAT ACCEPTS THE `javascript:` SCHEME AND REFLECTS IT INTO THE PAGE BODY — REFLECTED XSS ON AN INTERNAL SSO/OIDC PROMPT PAGE, MASS-REPRODUCED ACROSS EVERY SUBDOMAIN SHARING THE SAME LIBRARY.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT via directory brute-force: the logout page `https://carbon-prototype.uberinternal.com:443/oidauth/logout` redirected to `https://carbon-prototype.uberinternal.com/oidauth/prompt?base=https%3A%2F%2Fcarbon-prototype.uberinternal.com%3A443%2Foidauth&return_to=%2F%3Fopenid_c%3D1542156766.5%2FSnNQg%3D%3D&splash_disabled=1` — "the `base` parameter is taking a URL".

INTERACTION-BYPASS: the team summary records that "these pages were affected by a clickjacking vulnerability that made exploitation easier, since a click was required to trigger the XSS" — the prompt page lacks X-Frame-Options, so the one required click is clickjackable and the "requires interaction" downgrade disappears.

Medium as rated for one host; P2/P1 as an internal-SSO session compromise.

Rule: **a parameter that expects a URL will accept `javascript:` unless the scheme is explicitly checked; a body reflection on an SSO helper page is XSS with session access, and the same library on 20 subdomains turns one payload into an estate-wide one.**

NOT re-recorded as new: `javascript:` scheme acceptance by a redirect/dest parameter is ALREADY recorded (the "authorization-related sink accepts a `javascript:` SCHEME because the value is validated as a host/prefix" entry, §17.83 material) — so this entry admits only the DELTA atoms: the BODY reflection on an SSO/OIDC prompt page, the SAML-library fingerprint → one-payload-mass-replay method, and clickjacking as the interaction-bypass. §17 slot 17.262 is written as a DELTA.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/298176  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; read in full via the report JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/298176.json` (HTTP 200, 8,697 bytes, `application/json`, `vulnerability_information` 5,192 chars). Metadata as served: severity **critical**, weakness `SQL Injection`, CVE-2017-0914, bounty $2,000, reporter `jobert`, submitted 2017-12-15, disclosed 2018-04-27. FRESHNESS: 2017 and patched (CVE-2017-0914) — only the METHOD transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no GitLab instance was stood up; the Ruby snippets, the payload and both request/response pairs are quoted from the report body.
CLASS: SQLi IN A FRAMEWORK'S ORDER-BY REBUILD (`reorder(params[:order])`) — BLIND READ VIA AN ORDER-FLIP ORACLE (GitLab `MilestonesFinder#order`).
CORE METHOD:
  1. Read the finder chain: `Groups::MilestonesController#index` → `MilestonesFinder.new(params.merge(group_ids: group.id)).execute`; `execute` ends with `order(items)`, and `order` is `if params.has_key?(:order) then items.reorder(params[:order]) else … end` — "`reorder` is called without any form of sanitization. This leads to a SQL injection."
  2. Establish the oracle: create a group and two milestones; `GET /groups/<group>/-/milestones` with `Accept: application/json` returns your rows with their `id`s (e.g. `429944`, `429943`) in a known order.
  3. Inject a boolean into the ORDER BY with CASE: `(CASE SUBSTR((SELECT email FROM users WHERE username = 'jobertabma'), 1, 1) WHEN 'a' THEN (CASE id WHEN 429944 THEN 2 ELSE 1 END) ELSE 1 END)` — the inner CASE sorts YOUR row by column 2 only when the guessed character matches.
  4. READ the flip: the same request with `&order=<url-encoded payload>` — when the guess is wrong the rows return in the original order (`[{"title":"3",…429944},{"title":"4",…429943}]`); when the guess is right the order reverses (`[{"title":"4",…429943},{"title":"3",…429944}]`). "Once the order reverses it knows what the value of the character is"; iterate `SUBSTR(<>, N, 1)` to walk any column of any table.
  5. IMPACT as stated: "An attacker can extract all information from a GitLab instance's database, including private access and shell tokens. These can be used to elevate the user's privileges, which may lead to arbitrary code execution." (tested against GitLab 10.2.4 / gitlab.com).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an `order` / `sort` / `order_by` / `direction` parameter on a list endpoint passed to an ORM ordering call (`reorder`, `order`, `order_by`) instead of a whitelist; a JSON variant (`Accept: application/json`) of the same list endpoint that echoes row order; the order of rows *you* control flipping between requests (the cheapest possible binary oracle); error/timing differences when the ORDER BY expression is malformed.
CHAIN: an `order` parameter interpolated into `reorder()` (primitive: ORDER BY injection) → a `CASE` on your own rows flips their sort when a subquery predicate is true (primitive: blind boolean read of any table) → read `users.email` / private-access & shell tokens (escalation: credential theft inside the instance) → those tokens used with the instance's runner/CI features (final: privilege escalation to arbitrary code execution). Critical where the DB holds tokens/credentials.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any list endpoint with an `order`/`sort`/`order_by` param, create two rows you can see in the response; replace the sort value with `(CASE WHEN (<subquery>) THEN <expr> ELSE <expr> END)` (and with a `,`-appended second column) and diff the row order across requests — a flip you control is blind SQLi; then walk `SUBSTR(col, n, 1)` for the columns worth reading. Rule: **when a user-supplied sort value reaches the ORM's ORDER BY unsanitised you do not need an error or a delay — make the database reorder YOUR OWN rows and read the answer off the response.**
DEDUPE: `MilestoneFinder`, `reorder(params`, `groups/-/milestones`, `order param`, `sort flip` = 0 hits across the three write targets. The recorded ORDER BY SQLi material (A 12 / C 26) is the WordPress-shortcode family (`[display-frm-data … order_by=id order=…]` inside `admin-ajax.php` shortcode expansion) — a different entry point reached through a different framework path; the `milestone` hits (A 6 / C 3) are GitLab GraphQL global-id type confusion, and `reorder` (C 7) is sanitizer pipeline reordering — neither is this finder. §17 slot 17.263.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1705717  2026-11-08

Metadata as served: severity **critical**, weakness `Command Injection - Generic`, CVE-2022-31020, bounty $2,000, reporter `shakedreiner`, submitted 2022-09-20, disclosed 2022-10-20. FRESHNESS: Sept 2022 (~4 years) and patched in indy-node — the handler is fixed; the METHOD (authorization evaluated AFTER the dangerous call; an undocumented field reaching a shell-out) transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no indy-node network was stood up; the code snippets and the JSON request are quoted from the report body.
CLASS: UNAUTHENTICATED COMMAND INJECTION — AN UNDOCUMENTED FIELD REACHES A SHELL-OUT BEFORE THE ROLE CHECK RUNS (`POOL_UPGRADE.package` → `dpkg -s <pkg>`).
CORE METHOD:
  1. TRACE THE HANDLER: `indy-node/indy_node/server/request_handlers/config_req_handlers/pool_upgrade_handler.py` — `additional_dynamic_validation` accepts an undocumented field `package`; when non-empty it flows `self.upgrader.check_upgrade_possible` → `NodeControlUtil.curr_pkg_info` → `cls._get_curr_info`, where `cmd = compose_cmd(['dpkg', '-s', package]); return cls.run_shell_command(cmd)` — "the user supplied name is then concatenated to the string `dpkg -s` and is run as a system command without any sanitization."
  2. INJECT A COMMAND: the `package` value is `a ; <shell command>` (`"package": "a ; python3 -c '<reverse-shell one-liner>'"` in the PoC) — the `;` closes `dpkg -s` and starts yours.
  3. SATISFY STATIC VALIDATION with a well-formed SIGNED write request (the report's own JSON fields): `identifier`, `operation.action:"start"`, `name`, a future `schedule` map, `sha256`, `type:"109"`, `version:"1.1"`, `protocolVersion:2`, `reqId` and a `signature` — "the request should be properly signed by any identity in the network (no role needed)".
  4. THE BYPASS: the docs say `POOL_UPGRADE` is Trustee-only, "however, we can run this exploit being a client without any roles in the network… the authorization that the `POOL_UPGRADE` handler performs, happens only **after** the package information has been fetched (using `self.upgrader.check_upgrade_possible`). Meaning any client can trigger the vulnerable code path and execute code on all the network's nodes."
  5. DELIVER: connect to the node's CLIENT port (ZeroMQ) using the node's public CURVE server key (public info; obtainable from the genesis file and convertible per `indy-sdk scripts/test_zmq/src/main.rs:136`) — or run the report's pytest repro (`exploit_test.py` inside `indy_node/test/`, disabling the test-mode patch first with `sed -i '/def patchNodeControlUtil().*:/{n;s/.*/    yield/}' conftest.py`, then `pytest -s exploit_test.py`). Impact as stated: "Breaking the network's consensus, stealing every identity, getting to run code on all of the nodes."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a privileged action whose handler performs the dangerous operation BEFORE the authorization check (read the handler top-to-bottom and locate the authz call relative to the sink); message-oriented/RPC protocols where any network identity may sign a request and roles are enforced late; request fields that are undocumented (`package`, `path`, `name`, `cmd`, `bashrc`) in the schema/validation; a field concatenated into a shell command (`dpkg`, `apt`, `tar`, `git`, `sh -c`).
CHAIN: any identity (no role) can produce a valid signed `POOL_UPGRADE` (primitive) → the handler fetches package info before checking Trustee authorization and concatenates the undocumented `package` field into `dpkg -s` (primitive: remote command execution as the node service) → the injected `;`-command (a reverse shell in the PoC) runs on every node the signed request reaches (escalation: RCE across the network) → consensus is broken and every identity's keys/state are readable (final: total compromise of the network and its identities). Critical.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any role-gated RPC/endpoint, read the server handler and ask "does the sink run before the authz check?"; send the message as a low/no-privilege identity; put shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&&`, `$( )`, backticks, newline) in EVERY string field and watch for a callback; prefer undocumented/newer fields. Rule: **a role check that executes after the dangerous call is not a control — find the sink, then ask which side of the authorization check it sits on.**
DEDUPE: `POOL_UPGRADE`, `indy-node`, `dpkg -s`, `privilege check`, `authz after` = 0 hits across the three write targets. §17 slot 17.264.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/262230  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; read in full via the report JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/262230.json` (HTTP 200, 6,366 bytes, `vulnerability_information` 2,695 chars). Metadata as served: severity medium, weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - DOM`, bounty $2,000, reporter `jelmer`, submitted 2017-08-22, disclosed 2017-09-26. FRESHNESS: 2017 (~9 years) — tinymce 2.4.0 and its filter-confusion bugs are long fixed; only the DELIVERY method transfers. HONESTY: the reporter states plainly "While I couldn't get a tinymce XSS to trigger" — this is a delivery-method entry, not a demonstrated XSS.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no editor was targeted; the PoC HTML and the candidate payload list are quoted from the report body.
CLASS: HTML5 DRAG-AND-DROP AS THE DELIVERY OF ATTACKER HTML INTO A RICH-TEXT EDITOR ON ANOTHER ORIGIN — DEFEATS `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (the payload rides the DRAG, not a click in a frame).
CORE METHOD:
  1. FIND the sink: `https://app.shopify.com//services/mobile_app/rte` loads a minified **tinymce 2.4.0** bundle from `https://cdn.shopify.com/s/assets/mobile_app/rte-bundle-f044a6c638b6c0500848c772dd5c86bf0eb2b27516c0860c6d3ddafde42231e2.js` — a known-vulnerable version, but "in order to trigger them the attacker needs access to tinymce's functionality".
  2. GET ACCESS WITHOUT FRAMING: put your HTML on the drag clipboard during `dragstart` and then navigate to the editor page — the attacker page holds `<div draggable="true" ondragstart="event.dataTransfer.setData('text/html', '<img src=\'https://cdn.shopify.com/shopify-marketing_assets/static/shopify-favicon.png\'/>'); document.location='https://app.shopify.com//services/mobile_app/rte'">drag</div>`.
  3. RIDE THE REDIRECT: "Immediatly after the drag the attacker redirects the user to Shopify. This does not violate the XFO 'DENY' setting" — the drag payload survives the navigation, so X-Frame-Options never comes into play.
  4. DROP ANYWHERE: "Victim releases the mouse button after loading the tinymce and the dragged data gets rendered by tinymce (tinymce is fullscreen so it doesn't matter where you drop it on the screen)" — the PoC proves RENDERING (the favicon appears).
  5. THEN the library's filter-confusion payload set (each with its upstream reference): `<a href="data:text/html;base64,PHNjcmlwdD5hbGVydCgiWFNTIik8L3NjcmlwdD4=" target="_blank">Firefox</a>`; `'">><marquee><img src=x onerror=confirm(1)></marquee>"></plaintext\></|\><plaintext/onmouseover=prompt(1)>` (tinymce issue 3114); `<HTML xmlns: ><audio><audio src=wp onerror=alert(0X1)>` (H1 #81736 / tinymce issue 2356); `&ltg;?">&ltg;iframe SRC=&#106&#97&#118…>` (numeric entities hiding `javascript:alert('XSS')`, tinymce issue 2132).
  6. The report's own impact note: "Considering the things that live under this subdomain + CSRF token handout on page successful exploitation of this could get pretty disastrous."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a rich-text editor / HTML-rendering route (tinymce, CKEditor, Quill, a WYSIWYG, a paste/import-HTML view) on a sensitive subdomain; `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or `frame-ancestors 'none'` (which stops IFRAME delivery only — test drag delivery anyway); a known-vulnerable editor version; an editor that accepts `text/html` from a drop or paste.
CHAIN: a vulnerable editor library that renders attacker markup (primitive: untrusted HTML reaches the editor's sanitizer) → HTML5 drag-and-drop carries the `text/html` payload across a redirect into the editor on the app origin, past `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (escalation: attacker markup in a privileged origin without a framing click) → a filter-confusion payload executes as DOM XSS there, where the CSRF-token handout and sensitive assets live (final: session/CSRF-token theft → act as the admin). The report stopped after RENDERING; the execution link is the unproven part and is recorded as unproven.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any app whose HTML sink is protected only by `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors`, try drag delivery — an attacker page with a `draggable` element whose `ondragstart` runs `event.dataTransfer.setData('text/html', '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>')` and immediately `document.location='<target>'`; drag it, let the page load, release over the target and check whether your markup is rendered/executed in the target origin; then throw the editor's known filter-confusion payload set at the exact version. Rule: **X-Frame-Options prevents delivering markup through a FRAME, not through a DRAG — a drag started on the attacker page and released after a navigation lands the `text/html` payload in the victim app's editor.**
DEDUPE: `tinymce`, `dataTransfer`, `cors proxy` = 0 hits across the three write targets; the recorded `drag` hits (A 17 / B 15) are "Drag and Pwnd" (VS Code ASCII/PTY drag) and drag-and-drop-into-a-terminal — command-injection sinks, not browser delivery of HTML into an editor. §17 slot 17.265.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1540906  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6; like source 1 this is a `visibility: no-content` disclosure — the JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/1540906.json` (HTTP 200, 11,406 bytes, `application/json`) returns an EMPTY `vulnerability_information` (0 chars) but a `summaries` array with the REPORTER's own summary (researcher `ian`), which names the route class and both impacts; the exact request shape was then pinned from two adjacent sources opened this pass — the **nuclei template** `http/cves/2022/CVE-2022-24856.yaml` (raw.githubusercontent.com, HTTP 200) whose only request is `GET {{BaseURL}}/cors_proxy/https://oast.me/` matched on the collaborator body, and the **FlyteConsole advisory** `GHSA-www6-hf2v-v9m9` / CVE-2022-24856 ("It also passes the headers along, which can be very dangerous"). Metadata as served: severity medium (program, CVSS 6.1) while the CVE is rated 9.1, weakness `Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)`, bounty $2,000, submitted 2022-04-14, disclosed 2022-05-26, asset "Uber Assets". FRESHNESS: Apr 2022 (~4.5 years); the `cors_proxy` route was deleted in flyteconsole 0.52.0 — the METHOD (an unauthenticated proxy/URL-fetch route = full-read SSRF) is alive wherever such a route survives.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Flyte instance was stood up.
CLASS: UNAUTHENTICATED "CORS PROXY" / URL-FETCH ROUTE → FULL-READ SSRF (response body returned, request headers forwarded) → CLOUD METADATA / INTERNAL SERVICES, PLUS REFLECTED XSS BY PROXYING AN ATTACKER HTML DOCUMENT.
CORE METHOD:
  1. RECON: a Flyte Console instance was found on `flyte-poc-us-east4.uberinternal.com`; auditing FlyteConsole's open-source code exposed "an unauthenticated route for a 'CORS proxy'".
  2. EXPLOIT: `GET /cors_proxy/<absolute-url>` — the template's own request is `GET {{BaseURL}}/cors_proxy/https://oast.me/` (single request, matched on the returned collaborator body). Reporter: "a classic server-side request forgery issue, allowing us to pass an arbitrary request to be performed by the server and read the response."
  3. FULL READ + METADATA: the response BODY is returned, so internal-only resources are readable — aim it at the cloud metadata service and at other unauthenticated internal URLs (advisory: "the attacker can access the internal metadata server or other unauthenticated urls"). HEADERS TOO: "It also passes the headers along, which can be very dangerous" — your headers are forwarded upstream (a header-spoofing/auth primitive against internal services).
  4. SECOND IMPACT — reflected XSS: "This also allowed reflected cross-site scripting as we could proxy arbitrary HTML documents through it" — point `/cors_proxy/` at an attacker-hosted HTML document and the internal origin serves it as its own content.
  5. FIX as the differential: "The patch deletes the entire `cors_proxy` as this is not required for console anymore" (flyteconsole 0.52.0; all earlier images yanked).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any endpoint a URL is handed to and whose body comes back — names like `proxy`, `cors_proxy`, `fetch`, `preview`, `thumbnail`, `render`, `import`, `unfurl`, `webhook-test`; a route present in the app's own source but never linked in the UI (audit the open-source code / the JS bundle for unlinked routes); a response that returns an OAST hit; a `Content-Type` that follows the remote target (proxied HTML = same-origin HTML).
CHAIN: an unauthenticated URL-fetch route (primitive) → the server fetches an attacker-chosen absolute URL, returns the body and forwards attacker headers (primitive: full-read SSRF + header pass-through) → read the cloud metadata service / internal unauthenticated services from inside the perimeter (escalation: cloud IAM credentials → the classic SSRF-to-RCE path) and/or proxy an attacker HTML document to run script in the internal origin (escalation: reflected XSS) → stolen cloud credentials used against the account, or script in an internal origin (final). The program rated it medium (CVSS 6.1); the chain reaches critical (metadata credentials / RCE) on a cloud instance with an assumable role.

Metadata as served: GitLab, "Stored XSS in repository file viewer", severity **medium** (team, CVSS 4.1), weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored`, no CVE, no bounty, reporter `kannthu`, submitted 2021-01-06, disclosed 2022-05-19. FRESHNESS: Jan 2021 (~5.8 years) — the swagger-ui/DOMPurify version in GitLab's viewer is long updated; the METHOD (old-sanitizer attribute injection in a spec viewer + `?url=` universal delivery) transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no GitLab instance was stood up this pass; the payloads, the `?url=` URLs and the impact sentences are quoted from the report body.
CLASS: STORED XSS VIA AN OLD **DOMPurify** INSIDE THE APP'S OWN **OpenAPI/Swagger VIEWER** — the sanitizer admits arbitrary HTML **attributes** (only `<script>` is stripped), so markup injected by a SPEC you control reaches the viewer page; CSP is then defeated with the app's own same-origin remote-script anchor, and the viewer's `?url=` parameter makes the delivery valid on ANY repository path.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK: GitLab renders a repo's `openapi.yaml` through an old swagger-ui whose bundled DOMPurify "allows an attacker [to] inject any HTML elements with any attributes (except script tag) on the page". The tested path: `https://gitlab.com/kannthu/asdasdas123/-/blob/master/openapi.yaml`.
  2. INJECT VIA THE SPEC: the strings you commit in the OpenAPI document are rendered into the viewer DOM, so put your markup in the spec. The old DOMPurify keeps attributes, only dropping `<script>`.
  3. CSP CONTEXT (report verbatim): "The XSS in POC requires 1 click anywhere on the page to execute, because of CSP that does not allow to execute events from HTML tags. (f.e. `<img src=1 onerror=alert(1)>`)." So you do NOT rely on an inline handler; you arm the injected markup with GitLab's OWN rails-ujs remote anchor (the CSP bypass from https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/213273, report verbatim):
     ```html
     <a
       data-remote="true"
       data-method="get"
       data-type="script"
       href="/wbowling/wiki/raw/master/test.js"
       class='atwho-view select2-drop-mask pika-select'>
     </a>
     ```
     — a same-origin `<a data-type="script">` that fetches and EVALUATES `href` as script on click; `script-src 'self'` allows it because the borrowed `.js` is served from the app's own origin. (Entity-encode it inside the spec so the sanitizer sees text and the renderer emits the live anchor.)
  4. UNIVERSAL DELIVERY VIA `?url=`: append `url=<your raw spec>` to the viewer URL of ANY repository's OpenAPI file and the viewer loads YOUR document instead — verbatim repro: `https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/build/omnibus-mirror/alertmanager/blob/master/api/v2/openapi.yaml?url=https://gitlab.com/kannthu/asdasdas123/-/raw/master/openapi.yaml`; "Click anywhere on the page → You should see the alert box". The XSS fires on a file you do not own.
  5. IMPACT (report verbatim): "The stored XSS is triggering for any user that opens the page and clicks anywhere on the page. The PoC can easily be extended to steal the user's CSRF token and to take over the victim's account." (one click required).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any in-app DOCUMENT VIEWER that renders a file you can commit (OpenAPI/Swagger/RAML/AsyncAPI yaml, notebooks, markdown, generated API docs); a pinned OLD DOMPurify / pre-3.x swagger-ui in the bundle (a version chokepoint that admits attributes); a query parameter that overrides which document the viewer loads (`?url=`, `?configUrl=`, `?spec=`, `?file=`); a page with `script-src 'self'` that ALSO ships a rails-ujs/turbo `data-type="script"` (or any "load this same-origin .js") helper bound by class.
CHAIN: attacker commits an OpenAPI spec carrying DOMPurify-passing markup + attributes (primitive) → the app's own viewer renders the spec and the old DOMPurify lets arbitrary HTML ATTRIBUTES through (primitive: attribute injection into the viewer origin) → the injected `data-remote data-method=get data-type=script` anchor loads a same-origin `.js` on one click, satisfying `script-src 'self'` (escalation: script execution in the gitlab.com origin) → read the CSRF token / act as the victim (final: account takeover). The `?url=` parameter upgrades "my repo's viewer" to "any repository's viewer URL" (final: delivery on a path you do not own, on any project).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find an in-app viewer that renders a document you can commit; put attribute-injection markup into the document and open it — if arbitrary ATTRIBUTES survive the sanitizer (only tags filtered), the sink is live. Then be CSP-aware: chain a same-origin script load (a rails-ujs `data-type="script"` anchor, or any existing "fetch a same-origin .js and run it" widget on the page). Finally hunt a loader override — point `?url=`/`?configUrl=`/`?spec=` at YOUR document and reload the viewer of a repository you do not own. Rule: **an old sanitizer in a spec viewer leaks ATTRIBUTES, and attributes are enough — the CSP is beaten by the app's own same-origin remote-script anchor, and `?url=` turns a self-XSS into an any-page XSS.**
DEDUPE: `1072868`, `openapi.yaml?url=`, `swagger-ui`-as-a-repo-blob-viewer sink = 0 hits as a technique across the three write targets. RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT (reviewed, NOT re-recorded): the `?configUrl=data:text/html;base64,…` Swagger-UI entry (ledger, source #1444682, Jamf) loads a whole attacker DOCUMENT as the config — a different primitive (document load) from spec-BODY attribute injection; the `data-remote="true" data-method="get" data-type="script"` rails-ujs CSP bypass is ALREADY recorded twice (the ReferenceRedactor entry #836649 and the `safe_params`/`script_name` entry, ledger ~line 4431) and is cited here, not re-recorded. §17 slot 17.267.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no GitLab instance was deployed this pass; the Octokit request/response shapes are quoted from the report body.
CLASS: AUTHENTICATED SERVER-SIDE **POST** SSRF — a repository-integration "connectivity test" makes the server's OWN API client (Octokit) POST an app-signed commit-status to a user-supplied URL, FOLLOW the attacker's `302` into the internal network, and ECHO the internal response body back in the UI error.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Establish the CONTROL: sign in as ANY user, create a project, add a `.gitlab-ci.yml` (the report's stock config) so at least one pipeline exists — the GitHub integration reports a commit STATUS, so a pipeline/commit must exist ("Before a minute to make sure the pipelines are created based on the GitLab CI configuration file").
  2. Settings → Integrations → GitHub: set the repository URL to YOUR host, e.g. `http://<remote_ip>/1/2`, then click the **"Test settings and save changes"** button.
  3. OBSERVE the server-side request — it is an AUTHENTICATED POST straight to you (report verbatim):
     ```
     POST /api/v3/repos/1/2/statuses/5509244fe4919b85f5c1e0e1a2340805055c32d9 HTTP/1.1
     Accept: application/vnd.github.v3+json
     User-Agent: Octokit Ruby Gem 4.9.0
     Content-Type: application/json
     Authorization: token ***
     Host: remote_ip
     Content-Length: 158

     {"context":"ci/gitlab/master","description":"Pipeline passed on GitLab","target_url":"https://gitlab.com/jobertabma/123/pipelines/36992118","state":"success"}
     ```
  4. ANSWER WITH A REDIRECT: reply `302 Found` with `Location: http://127.0.0.1/` — Octokit FOLLOWS it and re-issues the request inside the perimeter (POST-capable; the `Authorization` header rides along).
  5. READ IT BACK: the internal response body is returned through the app's error message — the report demonstrates `127.0.0.1:80`, `:8080` and `:22`.
  6. ESCALATE (report verbatim): "make arbitrary `POST` requests in a GitLab instance's internal network. It can also be used to connect to cloud provider's instance metadata API, which may result in the ability to execute commands on the machine."
DETECTION SIGNAL: any integration / connector / webhook **"test connection" / "save & test" / validate** action that fetches a user-supplied URL server-side AND uses a client that FOLLOWS redirects (Octokit, Go `net/http`, curl `-L`, `requests`); an outbound request that carries the APP'S OWN credential to the URL you control (`Authorization: token …`, a Bearer, an HMAC); a UI that echoes the fetched response body/headers in an error or preview pane (full-read, not blind); server-side code that builds the outbound URL path as `<yoururl>/api/v3/repos/<n>/<n>/statuses/<sha>` (a forced path you must neutralise with `#` or a redirect).
CHAIN: any authenticated user with a project (primitive: create a repo integration) → the server's Octokit client POSTs the app's own authenticated commit-status to the attacker URL (primitive: a controllable outbound AUTHENTICATED request) → the attacker's `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1/…` makes Octokit re-issue the SAME authenticated POST inside the perimeter (escalation: arbitrary authenticated POST + redirect-follow SSRF) → the internal response is echoed in the UI (full-read) → aim it at `169.254.169.254` metadata → cloud IAM credentials → command execution on the machine (final, per the report).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every "test connection"/"validate"/"save & test" integration action: point the URL at your collaborator, confirm the request arrives FROM THE SERVER, and record (a) the METHOD and (b) whether the app's own Authorization/API token is attached. Then answer `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/` (and `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`) and read the internal body back from the UI error / logs. Rule: **an integration test is not a harmless GET ping — if the client follows redirects you get an AUTHENTICATED POST into the internal network, and if the app echoes the response you get a full read of it.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): the generic pattern "a webhook/integration TEST button is an SSRF primitive" is ALREADY recorded (Bugbountyskills.md §2.3, source #2301565) and "redirect chain → internal/metadata" is recorded (§2.4, #878779 / #632101; and the glusterfs `resturl` PoC#2 at ledger source #776017). DELTA (new): the test flow reuses the app's OWN AUTHENTICATED POST — Octokit posting a commit-status WITH `Authorization: token` — so this is a POST-WITH-CREDENTIALS into the internal network, not a read-only GET ping; and the internal response body is ECHOED in the UI error (full-read). 0 hits for `446593`, `Octokit Ruby Gem`, `Test settings and save changes`, `api/v3/repos` across the three write targets. §17 slot 17.268.

     ```json
     {"operationName":"ThemePublishLegacy","variables":{"id":"gid://shopify/OnlineStoreTheme/[THEME_ID]"},"query":"mutation ThemePublishLegacy($id: ID!) {\n  onlineStoreThemePublish(id: $id) {\n    theme { id __typename }\n    userErrors { field message __typename }\n    __typename\n  }\n}\n"}
     ```
  4. SUBSTITUTE AND REPLAY: run the same request with the PAID theme's id in `variables.id`; refresh and the PAID theme is "now publish & active" — no purchase check fired.
  5. CONSEQUENCE (report verbatim): "after the theme is published, it seems like we own it" — the yellow "Theme trial" badge disappears and you can rename, edit and download the theme files: "install paid theme without purchasing it could lead to content stealing and lost of profit. There is also some unwanted information disclosure since we can edit the theme code and download the files after its published."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a storefront/marketplace where a PAID asset can be INSTALLED/attached as a trial and the UI shows a badge/gate ("Theme trial", "Trial", "Preview"); a publish/activate/enable/download action sent as a GraphQL `mutation` or REST call carrying ONLY the object's global id (`gid://…`) with no entitlement field; an entitlement enforced in the UI/model layer but ABSENT inside the state-changing mutation itself.
CHAIN: ordinary merchant account (primitive: install a paid theme as a trial — free) → read the paid theme's global id from a UI URL and replay the app's own publish mutation with that id (primitive: no purchase check in the mutation) → the paid asset is published and becomes editable/downloadable (escalation: ownership of an un-purchased asset = content theft) → vendor revenue loss at scale + access to the paid theme source (final: business impact; program rated low, impact is per-asset).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any store/asset flow with a purchasable object: perform the action on a FREE item while capturing the state-changing mutation (publish/activate/enable/claim/download), then swap in the id of a PAID item you hold only as a trial and replay it. If the paid item activates, the gate was client-side. Rule: **capture the mutation for a free item, substitute the paid item's id, and see whether the server re-checks entitlement — an id you can read from a UI URL is enough.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): this report family is ALREADY recorded — ledger entry SOURCE #953083 (same program, same title, same reporter `saltymermaid`, same `ThemePublishLegacy` / `onlineStoreThemePublish` endpoint, ledger ~line 6472) documents the **TOCTOU RACE** variant (replay the publish DURING the install, just before the last `ThemesProcessingLegacy`). DELTA (new, and STRONGER): #927567 needs NO race and NO timing — the entitlement check is simply ABSENT when replaying the publish against an already-INSTALLED (fully downloaded, trial) paid theme; a hunter who follows only the recorded race entry would wrongly believe precise timing is required. `927567` itself = 0 hits as a recorded report across the three write targets. §17 slot 17.270.
